Question: How likely was it for a soldier to survive two battles in a row in the Napoleonic era?
Answer: Casualty rates were actually very low back then, battles were not won or lost by killing the enemy to the last man, but by routing them. During the battle of Austerlitz Napoleon lost 1305 men, out of 65,000 to 75,000 which is between 1.74% and 2%. That is a pretty good chance of surviving the battle on Napoleon’s side. In fact, consider the Old Guard, if you have not heard of them, they were the most loyal and elite veterans who fought for Napoleon. The criteria to become one was as follows: At Waterloo, Napoleon commanded at least 5669 such Old Guards. And several thousand more Middle Guards, who were also veterans though not to the same degree. Considering how many of these very long time veterans were around, it should be obvious that surviving battles were the norm, and veteran soldiers were highly appreciated in the French army.

Question: Did the soviets have a valid justification going to war with Finland during 1939? The common narrative is similar to the modern day Ukraine war where a bigger country threatened a smaller one without any reason.
Answer: The Soviet justification was based mostly on the Shelling of Mainila, in which the Soviets claimed that the Finns had shelled a small village on the border. However, this was a falseflag operation carried out by the NKVD to provide a casus belli. This casus belli was justification enough at the time, but honestly quite little was needed. The real reasons for the attack had nothing to do with it of course. The reason why it was done was because of Finland’s pro-German policies, refusal for Soviet cooperation and the proximity of the Finnish border to Leningrad. All of which greatly concerned the Soviets in 1939, expecting a future war with Germany. No country has ever threatened or indeed done anything “without reason” whether it is big or small. National policy is not like picking food from a fridge, it usually takes a little more effort and consideration.

Question: How big is the gap between Russia and the USA in terms of military? Don't be biased.
Answer: The current military gap between the USA and Russia, quite depends on which aspect. To honestly say that a country has military power as a single static value doesn’t make sense, like wise, simply pointing to a past operation as an anecdote is a fallacy, and only marginally gives an indication of what experience shapes the ideas of the respective military. Let’s start with the highest level of capability. Russia and USA are nuclear superpowers, no matter what people claim about them otherwise. They are peerless in their ability to destroy the world, both maintain thousands of nuclear warheads and delivery systems. Even China only maintains 10% of the warheads of either Russia or USA. In this respect there is no gap, and both nations are peerless. If we talk about projection power, the USA is the only true superpower and peerless in their ability to deploy their air and naval forces around the world, usually for influence and punitive actions. Russia is a regional power, they can project only with the consent of host countries, or within their immediate region, such as Ukraine and Georgia, but the very idea that Russia could militarily influence anything in for example South America is close to unthinkable. In terms of actual naval power, the US Navy is almost certainly the most powerful navy in the world, even with Chinese naval power reaching new heights, it is still a regional and very inexperienced navy, while the Russian navy is more experienced, it is under funded. The US navy is very experienced, very well equipped, and very well funded. It is a very well organized US military arm and the basis for most of it’s power. In terms of air power, the US also has a clear edge. The US maintains the only large fleet of stealth aircraft, the largest fleet of AWACS, the only truly capable carrier based air force, as well as an overall advantage in numbers. However, the Russian air force is no joke, they are highly capable and have a large percentage of modern aircraft, what they lack in stealth they make up for in advanced missiles and carriers for them notably the MiG-31 with Kinzhal air to ground missiles, and R-37M ultra-long range AA missiles, both have proved highly effective in a near peer conflict. The Russian air force also have a lot of experience fighting in high ECM and high AA environments, which no US pilot can claim, as the enemies of the US rarely have any air defense at all, and they tend to fly their planes like AA missiles barely exist. The gap here might not be as great as one might think. In terms of Army, the Russians maintain a larger force than the US, additionally, the US are facing very serious problems with manpower, being an all volunteer army, Russian shortages can easily be fixed with conscription, and they maintain a reserve more than 10 times the size of the USA. As we can see from current conflicts, in a serious war, the ability to replenish casualties is very important, and the USA does not have this nearly to the same extent. Additionally, the Russian ground forces are now staffed by experienced officers and troops, who know how to conduct trench warfare and urban warfare on the modern battlefield against near peer adversaries. Again, no soldier in the US army can claim the same. The equipment of the Russian army is also rapidly adapting to the realities of modern warfare. Everyone laughed at the Russian cope cages in the beginning of the war, no one is laughing now. The Russian tactic for drones was correct, and everyone who is facing drones now copies the Russians, not the other way around, just ask the Israeli cope cages. Finally, the Russian ground forces have a very large, and very experienced and successful drone corps, which is now integrated at company to battalion level which includes an electronic warfare anti drone component. This is not a small advantage, and without a doubt this is going to be an essential part of any modern army in the very near future, but western militarizes including the USA are only barely beginning to do something like what the Russians already have in terms of drones. In short, in terms of ground forces, the Russian army is probably ahead of the USA and this is the area with the biggest difference in experience and innovation. In summary, this is my opinion: Nuclear, the two forces have parity Projection power the US has peerless lead over Russia Naval forces the US has a significant lead over Russia Air force, the US has a lead over Russia Army, Russia has a significant lead over the USA

Name: Carl Hamilton
Question: How do you view the popularity of "Black Myth: Wukong" and the spread of Chinese culture?
Answer: The significance is properly significantly overrated, the fact people made it into a political thing is completely silly to me. First, let me talk about its popularity. The vast majority of players are Chinese, this is quite obvious from 2 reasons, the first being that when it is night time in China, the playerbase drops from 2 million to around 240,000, a drop of about 88%. The second reason is if you go to steam reviews, and turn on simplified and traditional Chinese language reviews, the number of reviews increases to 497,279 reviews, out of 558,953 reviews in total. If I turn on Danish reviews only, there are 29 reviews in total. That means in total 89% of all the reviews I can see, are Chinese. And that is probably indicative of the actual distribution of players in the world. So, about the idea this is a global phenomenon, I would say, not really. It’s a Chinese phenomenon, and I think people have just forgotten there are actually a lot of Chinese players. So many of them have probably converged to play this because of the following reasons: I do not think this game will spread Chinese culture all that much to be honest, and I do think the game is actually all that special. There haven’t been many games like this which has come out of China at all, but there almost certainly will be in the future. The novelty of being one of the first AAA games to get all the corner stones correct in the Chinese game industry and translate and successfully launch the game internationally, is probably not going to be a common occurrence. There is also the point here that the game isn’t really promoting Chinese culture per say, Wukong is based on the Chinese novel journey to the west, and it is essentially a fantasy novel from the late 1500s. It is a classic Chinese novel, but the game doesn’t really do a good job of explaining that, in fact the introduction to the game makes no sense what so ever, without a fairly decent understanding of Chinese culture already. It explains very poorly this setting as the game progresses as well. In a way it makes as much sense as the world building in Elden Ring and Dark Souls, however, the game is based on real culture and novels, so the fact that it is disjointed confusing and non-nonsensical in its introduction, is not really a great cultural hook at least. From a technical point of view, the game is honestly nothing special. It uses Unreal 5, which goes a long way to making the game pretty, but they really do let the engine do the heavy lifting. The initial chapter environment is maybe 80% brushed with auto generated foliage. A minor criticism, but shallow water are merely texture surfaces, that you stand on, which is a bit of shame as there is a fight in deep water, which is beautifully done. The game has some cool features graphically, but it is not a very complex or deep game compared to Elden Ring for example. I would say, it is one of the better Dark-Souls-like, far better than Lies of Pi, which was released last year, which was frankly so generic. The game lacks different weapons, play styles and multiplayer, and for this reason I think it will quite quickly disappear from the top of steam once players finish the campaign. In short, the global popularity of Wukong is greatly exaggerated, I don’t think it is some secret way of spreading Chinese culture. Clearly, the developers really liked the story that the game is set in, it’s a labour of love, that has released in ideal conditions, and all the media talk it is getting is completely ridiculous, and in some cases reeks of jealously. Unfair criticism against Asian games is completely common in the west, not just because they are Chinese, Elden Ring, Stellar Blade, Once Human and several other recent games also faced completely unwarranted criticism in the west, but were still easily commercial successes. I hope the next big Chinese game will do a different classic Chinese novel, Romance of the Three Kingdoms preferably, but I’ll take Watermargin if I have to.

Question: Did WW2 partisans in the U.S.S.R. and Nazi occupied Europe have a major effect on the course of the war?
Answer: Partisans in WW2 were part of the calculation that resulted in the defeat of Nazi Germany. Partisans were active nearly everywhere at some time or another, mostly organized by the underground communist parties of Europe in the occupied territories. This was not limited to the USSR or Yugoslavia despite their highlights. Partisans carrying signs saying “we shot at Germans” before being executed in Minsk 1941. The partisan movements had 2 very important tasks which they generally carried out quite well. Firstly, they complicated Axis logistics, prevent crucial supplies from reaching the front, or raw materials from reaching the factories. Secondly, they tied up significant amount of troops that would otherwise have been used on the front line. In 1943, the Germans needed 550,000 regular soldiers in anti partisan activities in the USSR alone. To put this into perspective, the combined German and Italian forces facing the British in Egypt in 1942, was almost 120,000. Almost 10 times more German soldiers were used for anti-partisan activities in the USSR alone in 1943, than all the German soldiers who served in North Africa. Another quite significant area of operations was France, in which around 200,000 partisans were operating, roughly half of which were communists, and the other half were various factions nominally supporting De Gaulle, all of them were important in intelligence gathering and interdiction against the Germans before D-day, and often helped the allies in combat operations with accurate and up to date intelligence. I would say, that the partisan activities were not decisive in the outcome of WW2, but they were important, and they were heroic.

This in turn created a large well educated and productive middle class which contributed greatly to the ability to create technology through skilled and motivated people. The problem with the new cold war, is that our base for rapid technological development is disappearing, we are destroying all the welfare mechanisms that gave a vibrant middle class in the western world, and frankly at this point China probably offers a better deal for anyone who wants to be part of the Brain drain movement keeping certain countries in the state of “resource exploitation”. Question: If the Nazis defeated the Soviets prior to Dday, what would have happened in the Pacific? Would the allies fight on two fronts? Sue for peace? Would the Nazis come to the aid of Japan? What other scenarios may have occurred?
Answer: This was an impossible outcome. The best possible outcome that Germany could have hoped for in their wildest dreams, was that the USSR would simply give up and accept a terrible peace deal in which Russia west of the Urals became part of Nazi Germany. Even in such a far fetched case, Germany would still not even be able to get to Japan if they wanted to. Robert Harris imagined in his book Fatherland, a situation in which Germany would still be having a perpetual war against the Soviets even in 1964. More likely though, Germany now occupied a gigantic territory, and even with the vastly reduced population they intended, they were facing down something close to 100 million people with nothing to lose. Even if Soviet industry completely ceased to exist, which is quite unlikely as much of it was already beyond the Urals, the USSR would continue fighting with what ever they had, even if they had to rely 100% on lend-lease they could still fight. This leaves the question, how many people did the Germans need to occupy and protect their new eastern border? The answer is certainly quite a lot. Additionally, Japan as a naval power was finished after Midway, their losses in 1942 were irrecoverable for Japan, and their defeat was merely a matter of time. Even if the western allies were forced to defeat Japan first, and then focus on supplying the Soviet remnant, and plan a new invasion of Europe in 1946 or something like that. They could have, and would have done so. Also there is the matter that the allies would almost certainly have nuked Germany in 1945. No matter how I see it, the Axis powers had sealed their ultimate fate in 1941, both the USSR and USA had the capacity to defeat Nazi Germany alone. Without each other, the war would have been longer, harder, deadlier a worse outcome without a doubt. But Nazi defeat still remained a certainty, the question was mostly about the human cost of the show.

Question: When the Nazi-Soviet Non-Aggression Pact was signed by Germany and the USSR, why didn't they coordinate their invasions of Poland to both be on September 1, 1939?
Answer: The Non-Aggression pact was not a military alliance and didn’t in any way shape or form stipulate military assistance in any circumstance. Quite specifically the the secret protocol of the Molotov-Ribbentrop pact, stipulated that in the event of any political or border rearrangement, there would be a non-intervention. Whether Poland would exist at all, was not stipulated either, but it was agreed that the two powers would essentially negotiate this at a later point. When the Germans invaded, they succeeded so swiftly that the Soviets primary concern was probably whether they would uphold their deal at all. If Germany occupied all of Poland in just a matter of weeks, while the Soviets sat back and then demanded eastern Poland be transferred to them… Well the Nazis would likely not have done it. There would likely have been foot dragging and excuses made to drag out that process, potentially until the Germans invaded the USSR anyway. Bear in mind that in 1939, the Soviets were aware of the German invasion plans of the USSR, and they feared this very much, the decision to promptly also invade Poland was made likely because of Germany’s swift success and a desire to guarantee the agreed upon sphere of influence. That is why they did not coordinate anything with Germany.

Question: Why did NATO not just disband after the Cold War ended? Wouldn't that allow Russia to drop its concerns about NATO expansion?
Answer: As you can see, there are many emotional responses to this which requires you subscribe to either a view of NATO as inherently good, or NATO as inherently evil. This is nonsense explanation made for the purpose of merely promoting peoples’ personal politics and hatreds. It does however offer no insight into the reality of how state policy and especially interstate policy is created and carried out. NATO didn’t disband, because NATO is power and influence. Power and influence are tools of security, economic advantage, and cultural stability. NATO did not continue to exist to oppose Rusisa, it existed because no country ever wants to make a decision in which they actively diminish their own power and influence. Because doing so brings no advantages, and potentially worsens your country’s position in the aforementioned categories. Countries will always seek the greatest advantage possible, not the greatest equity. Russia was not seen as a threat in the 1990s, and essentially the expansion of NATO was a result of that, as Russia is not seen as a threat, expanding NATO improved the advantage in the aforementioned positions. Ironically, if Russia had been perceived as seriously posing a threat in the face of NATO expansion, it would never have happened. That doesn’t mean that NATO expansion was aimed deliberately at threatening Russia either. However, as NATO increases it’s advantage in those areas, you have to ask yourself the question: “increased advantage relative to whom?” The answer is obviously Russia. So while the expansion was not made as an aggressive move, it reduced the Russian, economic advantage, security position and cultural stability. It is in a completely objective and non-aggressive way entirely in NATO’s interest to expand, and it is in a completely objective and non-aggressive way entirely in Russia’s interest to not have NATO expand. Material, security and cultural influence positions is how countries maintain their power, and they will pursue these goals to maximize their position. This is called the theory of offensive-realism, and it has so far been quite good at predicting international politics.

Question: How adept were the Soviets in railway logistics from WW2 to the Cold War? What could they achieve that most or no other country could do?
Answer: The Soviet logistics system, and arguably even the modern Russian one, were designed around railroads. Railroads are very efficient in general, I wouldn’t say there was anything that the Soviets could do with trains that others couldn’t do in theory, but they did have a few advantages. The Soviets worked on a centrally planned economy, and so the entirety of the rail logistics network could be planned and operated from a single point. The Soviet factory network was built to incorporate the rail network as efficiently as possible, and during the relocation of Soviet industry in 1941, the location of factories were organized to reduce the amount of necessary transport as much as possible. This made the network highly efficient. On the front, the Soviets were known for their armored trains which were quite difficult to ambush, they usually pushed an empty rail cart in front of the locomotive in case mines were placed on the tracks to avoid losing a locomotive to a demo charge. The permanent railroad troops were also able to lay down new tracks shockingly fast, as well as convert between Soviet and German rail gauges. Finally, the Soviet equipment were all aimed at this as well. The Soviet primary flatbed rail cars were able to carry either 50t or 100t. Soviet requirements for things like tanks specified less than 50t weight, so that any flatbed could still carry even the heaviest Soviet tank, and the 100t flatbeds could carry 2. Likewise the width of Soviet tanks were such that they always fitted perfectly on the flatbeds. Every Soviet equipment were designed from the beginning to fit on rail transport, solving many logistical issues from the factory side. Performance specifications were never allowed to take precedence over logistics specifications, and while that gives many a wehraboo a smug tone when discussing tank performance, but ultimately logistics is a prerequisite for any strategy and usually determines your force ratio and ability to achieve fire superiority.

Question: How significant were explosives and propellants supplied by American lend-lease to the USSR?
Answer: Explosives delivered by the Americans was very significant, particularly from 1943 and onwards. In my personal opinion it is not as significant as for example trucks, it appears it was one of the most important categories, details to follow. It is not so simple to say explosives and propellants, due to the fact that there are many explosives. Even the Russian sources I was able to gather, some with help from people here on Quora, doesn’t seem to fully detail the explosive and powder production. Indeed there are some holes in the information in Russian sources with confusion in regards to production in 1942. The explosive most well known is probably TNT. The Soviet Union produced some 273,193t during the war, while they received 88,525t of TNT through lend-lease (24.5%). However, that’s not the hole story, TNT is produced with toluene being the primary precursor, which was produced in the USSR at the tune of 95,865t while 64,000t was delivered through lend-lease (40%) according to Dmitry V. Gavrilov. However, the statistical archives show 208,100t of toluene produced. This might include the lend-lease delivered, if the record keeper didn’t differentiate. Either way, it seems Gavrilov is unable to account for at least 40,000t of toluene. The toluene was delivered mostly between 1943 and 1945, the toluene delivered near the end probably didn’t have time to be turned into TNT before the war ended, so we know that part of the TNT certainly was produced using lend-lease material, but probably less than the percentage, the exact number is probably not known. Additionally, we should consider the temporal aspect, explosive deliveries began in 1942, but only became significant in 1943 increasing in 1944. For the key battles of Moscow, Stalingrad and Kursk it played little role, but probably allowed for an increased throw rate of artillery during the Bagration offensive in 1944. Finally there are two factors which are difficult to account for. I do not have the data to speak definitively on propellant. Question: How effective were Soviet heavy tanks in WWII?

The KV-1 was not as relatively good in the beginning of the war, though it still performed better than the T-34. Question: In World War II, what was the difference between "armor piercing ballistic capped" and " armor piercing, capped, ballistic cap" ammunition? Which was more effective?
Answer: Armour piercing ballistic capped (APBC) and armor piercing capped ballistic cap (APCBC) both feature a lightweight cap meant to improve aerodynamics. The APBC round underneath have a slightly blunt nose which is made of hard steel, which improves performance against sloped armour due to the effect of normalization when hitting angles. The APCBC features a soft nose under the ballistic cap, which increases the effect against normalization even more, while leaving the sharp hard core. Normalization of shells might be a little counter intuitive, but essentially what happens when you hit a sloped armour, is that the shell will have force exerted in the direction of the slope. This means that during penetration, the armour piercing round will tilt upwards. That means that sloped armour actually offered additional protection beyond it’s line of sight thickness. If the angle of impact was high enough, this effect would actually cause the projectile to deflect off the target entirely. The APBC was probably marginally better against flatter armor, such as those featured on German tanks, while the APCBC was better against heavily sloped armor. It makes sense then that the Soviets favoured the APBC design, while the Germans favoured the APCBC design. As WW2 came to a close and everyone switched to heavily sloped armor, the Soviets began work on a 100mm APCBC design called the BR-412D which was to replace the APBC design for the 100mm gun the BR-412B. The APCBC would be the primary AP round for the Soviets in post WW2, until the introduction of HEAT and later APFSDS.

If we look at the top 10 Soviet aces this is quite well reflected in their aircraft use. 4 out of the 10 flew the P-39, 4 flew the La-5, 3 flew the La-7, one which from the P-39 to the La-7, Alexander Pokryshkin was offered the switch but refused. Only 5,000 La-7s were built and so there was not enough for everyone. Despite it’s good reputation, none of the top Soviet pilots ended the war on the Yak-9.

Question: Some say Japan didn’t surrender in WW2 because of the nuclear bombs, but because the entry of the USSR into the war. How true is this?
Answer: It has a lot more truth to it than most people are willing to admit today, let me set up the premise for you. Tokyo March 1945 On the 9th of March 1945, 334 B-29 heavy bombers dropped incendiary bombs all over Tokyo. In a matter of a day they had killed roughly 100,000 civilians and destroyed 25% of the entire Tokyo area. More people died in Tokyo on this one day, than the total deaths resulting from the nuclear bombing of Nagasaki (60,000–80,000). Recovering of corpses in the Tokyo Area March 1945 The man behind the US terror bombing campaign Curtis LeMay, made a survey in 1943, for the use of napalm against civilians, and concluded with his analysts, that fire bombing the 6 biggest cities in Japan could result in half a million dead civilians, roughly 8 million homeless, and 3.5 million needing to be evacuated. This campaign was approved and in March 1945, and after Tokyo, Osaka, Kobe, Yokohama, Kawasaki and Nagoya were also essentially destroyed and by all accounts LeMay was correct and the fire bombing killed the estimated amount. Shizuoka after it was fire bombed in June 1945 It did not stop there, after the big cities, the US campaign focusing on cities ranging from 60,000 to 300,000 in population. Before the nuclear bombing began, 64 cities had been completely destroyed by fire bombing already. When the nuclear bombs destroyed Hiroshima, the Japanese didn’t panic at some American wonder weapon. They just figured it was another city destroyed. Far smaller than many of the cities already destroyed. The loss of 64 cities including Tokyo, hadn’t made the Japanese surrender, why would two more? That isn’t to say the Japanese didn’t understand what nuclear weapons were, they did. And they did recognize it after a few days. The bombing itself was nothing new to the Japanese however. What was new in 1945, was the loss of Manchuria. It should be understood that Japan wasn’t ruled by Emperor Hirohito, and even if he himself was persuaded by the nuclear weapons, which might indeed be the case, that was not enough to make the military dictatorship step down. They still controlled a massive part of China and all of Korea. The Kwantung Army in Manchuria had been staunch supporters of Tojo, and constituted a big part of the material base for the Japanese Empire. When the Soviets invaded and defeated the Kwantung Army in just a few days, not only did they deprive the Japanese of their materials, they had also effectively destroyed the power base of the Japanese military dictatorship, and demonstrated that even the veteran Japanese forces were no match at all for the Soviet military. The Japanese leadership (correctly) assumed that if the Soviets helped in invading Japan, they would occupy part of it, and likely insist of a total dismantling of the Japanese social structure. The Americans on the other hand were more open to keeping the wealthy elites in power and letting the Japanese Emperor continue. This influenced their decision to surrender faster. The nuclear bombing was a factor, but it was a small one. The absolute state of catastrophe was already arriving in Japan. By fall of 1945, had the firebombing continued and the Soviets helped the invasion, a depleted Japan would have had to face off two armies, while having a massive starvation due to rice crops failing to be harvested. Whether or not the nuclear bombing had happened, Japan was finished. Japan was merely hoping to make it so difficult for the Americans to achieve a quick victory, that they would negotiate one, with the arrival of Soviet forces, there was no hope of such a thing, as even if the Americans refused to invade Japan, the Soviets would do it anyway. [Edit] Additional context from the Japanese primary sources, confirms what I have said here, I should have included this in the original answer, there are two points I would like to very briefly make. In the comment section, I expanded on the Emperor’s speech of 15th of August. But I would like to point out that Emperor Showa was not in control of Japan during WW2. I would also like people to consider, that the Japanese motives are not a mystery. Instead of speculating of making up fantasies as has happened in the comment section, you could simply go read a Japanese history book, the Japanese are not fairies, they can be asked, if nothing else, try google translate the Japanese version of wikipedia for the surrender of Japan, and see how many times the Soviet Union is mentioned (it’s a lot).

Name: Carl Hamilton
Question: How did the quality and quantity of the Soviet Union's aircraft industry compare to that of the US?
Answer: This depends quite heavily on when we are talking, and if we are talking civilian or military. In general the military industry was not as sophisticated as the American one, while in many areas the civilian aircraft industry took the lead in other cases. I’ll start with the civilian one since it is much simpler. The Soviets created the Tupolev-104, which began service on the Moscow-Omsk-Irkutsk route in the Soviet union in 1956. This was the first successful jet-line passenger service in the world, and would mark Aeroflot as one of the leading air line services for the remainder of the cold war. The Boeing 707 would become a ubiquitous aircraft, but first flew in 1958. Another popular American aircraft was the DC-8. It should also be noted the British de Havilland Comet, was the first actual jetliner, but was withdrawn from service after several crashes within the first year of operation. Turns out they had not stress tested the aircraft before putting passengers in it. During the cold war both American and Soviet aircraft companies made a string of successful passenger jets and cargo planes, which were fairly similar. The Soviets did manage to create the first supersonic jet-liner the Tu-144, the Concorde was made as a very similar aircraft the year after. During WW2, US aircraft manufacture was of very high quality and quantity as well. The Soviet aircraft industry struggled in WW2 quite a lot, due to a shortage of materials for aircraft, including aluminium. This meant that many early aircraft of the USSR were mostly wood, additionally Soviet aviation fuel did not contain as much octane as American fuel, which limited engine operations and thus Soviet flight performance was not as good in general. Design wise, the Soviets were doing quite well though. The La-5, La-7, Yak-3, Yak-9 and of course the IL-2 were all excellent and effective designs, despite their limitations. Notably, the Soviets favoured fuselage mounted cannons and emphasized pilot skill in aiming, this became the standard everywhere after WW2, so they were ahead of the Americans in gun placement. On the other hand the US produced some of the best aircraft of World War 2, including the famous P-51 which was likely the best escort fighter, the P-38 lightning long range fighter, the naval fighters F6F, F4F, F4U, a slew of bombers including the B-17, B-25 and of course the B-29, which was in fact so good the Soviets copied it as the Tu-4. Following WW2, the Soviets and American competed in aircraft on a more even level. By the Korean war the Soviets had closed the gap and the MiG-15 jet fighter performed equally well to the F-86 sabre aircraft, with some minor advantages on both sides. In the 1950s however, the US would once again take the lead in aircraft technology. Most importantly, the US won the race to create an effective air to air missile, the AIM-9 sidewinder. Other missiles existed, but this one actually worked. The Soviets copied the missile as the R-3. The famous MiG-21 fighter was created by the Soviets, and was an excellent little aircraft able to challenge US air forces in Vietnam, however the F-4 Phantom created about the same time, was without a doubt higher in performance. US fighter aircraft of this period also tended to be much more multirole, offering quite flexible CAS, while the Soviets relied almost entirely on the Su-7 for tactical air support. For bombers the Soviet and American both had an effective long range nuclear bomber, namely the American B-52 and the Soviet Tu-95. In the 1960s the Soviets would take the lead in bombers, with the introduction of the Tu-22 and later Tu-22M the Soviets created supersonic jet bombers which the US did not have an answer to. The US would not acquire a response until 1986 with the B-1 lancer. In tactical aviation, the 1960s was a bit of a slumber in new aircraft, time was spent improving current models, except the US introduction of the F-111 which was a good tactical bomber, far surpassing the Soviet Su-7. However, many designs were being developed in the 1960s. On the year of 1970, the Soviet air force drastically changed. In the same year they introduced the new MiG-25 high altitude fighter, the fastest armed aircraft ever created, armed with the fastest and longest range missiles at the time. The MiG-23 was introduced as a much more capable replacement for the MiG-21, the Su-7 was upgraded to the Su-17 with a slew of guided weapons, and soon after the Su-24 was introduced as an equivalent to the F-111. The US was not sitting idle either, and would soon regain superiority in the air with the introduction of the F-14 in 1974. The F-14 was the beginning of a new generation of aircraft and was at its introduction unrivaled in performance. Just two years after the F-15 was introduced, as the world’s premier air superiority fighter. These aircraft could carry significant number of missiles, had good flight characteristics and avionics. The MiG-23 could only carry 2 long range missiles, and 4 very short range missiles. While the F-15 could carry 4 long range missiles as well as 4 short range missiles. Additionally the R-23 was not as potent as the AIM-7 sparrow, though the R-24 missile made for the MiG-23 was meant to be an upgrade over the AIM-7. These American super aircraft, were however quite expensive, and so a cheaper alternative was made in the F-16, which delivered much of the same performance but at a greatly reduced cost, allowing the mass production of the highly capable new series of aircraft. The Soviets struggled to compete with these new aircraft, but had some tricks up their own sleeve. In 1981 they introduced the MiG-31 which was the first fighter aircraft to feature an electronically scanned radar, and active search missiles able to hit targets at over 120km away. Additionally the in the 1980s the Soviet began fielding the MiG-29 and Su-27 fighter aircraft, which were superior in performance to the F-16 and F-15. Additionally these aircraft had great innovations including the first off-bore short range missile the R-73, long range IR missiles in the R-27T, and a helmet mounted sight, which allowed pilots to fire missiles at aircraft they were looking at without having to point their own aircraft at it. In close range fighting they were considered even by western pilots as wonders. Quite uncharacteristically of the Soviets however, they were not mass producible, and the Soviets ended the cold war, outnumbered quite severely in this generation of aircraft. The US and Soviet aircraft industries produced many great technological advances. On the whole the Soviets produced more aircraft, except in the 1980s. But I think it will not be uncontroversial to say that in general the US had the advantage of producing the best performing aircraft in general for pretty much the duration except the 1980s.

Question: In the mid-1970s, how overmatched were Soviet tanks in comparison to NATO tanks? Would NATO have been able to resist columns upon columns of advancing T-62, T-64 and T-72 tanks?
Answer: You pick the height of Soviet superior in armour technology as a time period. Not only was NATO severely outperformed in terms of Soviet quality, they were also outnumbered quite significantly. Let’s take the year 1976, by this year, the Soviets had a whopping 30 T-80 tanks, that’s fairly irrelevant so let’s ignore that. They had 1,967 T-72 tanks, but most importantly, 4,093 T-64 tanks. Additionally they had roughly 20,000 T-62 tanks and additional T-55 tanks, roughly 48,000 tanks in total in the field. In Europe NATO could field roughly 6,000 tanks according to the RAND report, “Assessing the Conventional Balance In Europe 1945–1975”. While estimating that the Soviets could field roughly 23,000 tanks in central Europe. RAND assessed that NATO would need 3 weeks to increase it’s tank numbers to just 8,000, mostly reinforcements from the USA. As Such, in terms of tanks, the Soviets were outnumbering NATO by at least 4 to 1, and most likely quite a bit more than that in practical terms. Now let’s talk about quality, we can start by looking at the most important front line MBTs of the 1970s. A quick summary if available here: Let’s talk about protection first. The Chieftain’s armor was quite sloped, in a line of sight, the armour was nearly 380mm, however, the reason why I have displayed thickness will become apparent soon. Only the T-64 had composite armour, which wile 205mm thick, was equivalent to 440mm vs kinetic penetrators and 575mm vs HEAT penetrators. The composite armour made it practically immune to HESH rounds from the front. Now note the APFSDS ammunition. APFSDS has a nasty tendency of reducing the effectiveness of sloped armor due to interesting physics regarding normalization. For example the 3BM-3 115mm round on paper penetrates 270mm at 2km range. This should not allow it to penetrate the Chieftain from the front. But it did, and if you like to see how you can look up 3BM-3 vs Chieftain on Youtube and go for SY simulations channel. If you’re not happy with that, consider that Iraqi T-62s destroyed Iranian Chieftains in the Iraq-Iran war without any problem from the front. The NATO plan was to rely quite heavily on other anti tank weapons against Soviet tanks, which was a bit of a problem with the T-64, as stated the 575mm vs HEAT made it practically immune against all NATO anti tank missiles at the time. The best NATO AT missile was probably the TOW and it could penetrate 430mm, an upgrade the I-TOW could penetrate 630mm but did not appear until 1978. In short, NATO was severely over matched in tanks both in quality and quantity in the 1970s, which is why the Leopard 2, Abrams and Challenger tanks were made. The ultimate plan to stop Soviet armored columns in the 1970s, was quite simply tactical nuclear weapons.

Name: Carl Hamilton
Question: How did Russian losses of the T90-M tank hit 100 when according to Oryx, Russia only had 67 to begin with?
Answer: There are multiple ways to arrive at such a number, the most likely one is that Oryx isn’t very reliable. Allow me to demonstrate. This in Oryx’s count T-90M Destroyed Nr. 53. What you actually see is the aftermath of an FPV drone detonating on the front armour of the T-90M. There is no visible damage at all, and I have never seen an FPV drone penetrate the front armour of a modern tank whether Ukrainian or Russian. Likewise this is T-90M Destroyed Nr. 39, this fire is coming from the explosive reactive armor on the front of the tank, the tank itself appears to have taken a prior hit disabling the engine, but it is quite obviously not destroyed. Oryx is extremely generous when it comes to assigning Russian losses, and extremely conservative when assigning Ukrainian losses. Even so, they claim currently only 5 captured and 53 destroyed. There is absolutely no attempt to prevent double counting either, in fact on Oryx the same picture is sometimes listed as both a T-80BV and a T-72B, counting not just twice but as different tanks. If you look at T-90M Captured Nr 4 and Captured Nr 5, you see that Nr 4 is a T-90M with a Ukrainian soldier next to it, while Nr 5 is a T-90M being towed away. How do you know this is not the same tank, first captured then towed? You don’t know. But it is counted as 2 separate tanks. Essentially, Oryx does not count separate instances, they count separate photographs collections, each new source is generally treated as a new instance of tank, and no questions are asked beyond that. Oryx represents an interesting collection of photographs from the war, it does not represent an accurate count of material analyzed with due process. Though the majority of its evidence is convincing enough, it does not hold up to scrutiny as a whole. Furthermore the number they have claimed is not 100 lost, but 53 destroyed and 5 captured. All of those damaged tanks which has thrown a track and are inside Russian controlled territory, will be recovered. Finally, of course, the Russians have not stopped producing tanks, and the number of T-90M in the field is far beyond 100 so losing 100 is certainly within the realm of possibility.

Question: Because the Soviet Union was resource independent, would it ever make sense for Stalin to attack Hitler first? (assuming Germany doesn't attack.) The risk vs reward is so much lower for Soviet's to attack first.
Answer: The Soviet Union was not resource independent, though they wanted to be and worked towards it. Never the less, the Soviets wanted to attack Nazi Germany. From 1934 to 1939 the Soviets tried to establish a way to destroy Nazi Germany before they were fully armed, having understood Hitler’s ultimate intentions quite well. Litvinov pursued a collective anti-Nazi alliance for 5 years before WW2. Additionally, and quite contrary to popular belief, the Soviet Union had appointed Maxim Litvinov, as the foreign secretary, a firm and true believer in collective security, and even disarmament. Litvinov improved the standing of the USSR considerably and tried very hard to build alliances with very hostile countries like the USA, UK and France. The USA not even having recognized the USSR as a legitimate state until 1933, when Litvinov convinced them otherwise. I am mentioning all this, because Litvinov was no figurehead, but a true driver of Soviet foreign policy, and in 1935 he accomplished a security agreement with France and Czechoslovakia. This was clearly aimed at Germany, but there were two big problems. Firstly France never fully committed to it, secondly Soviet troops could not easily arrive in France nor Czechoslovakia in case Germany attacked, neither could they directly engage the Nazis as they did not border them. This meant that the USSR needed a military access assurance from either Poland or Romania which did not arrive in 1935, and further didn’t arrive in any subsequent discussion of European collective security. It should be noted that until 1939 Poland was quite close to Nazi Germany, having immediately signed a non-aggression pact in 1934, and as late as 31st of October 1938 the Polish Ambassador in Berlin was discussing with Von Ribbentrop interesting things like breaking up the remaining Czechoslovakia and emigration of Jews. Indeed Polish leadership had envisioned Poland as a rising power of central Europe, but had lost out on the ability to influence Hungary, Slovakia and Romania. Rather than seeing the writing on the wall however, Poland decided to rely entirely on France and Britain for security, and continued to refuse Soviet aid in the case of war, unable to settle it’s differences. After 5 years of rejections to form the coalition against Nazism, the Soviets perceived the intentions of the western countries + Poland, as being overtly anti-Soviet, suspecting (quite rightly for the most part) that the western countries were hoping that a German-Soviet war would be the outcome, and would allow them to sit back and watch their European rivals destroy each other. Famously the caused the Soviets to sign a fateful treaty with Germany instead. It would have made perfect sense to attack Hitler first, but geographically the Soviets were never able to do that until after the Germans had taken Poland anyway. The Soviets did not wish to fight Germany alone, and was unable to secure any collective security treaties from the western powers. As such it never happened, though they very much wanted to.

Name: Carl Hamilton
Question: What were the qualitative and performance differences between concurrent models of the T-34 and M4 Sherman over the years of WWII?
Answer: By the time the M4 Sherman entered production, the best variant of the T-34–76 tank was already in production for a few months. The T-34 Mod 1943, was actually made in May 1942, while the Sherman production began in the summer of 1942. Prior to that the Soviets had T-34s and the US did not have Shermans so in the period where the Soviets had a T-34 and the Sherman didn’t exist, the T-34’s most close analogue from the USA was the M3 Lee, which did not have a main gun in the turret, and was widely considered inferior to the T-34 in most aspects. The M4 Sherman being an evolution of course also improving on the M3 design in every way. The T-34 Mod 1943, had advantages in track width making it better for muddy and snowy conditions than the Sherman, overall the armor of the Sherman and T-34 Mod 1943 was fairly similar, as was the firepower. The Sherman had slightly better penetration with solid shot ammunition, while the T-34 had better post penetration effects due to firing APHE. The biggest advantage and difference at this point, was that the Sherman featured a three man turret and came with radios on all tanks, which was not yet the case for the T-34. From 1944 T-34 production switched to the T-34–85 and the US introduced the Sherman 76 variants. The T-34–85 closed the earlier advantage of the Sherman, by introducing a much better turret with heavier armor, 3 crew positions, radios on all tanks and good copulas. The Sherman 76 had a good penetration as did the T-34–85 but in terms of firepower the T-34–85 had a much bigger HE-FRAG round increasing effectiveness against infantry and buildings, while being about equal in armor penetration. In short, the M4 Sherman was better than the standard T-34–76 in most cases other than mobility, but not as good as the T-34–85 even with the 76mm gun. It should be noted that both tanks were excellent in general, and well liked by their crews, they served side by side and generally no decisive difference was found and they could be deployed in similar ways by the USSR which operated both.

Name: Carl Hamilton
Question: What were the flaws of the M4 Sherman tank and why did it struggle against German tanks in World War II? Did the Japanese or Soviets face similar issues with their own tanks during the war?
Answer: The Sherman tank was an excellent design, and honestly had relatively few flaws. Now many people will point out that the Sherman tank’s performance against so and so enemy wasn’t perfect. This is irrelevant. When creating a design there are always choices to be made, you cannot have a speedy 70 tank heavy tank with a low fuel consumption in 1943. Giving a design performance in one area will decrease its performance in another. The commonly listed flaws of the Sherman tank is the inability of the Sherman tank to defeat German heavies like the Panther and Tiger from the front, and armor which was too weak to stand up to German 88 and long 75mm guns. Well, that is certainly true. However, Sherman tanks spent the vast majority of their time supporting infantry, against soft targets like other infantry, bunkers and lightly armored vehicles. The Sherman excelled at this without any issue what so ever. In the entire campaign in France, the US only encountered 3 Tigers, and defeated all of them. So what does it matter? Similar criticisms are often levied against the T-34, which had far more struggles in the beginning of its production. The T-34–85 was truly a masterpiece design for WW2, as was the Sherman. The T-34–85 and the Sherman had different weaknesses, but both were capable of dealing with all threats on the battlefield as long as they were deployed correctly with their combined arms elements. The Sherman armor and gun firepower, was completely standard for a medium tank, combined with excellent material quality, high reliability, and most importantly of all massive availability able to support US troops everywhere once production picked up. The Japanese had no mass produced equivalent of the Sherman tank, and generally had weak armor components for the entire war, this was never a priority for the Japanese as they mostly fought unarmored Chinese and island hopping campaigns against the Americans in which tanks were just not very decisive.

Name: Carl Hamilton
Question: Why is it okay to blackwash every historical figure in media lately?
Answer: It is not okay, and there is very often push-back against that kind of deliberate falsification of history. The reason why this happens as at all, is because of corporate pandering and poor understanding of social theory in the first place. You are probably aware that you don’t have to go back far, before black people in American media at least, were quite poorly represented both in quantity and in character. Good old King of Norway from the Vikings TV show On the social theory end, you’ll see that quite a lot of people feel that people need someone to look up to in a media form, and think not much further than this. Hence why both heroic fantasy characters and historical characters should be black in order to give black people something to look up to. This is fairly stupid for multiple reasons: All of these seem fairly offensive to me, more so than a lack of black characters. This leads us to the corporate aspect, the reality of race in America is that white people overwhelmingly control institutions and wealth. From a corporate point of view it is more important to hide this fact than anything else. How does adding a black character change the income distribution in America? It doesn’t. There used to be token characters, put in shows for the reason of appearing progressive without actually making shows about them. This is not different, it’s just more blatant. We can keep the discussion about black faces in media, because that way we do not have to talk about the reality of the economy of the USA. Likewise, female and LGBT representation is free for corporations, these are excellent things to work with for them, because there is absolutely no down sides to it. People still consume the products on the whole, and the discourse centers around their inclusion which again doesn’t actually hurt the ruling class of the USA at all. If there was no forced inclusion of black characters, there would undoubtedly be far less of them and they would be far more logically placed in historical shows about our current topics. However, this is true only because black people in the USA have much less access to creating movies. According to statistics from worldmetric, 16.9% of characters are black, but only 2% of Academy Awards voters are black. As such black faces on screen are over-represented, but the people with power behind the scenes are grossly under-represented. If black people in the USA had the same resources that white people had on the whole, there would be more black directors, black writers, black producers, black studio owners. And at such point, why would inclusion initiatives even be necessary? Empowerment is not changing history to be devoid of racism in media, it is fixing the actual racism that causes massive wealth disparity in the present day. Poor people do not need role-models, they need money. Being poor is not a lack of character, it is a lack of cash and power. The black-washing as you call it, is mostly an upperclass attempt to appear as if they are trying to change things, without actually changing anything.

Name: Carl Hamilton
Question: How did the Chinese, Japanese, Vietnamese Soviet, and other military forces motivate their troops to participate in 'human wave' attacks in World War Two, the Korean War, and the Vietnam War?
Answer: They did not, because there isn’t any such tactic described in any of their doctrines. The term is almost exclusively used to denigrate other forces in an attempt at making them look primitive, where we are supposed to look civilized. There is a long standing tradition, that western people fight with quality while barbarian eastern people and other wrong colours, fight with numbers. This is obviously not true, but it is a very popular narrative. The idea of assaulting something with infantry, is quite often misconstrued as being human wave attacks, but the use of infantry in an offensive role is not anything particularly special. Everyone does this. In fact one of the most famous assault using human waves is the D-day landing. It was carried out in waves, it was done almost exclusively by infantry (due to many tanks sinking before getting ashore), yet when it is Americans, British and Canadians doing the waves of humans against a heavily fortified position in which they lose thousands of people it is not a term used, and if you look at the portrayal in media like Saving Private Ryan, it looks rather heroic. Unlike when you see Soviet attacks in Enemy at the Gates which are depicted as actively trying to get their own people killed and is indeed pure fiction as those things never happened, or movies like Taegukgi where the Chinese are more or less depicted as ants in some scenes. The reality is that infantry attacks happen, human wave attacks is a buzz term meant to insinuate inferiority and disregard for human life, I wrote about this several years ago.

Name: Carl Hamilton
Question: Did the Western Allies or Soviets use captured Panzerfaust?
Answer: The Soviets wanted a rocket weapons, but were not satisfied with the Panzerfaust, Shrek, PIAT or Bazooka. The reason for this was that the Soviets wanted something much longer range. The effective range of rocket or recoilless launchers in WW2 was very small, and what the Soviets wanted was something with the range of an AT rifle. The Soviets actually stuck with the AT rifles throughout the war, despite being offered both PIAT and Bazookas. The Soviets actually began a development program in 1942 called the Ruchnoy Protivotankovyy Granatomot - RPG. Which lasted nearly 20 years, the specifications set down to be able to hit an destroy a tank frontally at 300m was not met until 1961 when the RPG-7 went into service. Here is an LPG-44 from 1944. Unfortunately it only had an effective range of 75m. As the Soviet program to make anti tank rocket weapons proceeded quite slowly, the Soviets did not just capture and use Panzerfausts, but collected them into great stockpiles and began distributing them en-masse. And with official manuals in Russian, a picture of which can be seen below. However, the battle of Berlin showed that the panzerfaust was still not that great, not for anti tank, nor for other works like hitting buildings. In this battle German panzerfaust only managed to account for around 18% of Soviet tanks disabled, despite this being the ideal conditions for the panzerfaust, total absense of mine fields inside the city, and a large availability of the panzerfaust. In short, yes the Soviets used them from 1944 and on, they wanted something completely different, and they quite quickly dropped them again. Bonus point to the first person who figures out what it actually says in the first picture, I know you’ll like it. Oh and as for the western allies, they had their own Bazooka and PIAT what did they really need Panzerfaust for?

Name: Carl Hamilton
Question: When was Lend Lease most important to helping the USSR in its war against the Axis? In the initial battles of Operation Barbarossa and Russian victory at Stalingrad (1941-43), or during the Soviet offensives from 1944-45?
Answer: We know this quite well actually, and I will commend the questioner for phrasing this question so well, because this is exactly the essence of the discussion on lend-lease which is almost always missed when people talk about this online. I can answer this quite accurately I believe as well. We are talking about the chronological significance and the relatively quantitative significance of lend-lease. This happens to be my great research passion to look at things in this way. The first bit we have to understand is that almost no lend-lease actually arrived in 1941, of the first period most arrived in the first half of 1942, so this is after the Battle of Moscow. It is not unfair to say that lend-lease played almost no role in this battle. If we look at the next period, from July 1942 to June 1943, we cover the period of Stalingrad and leading up to Kursk. At the height of the Stalingrad offensive (Operation Uranus) some lend-lease equipment was beginning to be seen in earnest, particularly trucks and aircraft. Note also the quantity delivered here was more than twice that of the period period. During Kursk in 1943, and until operation Bagration in 1944, the largest amount of lend-lease was delivered, and it was again nearly double of the previous period. From this period the Soviets also began receiving better quality items such as the Sherman tank, rather than M3 Lee or Valentine. The most overlooked category is not trucks, which is known, but aircraft, in which lend-lease aircraft made up almost 10% of the total inventory which is quite significant, additionally the aircraft delivered like the P-39 was probably some of the most beloved lend-lease equipment out of everything, the Soviets had complaints about much equipment delivered, but very little about the P-39 aircraft which they thought was excellent, and it was a real ace maker with Grigory Rechkalov, possibly the best allied pilot in WW2 (Along with Ivan Ivan Kozhedub), flying this plane against the Germans to a tune of 61–65 planes shot down, the vast majority in the P-39. In the final period, for the Battle of Berlin and prior offensives, I would say lend-lease did not matter for the simple reason that the war was guaranteed won at this point. Additionally this was the period in which the Soviet industry had recovered the most and was able to handle most shortages anyway. The answer is of course it was the most important from mid 1943 to mid 1944. Not just because of the above reasons, but also because if we consider the Soviet supply situation. Yes the Soviets had the greatest shortages in 1941–1942, but they also received the smallest amount of material. In 1943–1944 they received the most, and also best. The industrial output in 1942 was the worst of any year, but 1943 was only slightly better. However, 1943 had ambitious military plans, that required more material. The Soviets would likely have won the Battle of Kursk anyway, but the lend-lease helped in making it such a comfortable victory, that the Soviets had material enough to immediately make a large counter offensive which was hugely successful. The extent of this success without lend-lease would have been smaller. Additionally, 1943 was the year in which food imports mattered the most. The Soviet agriculture had is worst year of the war, but on top of that, their success in the spring offensive and later Kursk offensive, also meant they recovered millions of more civilians who needed food. The combination of the worst food supply with a great influx of mouths to feed meant that kilo for kilo lend-lease food mattered the most this year. I hope people can appreciate that this answer does not answer the question of whether lend-lease carried the USSR, but in which years that lend-lease had the most use value which is the essence of the question. This is a more objective question and answer, because there is little subjective evaluation needed.

Name: Carl Hamilton
Question: Why did Russian missiles strike a children's hospital in Kyiv?
Answer: I do not think it is so easy to determine guilt in these cases and so quickly. Particularly not in such a complicated missile scenario where Russian missiles actually struck from all directions. Let’s look at some evidence which has already been posted. Striking elements: Striking elements were found on the day, and they certainly look like they are from an AA missile, though to me, they look more like they are from a BUK missile than from any western missile. There is another problem with this piece of evidence. This picture and the other pictures do not prove the location of collection. In fact from what I saw on telegram these fragments were shown in relation to another impact on an apartment building, which indeed looks like it was hit by an AA missile as it had minor damage, but a large fragmentation pattern. I would say these pictures of fragments are not indicative of much as of yet, based on the photos currently available we cannot source them the hospital unless there is an update on this I am unaware of. Video of Missile Arrival I first saw this reported as an AIM-120 missile, which I at first glance thought yes that might well be it. However, upon reflection and a closer look at the frames, it appears that there is a jet booster at the tail end of the missile. Though actually, the picture is blurry, and this might indeed just be a the tail fin of a cruise missile, with the missile flying upside down. Additionally, the missile is lacking top and bottom middle fins, as well as one tail fin for it to be an AIM-120. While it is possible, that an AIM-120 could be damaged to badly that it is missing 3 fins to give it that distinctive shape, that is a more complicated explanation than it is most likely a Kh-101 which already matches this shape much better. Additionally, the tail end of the missile is not leaving any smoke, unlike a air defense missile which was just fired with a solid fuel rocket engine. An AIM-120 would leave a smoke trail for several kilometers, and if it accidentally fell inside Kyiv and was launched from Kyiv it would not have gone that far. In short, the video appears to indicate this was a Russian cruise missile. Damage Assessment The footage of the destruction shows significant blast damage. Air defense missiles do not usually carry significant blasting warheads, and usually leaves wide spread fragmentation damage as they are designed to produce a fragmentation cloud to destroy aircraft, not buildings. It appears to me that that the missile hit the corner of the building, causing a downwards pressure wave that collapsed this section with the most severe collapse on the outside. The downwards shaped roof and the lack of a wide scattering of building material, means that the collapse was not caused by the explosion happening inside the building. An AIM-120 missile could potentially cause this damage, but only if it detonated inside the building after penetrating the roof. The 20kg warhead of the AIM-120 is smaller than even a regular 152mm artillery shell, additionally, it is not optimized for building damage as I said, and the blast direction is in a circle around the missile, not forward. The 400kg warhead of a Kh-101 could definitely collapse a building section, it is optimized for building damage, and could cause this even without detonating inside the building. In short, the damage assessment indicates, this was caused by a large explosive warhead, able to generate significant blast pressure without a large cloud of aerial fragments, such warheads are found on cruise missiles. Summary: The striking elements are inconclusive and too context free to really show anything. The video of the arrival indicates this was likely a Russian cruise missile. The damage assessment indicates this was likely a Russian cruise missile. I would say, that objectively speaking this was almost certainly a Russian cruise missile, it is very unlikely though not impossible it was an air defense missile, but all indicators show otherwise. As to why the Russians actually would want to do this, I suspect they didn’t. The most likely explanation is that the cruise missile was damaged flying through Ukrainian air defense, lost control and landed the wrong place. Another explanation could be that Ukrainian electronic warfare systems jammed the missile guidance, and it missed its intended target, we see this quite a lot on other missiles too. It’s also possible that Russian intelligence designated the target by mistake. Finally, maybe the Russians just enjoy hitting hospitals, because they are comically evil cartoon villains. I would wager the last one is not the reality, the second last one is also unlikely, as if it was designated as a targeted building, the Russians would not have hit it with just 1 cruise missile, but several. We saw 5–6 missiles land on the same industrial target close to this area, and just 1 hit this hospital. That to me seems to indicate a malfunction, caused by damage, electronic warfare, or maybe even just a manufacturing error. I hope this was objectively enough framed to be informative.

Question: Let's pretend that Hitler never went into the Soviet Union in 1941 or anytime thereafter. How would Germany have ultimately lost? Leave the American Military to the side for this, but if the Soviets attack they would have been slaughtered wholesale.
Answer: The Soviets would not have been slaughtered wholesale, they would almost certainly have won and much more so than they did in reality. You’re assuming that Soviets were innately stupid and bad at war obviously, in this respect you share your view with the Nazis. This is a fairly bad starting point so let’s correct that, because once you understand the reality behind the German success, you’ll see why the Soviets would probably have won. The Germans could not have attacked the Soviets at a better time, the Soviets were completely surprised by the fall of France, and had enacting multiple reforms and changes of equipment for the military, expecting to have several years to complete them. When Germany invaded in 1941, many Soviet tank formations were in the process of refitting, and were in the wrong place, often also not fully manned. When Soviet KV-1 tanks went into battle in the early days, they often lacked tank shells at all, unable to fire their main guns, they used just their machine guns. The Soviets were lacking officers and reserve materials, didn’t have a completed communications reform of their air force, not communications of their land forces which was in the process of modernizing to use radios. Let’s pretend that the Soviets did not have these problems. They had completed their reforms entirely and the year is 1943 or so. The Soviets have an armored force fully equipped with T-34s and KV-1s instead of the around 15% of their force as in 1941. The average Soviet infantry-man is armed with either an SVT-40 semi automatic rifle or a sub-machine gun, instead of a bolt action rifle. Every Soviet mobile formation has a full battery of Katyusha rocket launchers. The Soviet air force is mostly equipped with next generation tactical planes like the Yak-9 and IL-2, instead of biplanes and first generation monoplanes like the I-16. There is no lack of officers or raw materials, there is no confusion, and no loss of territory. Everything that the Germans were surprised by in low quantities in 1941, now exist in massive quantities, instead of hundreds of KV-1s without proper ammunition, you have thousands of KV-1s, all with radios, as was always the intention. Panzer III and short barreled Panzer IV which did fine against T-26 tanks and Valentines, had little to offer against T-34s, especially as the T-34 fielded would likely have been vastly different as the plans for the T-34M was already at the component testing scale in March 1941, but cancelled due to the need to mass produce immediately. Had the Soviets had more time, the T-34 would have had a three-man turret with a radio, additionally a significant number of T-34Ms would have been armed with the 57mm high velocity gun for tank destroying, a few of which were actually trialed in 1941, leading to the misconception that there was a T-34–57 tank in production. Below is the model of the T-34 with a three man turret. Many of the German tanks on the other hand were accelerated and put into production, exactly because of the shock of Soviet equipment like the T-34, KV-1, Katyusha and even the 120mm mortar shocked the Germans enough that they just reverse engineered it. Likewise the G-43 rifle reverse engineered parts of the SVT-40. German pre-war armament plans were not technologically ambitious like the Soviets were, and the disruption of the Soviet industry in 1941, was one of the heaviest blows imaginable. Even in the most farvourable scenario imaginable to the Germans, (the actual one) the Germans lost; were unable to take their strategic objectives. Not imagine the reverse, the scenario most favorable to the Soviets with Germany spending all it’s resources in the west. It would have been a slaughter yes, of Nazis. By the way, I am fully convinced that the British Empire and The United States could have won against Germany eventually even without the Soviets, provided they were willing to take the cost in human lives, they would certainly have been able to hold on for another 2 years if they had to until the Soviets were fully ready. In reality the Soviets defeated 80% of the German forces, but there is no reason why the heavy losses of 1941–1943 couldn’t have been done in the west instead, with the Soviets swooping in in 1943–1944 and just mopping up the remains. Germany lost WW2 due to their own arrogance, ignorance, prejudice and poor economic planning. They got incredibly lucky that they managed to get as far as they did, change some variables and things look worse for them in most cases, not better.

Question: Having defeated most of the German Army, in 1945 was the Soviet Army the best fighting force of WWII? How much better equipped, experienced, and professional were Soviet troops by 1945 than they had been in 1939/41?
Answer: The Red Army emerged from WW2 as a tired, but very well equipped and experienced fighting force. The Red Army had become specialized in dismantling enemies in the depth of their territory, and carrying out offensives consistently at high speeds through opposition. At the end of WW2, the Soviets showed how far they had come when they faced down the Japanese army in Manchuria. And delivered an overwhelming victory in in just 11 days. The Soviets captured over 800,000 square kilometers, for reference France is 643,000 square kilometers. In terms of equipment, there were quite drastic changes to the Red Army. The basic Soviet infantry division went from being a mostly rifles division, to being rough 40% automatic weapons, having organic self propelled guns and more than twice the amount of artillery throw weight compared to 1941. The detailed breakdown is here: Even more stark is the contrast between the armor units. In 1939 a Soviet tank brigade, such as 26th tank brigade, had 228 T-26 light tanks, the 15th tank corps had 461 BT-5/7 light tanks. Quite a lot, but very limited in capability. From 1939 to 1942 Soviets relied heavily on these obsolete light tanks. It wasn’t until 1943, that the T-34 medium tank became the mainstay of Soviet tanks. Additionally due to losses, Soviet tank corps were significantly reduced in strength during the early years of the war. Additionally of course, in the later war the Soviet tank corps were also supported by independent heavy tank regiments with IS-2 heavy tanks. No other army in the world had even close to the artillery firepower, heavy tanks availability, or automatic infantry weapons that the Soviets deployed. No other army had commanders experienced in the scale of land operations that the Soviets had. I would not go as far as saying that it was the best fighting force in general, but it might have been the best army. But there is more to a fighting force than that, for example the navy and air force. There is no objective way to measure this either. The only fact we can say for sure is that the Red Army was an order of magnitudes better in 1945 than in 1941, and armies like the Japanese one which was not prepared for what the Soviets could do the same way the Germans were, were simply rolled up.

Question: During WWII, since Japan directly attacked the USA & Germany did not, did Americans support the war in the Pacific more than the conflict in Europe?
Answer: The US population were already pretty hostile to the Germans before the Japanese attack and German’s declaration of war. It was understood that Germany was the preeminent partner in the alliance, and therefore USA adopted the policy of “Europe First”. Despite Japan’s actual attack, they were to be honest, little threat to the Americans in the short term, Europe was economically hugely important, most exports went this way, and most imports came from there. Not to mention, that even the Americans felt a strong cultural connection as most Americans still had family or known roots in Europe, particularly there was a cultural connection with the United Kingdom. Francis Pickens Miller wrote for Foreign Affair in July 1941, before Pearl Habour the following: The North Atlantic area is the cradle of our civilization, and the survival of the American way of life depends upon the survival of this civilization. For more than a thousand years our fathers have been building a common society on the shores of the North Atlantic. They built it by labour, by faith, and, when necessary, by arms. It is a civilization based upon a belief in the essential dignity of man, as expressed through representative government, limited by a Bill of Rights. The Atlantic Ocean has become the ocean of freedom.” There was also the consideration, that the primary allies of the USA was in Europe, namely the UK and USSR. While China held down the Japanese land forces, it was unthinkable that even in the very unlikely event of a total Chinese victory, that they would be able to do anything against mainland Japan or the Japanese navy. As such they were not as useful of an ally, despite their massive contribution to WW2. On the contrary, had the US lost the UK and USSR, it is difficult to imagine how they would have managed to defeat Germany at all. Therefore it was important to prop up both of these, and focus on their needs, with the majority of the US effort. I think the US public was largely aware of this as well, and there were not serious calls to change strategy to one based on vengeance rather than logic.

Question: It is historically established that communists adopt not only the word "leftism" but also the word "democrat". The name of the Russian party that gave birth to today's communism was "Russian Social-Democratic Labor Party". Do you understand now?
Answer: No, that is incorrect. The correct terms are left-wing and right-wing. This terminology comes from the way voting was historically done, by standing either to the left side or the right side of the room. It just so happened that the right-wing of the room was usually occupied by the conservatives, while the left wing of the room was occupied by the progressives. Confusingly, in Denmark the old conservatives was called “Højre” (Right) and the liberals still to this day being called “Venstre” (Left), which is now the the main right wing party, while the social democrats have not taken the left position. Communists historically, rejected the possibility of change through participation in a rigged game of elections, where the establishment had all the power. Their route was through revolution, and their idea of democracy was representation of the majority through class, not through elections. Communists have never desribed themselves as leftist, because it’s a word made by people too stupid to understand why it’s called left-wing, and it makes as much sense as rightist. Left-wing and right-wing are not ideologies, positions or policies. They are tendencies, and hints in which direction one leans. Lenin was briefly part of the Russian-social democratic labor party, that doesn’t mean that party gave birth to Soviet communism, it means Lenin part of it, but really this party wasn’t even a part after 1903, it was split between the Bolsheviks and Mensheviks.
