Question: One thing the British and the Russians agree on, is that American assistance was limited, and non-essential, in their defeat of Hitler. So, why do Americans still insist that they couldn't have defeated Hitler without American assistance?
Answer: The Americans like practically everyone, would like their history to be significant, the nationalist ones like every other nationalist, want their history to be better than other people’s history, because it gives a sense of superiority. That being said, we cannot say for sure what would have happened in an alternative reality, we can only say what happened in this one. In this one, the USSR, USA and UK defeated the Axis. American assistance in the real meaning, was not limited nor non-essential. The US deployed a very large military in world war 2, and defeated with their own military a significant portion of the Axis ground forces in Europe, and an even larger proportion of air forces and naval forces. I don’t think anyone should underestimate nor overestimate this, but certainly none of the US fighting soldiers should be considered as anything else than equal to any other soldier in the fight against Nazism. One of the other often noted aspects of US contribution to World War 2, is lend-lease. The US spent 50 billion 1945 dollars on lend-lease support for its allies. 31.4 billion went to the British Empire, while 11.3 billion went to the USSR. Of the 11.3 billion to the USSR 5.5 billion were military equipment, while the remaining were civilian goods and services. For the British, 13.3 billion were military equipment, while the remaining were civilian goods and services. Services includes payment to everyone involved in lend-lease on the US side, so this did not directly benefit the recipient countries. If we look at the amount of service members in WW2, we get a bit of a scale of contribution. 34 million Soviets served in their armed forces, and received 5.5 billion dollars worth of equipment, that is 162 dollars per Soviet serviceman in military equipment. 7.957.000 million people served in the British Empire’s military in World War 2 (Not including Canada), so with 13.3 billion dollars of military equipment, that is 1,671 dollars per British soldier. In short the British received more than twice as much equipment, for less than 1/3rd the amount of soldiers, a difference to be precise of 10.3 times. We can take an example of British reliance, the British produced 15,359 medium tanks, not counting the 8,275 Valentine as medium as they were less than 20t weight nor the 1,700 Covenanters, as it was a failure that was never issued to combat units. The British did also have 5,768 Churchill heavy tanks. But compare these 15,359 medium tanks this to the fact that they received through lend-lease 20,071 medium tanks, of which 17,184 were Sherman tanks. That means the US supplied more than 1 Sherman tank for every domestic British medium tank, and consider that the Sherman tank was better than all British medium tanks except the Comet. If the British had not received lend-lease from the US, their armored force in WW2 would have been very weak and reduced in size by about 50%. And this is being generous as those numbers include pre-war production for the British, which were mostly not used or lost in 1940. I’ve worked with other researchers in Denmark to do a more detailed analysis of the Soviet armored forces and lend-lease previously, I will post it again here. If we take all of the Soviet 131,700 tanks, and compare it to the 10,470 tanks received through aid, they made up just 7.9% of the total amount of Soviet tanks, and generally was not superior in quality. However, my data is better than so, and if you look below, we see a more realistic picture, as this is based on the actual Soviet inventory from the beginning of 1942, after the catastrophic losses in Barbarossa 1941, however bear in mind this data is not just US lend-lease but US and British lend-lease combined. In short, US contribution was significant in general, the material supplies to UK and USSR were vastly different, the Soviet military was enormous and their production big even without any US aid, the British was not. Without US lend-lease British WW2 contribution would have been significantly reduced without a doubt, in contrast, the majority of lend-lease to the USSR arrived only after the Soviets had already won Moscow (1941), Stalingrad (1942) and Kursk (1943).

Question: How is Operation Barbarossa viewed by modern Europeans?
Answer: There are certain different levels of interest, and I am sure this varies by country as well. But contrary to what a few cynics seem to think, I believe most people actually care about history in general, and quite a lot of people are at least aware of Operation Barbarossa. One of the most popular magazines in Denmark is simply called “Historie” and the most popular subject is WW2. That isn’t just for nerdy men either, my mother, my grandmother, auntie and plenty of laymen friends read this magazine. If you ask the average person who actually know more than this happened in WW2 and that the Soviets were invaded, you will probably get a variety of opinions. The most casual opinion is that the Germans cleaned the Soviets out because the Soviets didn’t have any officers, but eventually the weather got to the Germans. The Danish Faktalink, describes the operation as initially a blitzkrieg, but that Germany put themselves in a two-front war, additionally they highlight that from the beginning the Nazis wanted an extermination war and Einsatsgruppen were part of the retinue that committed war crimes from day one. It highlight the extermination of POWs and the Nazi ideology of Lebensraum. The Danish history magazine, goes into more military detail, and break with a lot of stereotypes. For example, they point out that while the Soviets didn’t have a lot of modern tanks, they did have the best ones like the KV-1 which was shocking to the Germans. Additionally they point out that while operationally the Germans were extremely skilled, they ignored their logisticians and equipped their troops poorly in comparison to Soviet troops which often had an advantage in better quality gear. When I talk to people here, they tend to be fairly reasonable about this, even in the current environment, very few lay people here, are under the impression that the Barbarossa was anything else than the German assault on the Soviets, and that the Soviets won but at a high cost. Danish magazines tend to treat the subject with respect and sobriety.

Name: Carl Hamilton
Question: How did the Soviet industry fare during Operation Barbarossa? Did they have enough resources to replace losses during major battles like Kursk and Stalingrad?
Answer: In 1941 during the catastrophe that was operation Barbarossa, Zhukov was chief of staff, and at one point he described in a memo from the Stavka, that the situation was “pretty difficult” and not very likely to improve. This is a slight underestimation. There are two ways of looking at it, one slightly optimistic and one slightly pessimistic. One the bright side, the Soviet Union persevered, were able to establish and increase their military industrial output and win the war, which is extremely impressive while losing so much of their territory. On the other hand, when Zhukov said the situation was difficult, what he meant to say in expressive words was that the Soviet economy was a bucket of dogshit on wheels going gown a hill at 100km/h towards a very solidly built brick wall. From 1941 to the end of 1942, the Soviet lost about 34% of their entire country’s output, including 48% of agricultural output, 32% of the civilian population and 23% of their factories. Disregarding the extreme military losses, that’s quite a thing to lose within 18 months. Imagine for a moment, that America was invaded, and their starting point was that America had lost from New York to New Orleans and to Chicago. This was the conditions, something America itself pointed out in WW2. In short, it’s difficult to even describe the scale of what the Soviets lost, and I can tell you that they did not recover their civilian society until the 1950s, that’s how great the devastation was. The fact that the Soviets were able to produce anything at all is impressive, the fact that they outproduced the Germans under these cataclysmic conditions, is a down right miracle.

Name: Carl Hamilton
Question: During WWII, did the Axis manage to exploit any of its captured Soviet territory before it lost it again — get in any grain harvests, mine any minerals, run any factories etc?
Answer: The Axis did exploit its Soviet captured territory but not very well. Soviet partisans were extremely effective in disrupting Axis plans to utilize the occupied territory. There was far less cooperation with the Nazis in most of the Soviet territory than in the rest of occupied Europe, the exceptions being Latvia, Lithuania and western Ukraine, which did have significant amount of Nazi collaboration. Whether through sabotage, non-compliance or other partisan activities, the Soviets were able to limit Axis exploitation of resources to around 14% compared to the rest of occupied Europe, according to Leonid D. Grenkevich The Soviet Partisan Movement, 1941–1944

Name: Carl Hamilton
Question: What impact will the use of FAB-3000 M-54, and possibly, ODAB-3000 heavy bombs with guided flight correction module have on the fighting in Ukraine?
Answer: 500kg and 1500kg bombs are perfectly able to destroy buildings, and the FAB-3000 offers little advantage in this regard. What it does do better is destroy bunkers. It is likely being implemented for this reason, the main impact this will have in the short term is likely that many of the front concrete bunkers of the AFU will no longer be as safe as they were before. That is the short version, if you want a real look into what these bombs actually are stick around. The above was destroyed with FAB-500 not FAB-3000. Arguably this is far more impressive than most of the screenshots and videos of the FAB-3000. The reason is because there were 4 FAB-500s above. But wait, 4 FAB-500, that’s like 2000kg of bomb, while 1 FAB-3000 is 3000kg of bomb, shouldn’t that destroy 50% more? No, you see, explosive power is not linear. What does this mean? Well for example 500kg of TNT would produce an incident pressure of around 10 PSI at 100m from detonation site. While 1500kg of TNT would produce an incident pressure of around 18 PSI at 100m from the detonation site. 300% more TNT gives you just 80% more pressure at 100m. Pressure is what collapses buildings, and is the most notable effect of bombs on video. 500kg of TNT creates 18 psi at 70m. So by this logic, if we want to cover an area with 18 PSI blast waves of TNT. 3 bombs with 500kg of TNT could cover an area of 46,000m2 while 1 bomb with 1500kg could cover an area of just 31,000m2. So you can see despite being the same amount of bomb, the more but smaller bombs is actually better at destroying something by area. However, there is more to this, this is just the primary blast effect. We also have the secondary blast effect, we can call this kinetic penetration using delivery body, or we can call it shrapnel. The Bombs are encased in steel, the FAB-3000 has only 1400kg of explosive filler, the rest is steel. When the bomb explodes the steel casing tends to go flying with an initial velocity of about 2,300m/s if my calculations using HMX is right. I know it’s more difficult to see on a still, but if you look below, you can see smoke and dust come out of this building on the eastern side, it is also quite apparent coming out on the western side of the building on the left. That’s not a incident pressure, that is fragmented steel traveling through a dusin layers of wall, and creating additional impact shrapnel through each wall inside those rooms. This building is still standing, but the inside is completely shredded, though this is not so obvious from the air. Finally, we have the ODAB variant. The thermobaric variants give up the ability to create a lot of high penetration shrapnel, in favor of creating a bigger pressure zone, and also adding an incendiary and non-linear direction of effect. That means, that the ODAB variants, tend to generate almost twice as big zones of destruction as their conventional RDX/HMX based counter parts, some thermobaric compounds are alleged to be 4 times more powerful than TNT (C-4 is 1.6 times more powerful). These bombs spread an explosive aerosol over an area then detonates it, this has the massive advantage that the aerosol can get inside buildings and other areas like bunkers or buildings, before detonating. This exponentially increases their ability to demolish, as well as almost guaranteeing termination of all life in the area, no matter what kind of cover is provided. No ODAB-3000 exists as far as I am aware. Due to their function thermobaric explosives scale a lot better than conventional ones do, and can cover massive areas with their aerosols if there is enough of it. The Russian FOAB would probably be an ODAB-7000, at this scale the FOAB allegedly provides the power of 44t of TNT, which is twice as much as the Davy Crocket mini nuclear weapon. Let’s hope we don’t see the use of such weapons.

Name: Carl Hamilton
Question: How important was it for the USSR and Germany to win at Stalingrad? If they lost the battle, couldn't the Soviets, with their larger population, resources & aid from USA have eventually defeated the Germans?
Answer: Couldn’t you say the same for every city? Every time they retreated to a new position, they lost people, material and industry. When did the Soviet arrive at the point where no more retreat was viable? Stalingrad? Vladivostok? The thing is that many people actually thought this. The problem is that while USSR was vast, the majority of everything was in the west, the areas which Germany was taking and occupying was the prime real estate of the USSR. In fact by the time of Stalingrad, Stalin issued the famous Order 227, colloquially known as “Not One Step Back” This is part of the text of Order 227, I think it is a very relevant primary source for the attitude as perceived by the Soviet Government at least, I doubt this would have been made if there wasn’t something to it. Some stupid people at the front calm themselves with talk that we can retreat further to the east, as we have a lot of territory, a lot of ground, a lot of population and that there will always be much bread for us. They want to justify the infamous behaviour at the front. But such talk is a falsehood, helpful only to our enemies. Each commander, Red Army soldier and political commissar should understand that our means are not limitless. The territory of the Soviet state is not a desert, but people – workers, peasants, intelligentsia, our fathers, mothers, wives, brothers, children. The territory of the USSR which the enemy has captured and aims to capture is bread and other products for the army, metal and fuel for industry, factories, plants supplying the army with arms and ammunition, railways. After the loss of Ukraine, Belarus, Baltic republics, Donetzk, and other areas we have much less territory, much fewer people, bread, metal, plants and factories. We have lost more than 70 million people, more than 800 million pounds of bread annually and more than 10 million tons of metal annually. Now we do not have predominance over the Germans in human reserves, in reserves of bread. To retreat further – means to waste ourselves and to waste at the same time our Motherland. J. Stalin Nr. 227, July 28, 1942 Contrary to popular belief, the public orders of Stalin was never a simple “do this”. The orders came with explanations for why they were being implemented, and the “not one step back” is a suggested slogan, not the actual legal part of the text. It was necessary to stop Germany, and Stalingrad really was one of the last lines of defense, it was an important component in keeping the Soviet oil fields, and it was an important industrial city. Could they have won anyway? Probably, but at a higher cost, and the cost was already too high.

Name: Carl Hamilton
Question: If UK & France immediately launched a major offensive after the Axis invaded Poland in 1939, would Germany have been defeated? Also, would the USSR have kept the part of Poland it had occupied?
Answer: Without a doubt Germany would have been defeated. Had the pressure been immediate the Germans would likely have defeated Poland swiftly anyway, but following this, they would have had to move their troops to counter western allied major offensive operations. Even if they succeeded in such a massive strategic move, they would without a doubt have been attacked in the rear by opportunistic Soviet forces. Facing a 2 front war, with far less resources on unfavorable conditions, the German military would almost certainly have been crushed in 1939 between the British, French and Soviet Forces, and without Italian help. The Soviets would likely keep their territory, as the western allies might indeed concede that those territories were in fact Belarus and Ukraine, and not wanting to make that into an issue that could start another war against the Soviet Union immediately after defeating the Germans.

Name: Carl Hamilton
Question: At some point in WWII, the USSR & Germany were going to break their non-aggression pact & fight. Why didn't the Soviets attack the Germans while they were preoccupied with the Battle of France in 1940?
Answer: That’s a fine question with quite a lot of facets to it. The premise you should be aware of is that Soviet intelligence were aware of German plans to invade the USSR in 1938, and they began a massive program of weapon modernization and army expansion. There is this meme that the USSR always had a massive army, but this is not the case. In 1930 before the rise of Nazism, the USSR maintained an army of 500,000 soldiers + a territorial militia. In 1933 the Nazis came to power and immediately began expanding their military. The Soviets responded by increasing their own force to 900,000 troops, and 1,300,000 in 1936, to roughly 3 million in 1939. However, the expansion goal of the Red Army, was roughly 6 million troops with the possibility to increase to 12 million. By 1940 this was not nearly accomplished, Soviet fighting in 1939 had revealed many weaknesses including a lack of trained officers, due to the rapidly expanding size of the military. New officers could not be trained nearly as fast as they were needed. The Red Army only reached their actual army size goal in 1943. An even worse version of this problem was faced by the USA when they expanded from 189,000 soldiers in 1939 to 3 million in 1942. The Soviets had attempted to build anti-German alliances with France, the UK, Poland and Czechoslovakia in the 1930s, but only the Czechoslovakians proved reliable, and were in turned betrayed by the others. By 1939 the Soviets were convinced they would have to fight Germany alone, but were not ready at all. As such while trying to finish their expansion and reform, they desperately wanted more time, which led to the Molotov pact, and later rather desperate attempts to delay a war with Germany. The Soviets had estimated that the war against France would probably last 4 years, but at least a couple, and figured they would be ready in 1942 or 1943 at the latest for an attack on Germany, preferably while they were still fighting France. The Soviets were not any less shocked than the rest of the world when France fell in manner of weeks instead of years. But it was too late, the Soviet reform had already begun, new weapons and formations were being introduced across the board, and many units were lacking officers who they had figured could be trained in the next 2 years. When the Soviet Union was invaded in 1941, it did not have what it wanted, which was a 6+ million strong army fully equipped with SVT-40 semi auto rifles, fully equipped with T-34s and KV-1s, and an air force with the new series of planes Yak-1 and IL-2. Some of these things would come in WW2, about 1943 in fact. This is why they didn’t just attack in 1940.

Question: What did the Nazi Party do for the German economy?
Answer: Though several parties can take credit for this project ultimately the Nazis were chief architects of some of the most rapid and extensive urban renewal projects in German history. Some of their plans had extremely long term economic implications, for example the effects of Nazism on Dresden provided work as late as 2005 for work on the renewal of Frauenkirche. Result oriented analysis of the work of the Nazi Party is a long process and one could explain it with a thousand more words, but I think it can be summoned up in a picture as the saying goes.

Name: Carl Hamilton
Question: If Soviet Russia couldn't defeat Poland in 1921 or Finland in 1939-40, how was the USSR able to defeat Germany & its Axis allies in 1945 during WWII?
Answer: In 1920 Soviet Russia, were not just fighting Poland. They were fighting a whole host of people, including the white Russian army. Poland did not fight the Red Army, Poland fought a fraction of it. The Red Army peaked at 5.5 million strong in the Russian civil war, at its peak the Polish fought around 900,000. This was still a very large force and the Polish managed extremely well, never the less had they fought the entire force of the Red Army they would have lost without question. As for Finland, as others have already pointed out, the Soviet Union won. Finnish nationalists very often control the narrative around this to the point that some people think they won. They did not, Finland lost and surrendered their territory. The story presented usually revolved around the failures of Kliment Voroshilov in 1939, and totally ignores that when Semyon Timoshenko became the commander of the Red Army in Finland, he assumed command on the 7th of January after just 3 weeks of planning, the Soviets attacked the Mannheim-line, which completely broke in 10 days of fighting, with a general retreat order for the Finnish coming in on the 15th of February, 2 weeks later the Finnish surrendered on Soviet terms. Again, the Finish fought only a fraction of the actual Red Army. The Axis in WW2, fought the entirety of the Soviet military machine, and a totally mobilized war economy. The fights with the Finish and Polish were not even important to the USSR. The lack of success in Finland initially resulted from incompetent commanders who were replaced, and an underestimation of the Finnish determination and skill. Once this was rectified a victory was quickly achieved. Germany and the Axis powers were much larger challenge that required every ounce of effort from the USSR and even so was a victory acquired as extremely loss in both blood and material.

Name: Carl Hamilton
Question: Are you upset that Ubisoft didn't add a Japanese man in Assassin's Creed: Shadows?
Answer: Not at all, I think that’s the least of the problems with the game, or rather it’s perfectly inline with what Assassin’s Creed is. It shows the total disregard for trying to get the setting right that Ubisoft has. Yasuke could easily have been done in a smarter way too, becoming samurai warrior in the less than 2 years Yasuke was in Japan is silly from a training point of view, and they could simply have made him an accomplished warrior already without making him Samurai, something that would make sense since they include Portuguese weapons and people, he could have been a gun specialist for example. So, honestly, Yasuke being the protagonist is not as bad as the fact that they butcher him as a historical person, they butcher Akechi, Oda and likely every other historical character as well, they’ll butcher the setting and they’ll get the culture wrong. In the grand scheme of things, it’s a minor thing, Assassin’s Creed series stopped being historically interesting to me about the time they ended the second one.

Name: Carl Hamilton
Question: Can you provide a comparison of German and Soviet losses (in terms of men and materials) during the Battle of Kursk?
Answer: This is far more difficult than it might initially seem to actually say. The first problem is that the two sides do not agree on when the battle of Kursk actually was. The Germans write that operation Citadel lasted until the 16th of July 1943, but the Soviet records show that defensive operations lasted until the 23rd. Wikipedia and other popular places, do not do a lot to make this clear unless you read the small footnotes. According to Soviet records (Krivosheev) the Soviets had 1,614 tanks and SPG guns destroyed or damaged during the defense of Kursk, Jonathan House and David Glantz wrote that the Germans had 323 tanks actually destroyed. Newer history books (which I have not read sadly) puts the number as 1,612 tanks destroyed and damaged. We have pretty detailed information of various Soviet armor group losses, but I was not able to find a list of completely destroyed tanks for the entire operation. However, the 5th guards tank army is probably pretty good indication. This was the tank army involved in the famous Battle of Prokhorovka, where the 5th Guards engaged the elite 2nd SS Panzer Corps, with the divisions Das Reich, Totenkopf and Leibstandarte SS Adolf Hitler. Of the 615 tanks the army had on hand, 374 survived the battle undamaged (60%), 113 were completely destroyed (18.4%) and presumably the remaining were damaged to various degrees (21.6%). Considering that this battle represented the most intense tank on tank fight, it is reasonable to assume that Soviet tank losses were not greater in other instances. By the way in case you are wondering why there are more survived T-34s for 29th tank corps than was on hand, it is because there was a reorganization after the battle to make the 29th full strength at the expense of other T-34 units. The total dead Soviet soldiers in the defense of Kursk was 70,330 according to Soviet records, and over 100,000 wounded. The German losses for this period is often said to be 11,000 KIA and MIA, but I have some severe trouble believing this. First of all, 6,3:1 in loss exchange is to begin with quite astounding, and it’s actually about the KD rate they were achieving during the absolute best days of operation Barbarossa. Which seems really odd, as the Germans were resoundingly defeated. From what I can gather, 3.2 million Germans were at the eastern front in July 1943, by October that had been reduced to 2.6 million Germans. Take into account that Germany mobilized nearly 2 million people in 1943 for the army. This is according to W. Victor Madeja from the book “The Russo-German War”. Call me crazy, but I find that Germany has an uncanny ability to lose 600,000 people between major known battles, but also take absolutely minimal casualties during one of the greatest battles in history. If Germany actually had the average KD ratio they claim of 5–7 the Soviet military losses in WW2, should be 21.5 million to 30 million. Yet it’s actual military losses were 11.2 of which only 8.7 were actually combat casualties. A ratio of 2:1 provided we pretend that no other Axis soldier than Germans existed.

Name: Carl Hamilton
Question: How does Germany honor the Soviet troops who liberated them from Nazism?
Answer: Germany has honored to near perfection their commemorations to Soviet troops who fought in WW2, most prominently the memorial in Tiergarten Berlin to the 80,000 soldiers who died in the Battle for Berlin. Germany has an official treaty with Russia and previously the Soviet Union, to honor the dead of WW2, and continues to do so no matter the political relations. The German governments of either political persuasion in Germany, has refused all attempts to vandalize or remove aspects or the entirety of these important war memorials, which has seen uninterrupted service as sites of commemoration since 1945. Additionally, I would say that Germany tends to have a less actively hostile attitude in their teaching of history, than many other western countries do, when it comes to the USSR. It’s not that they are above bias, but from my dealings with German teachers, historians and people who received an education there, I think they tend to have a reasonably sober view of the past in general. The most vehement voices suggesting that people were not liberated from Nazism by the Soviets rarely seems to come from Germans, but instead tends to be from those countries that suffered the least in WW2. Indeed, this view is probably heavily linked with poor understanding about what happened in countries occupied by Nazis, or a sympathy for the activities of Nazis in some weird cases.

Name: Carl Hamilton
Question: As WW2 wound down, did the Allied western nations consider an invasion of USSR, using surrendering Germans as frontline troops? Would this have been possible? Successful? If successful, what are the pros/cons of a newly occupied USSR?
Answer: No such a plan would almost certainly not have succeeded, but maybe not for the reasons which is commonly said. It is not simply that there were a lot of Soviet troops, there certainly was. The Soviets had 228 divisions against the western allied 80. Though Soviet divisions were about 17% smaller than US divisions. But I think there are several other considerations than merely the operational superiority of Soviet forces. In 1945, communism was at or close to it’s peak global popularity. It had just defeated Nazism, and unlike today, this was pretty much undisputed at the time. Communists were slated to win elections in places like France and Italy, and Labour did win in Great Britain. Western countries were rightfully scared of the massive backing communism and the USSR enjoyed from their own populations. If an attack on the USSR had been made, it would be betraying a current ally in the worst of ways, and most people would have been quite upset over this, not just the communists. But you could have expected revolutionary conditions in England and Soviet agents would quickly, and quite effectively no doubt stoke flames even in the USA. Another argument made, is that the a tactical victory would be possible thanks to nukes. This is false. The plan for operation unthinkable was made in May 1945, the first nuclear test was in mid July 1945, and the actual bombs for use were not ready until August 1945. So the surprise attack would have been conducted without nukes. Additionally, 2 nukes would have very little tactical impact on the battlefield, it would however have massive repercussions politically. Not only have you betrayed your ally, but you have resorted to the most horrific weapon ever seen and begun a campaign of instant genocide? Good luck selling that to your civilian population after 4–6 years of some of the worst warfare the world had ever seen. That is of course, if the bombers weren’t just shot down. It should be remembered that the US nuclear bombs were dropped on undefended cities. The Soviets had radars and 12,000 tactical aircraft in central Europe alone. That’s a pretty big difference.

Name: Carl Hamilton
Question: During the Cold War, just like how people in the Eastern Bloc emigrated to the Western Bloc to escape communism, were there also some people who emigrated from the Western Bloc to the Eastern Bloc to escape capitalism?
Answer: It is information which is quite difficult to search for, but it did indeed happen. From Denmark, Martin Andersen Nexø decided to move to East Germany in 1951, where he lived in Dresden until he died in 1954 (Age 84). He is probably the second most famous Danish author after H.C. Anderson, and his book Pelle Eroberen, is the most translated Danish work after Anderson as well, it is also a great book in my opinion by the way. It was made into a movie as well where no other than Max von Sydow plays one of the title roles (The priest from the exorcist, Blofeld from James Bond) Ollie Harrington, a famous American cartoonist and civil rights activist moved to East Germany in 1961 after his friend Richard Wright died. Harrington suspected that the US government were targeting black US civil rights advocates for assassination, he lived in East Germany until his death in 1995. Wolfgang Gans zu Putlitz an active anti-nazi resistance member before WW2, and British spy, and witness at the Nuremberg trials, defected to East Germany in 1954 out of disgust for the West German establishment and their rehabilitation of Nazi warcriminals. Perhaps one of the most famous cases is Ursel Lorenzen, a secretary at the NATO HQ from 1966 to 1979 passed essentially all NATO battle plans to the Soviet Union and defected to East Germany in 1979. Her whereabouts to this date is unknown. These are just some examples, generally speaking the USSR did not encourage obvious defection in the same way the west did. The west literally paid people to leave the Eastern Bloc countries and would take just about anyone for the propaganda victory. The Soviet approach was vastly different, they preferred their agents to stay inside western countries and collect data. The people defecting to the USSR tended to stay put, and work for the ideological course undercover. The Soviet spy network was well known to be vast, it included the Cambridge five, which were a British spy ring that were top placed in Mi5, and other very embarrassing positions. Those cultured enough have seen “Yes Minister” will remember Bernard saying: Well if I know it, I am sure the Russians know it. The Kremlin usually gets NATO defense information before it filters to us at Number 10 (British Prime Minister residence)

Name: Carl Hamilton
Question: Was Hitler just imitating Russia? Or did Germany also have a long history of genocidal wars of aggression?
Answer: Not at all, Hitler absolutely hated Russia, the Soviets, Marxists, Communism and considered the entire country to be secretly run by Jews, all of which he makes perfectly clear in his book Mein Kampf. There was however a country, which had racial laws very similar to Germany and was literally founded on genocidal wars of aggression. Let me furnish you with a quote from the American lawyer and historian of compartive legal history at Yale, James Q. Whitman’s book Hitler's American Model: The United States and the Making of Nazi Race Law: It is hard to admit the continuities between Nazism and the postwar European orders that replaced it. No one wants to be perceived as relativizing Nazi crimes… Nazism was not simply a nightmarish parenthesis in history that bore no relationship to what came before and after; nor was it a completely unexampled racist horror… The Nazis found examples and precedents in the American legal race order that they valued highly, while simultaneously deploring, and puzzling over, the strength of the liberal countercurrent in a country with so much openly and unapologetically sanctioned racism. We can, and should, reject the sort of simple-minded anti-Americanism that blames the United States for all the evils of the world, or reduces America to nothing but its history of racism. But there is no excuse for refusing to confront hard questions about our history, and about the history of American influence abroad. The Nazis had an idea of blood purity and race mixing, which was passed into law in 1934, indeed, the term “mischlinge” means “mixling”, and referred to mixed race people. This Blood Purity law and Race Mixing concept were taken directly from American laws. Not only is it obvious that it was, this is specifically mentioned multiple times in Nazi discussions in 1933 and 1934. US Senator Theodore Bilbo, said that “one drop of Negro blood placed in the veins of the purest Caucasian destroys the inventive genius of his mind and palsies his creative faculty”, the Nazis considered the One-drop rule too extreme. In 30 out of the 48 US states at this time, considered any marriage between blacks and whites, to be legally invalid, and combine this with 9 US states adopted the one drop rule verbatim, and another 8 states adopted it in practice. Virginia declared in the 1930s that more than 1/16th native American ancestry meant you were legally not white. Question: What makes the Soviet Union's T-34 tank superior to Germany's Tiger tank?

People meme that means that the Soviets threw hordes of T-34s at individual Tigers, the reality is that T-34s mostly faced: No tanks. Because if you have 43 tanks, and they have 1 tank, even if it is better, you can just attack where they have no tank. In 1943–1944 the length of the eastern front was roughly 3,000km. In june 1944, there were 241 operational Tigers for the eastern front. If you spread out every tiger, along the front, you’d still only have 1 Tiger op 12.4 kilometers, and since they actually grouped them in battalions of 45 and at minimum a company of 15 Tigers, you’d in reality have at best a tiger present every 200km of front, but you would have 3 T-34s for every single kilometer of front. This means at that only 1 out of 200 T-34s even faced Tigers. So it absolutely didn’t matter if the Tiger was better on paper. A tank which is so rare, it is not present on 99.5% of the front, might as well not even exist. It just has no impact on the outcome of the war. A tank that is present everywhere, all the time, every day and in great numbers. That is how a war is won.

Question: Where did the Germans send most of their tanks between the Western and Eastern front in 1944, specifically after D-day?
Answer: Overwhelmingly it was the eastern front, but we can go into details about this. Prepare for statistics. I happen to have researched this quite recently in the German Federal Archives. The answer to this lies in the Quartermaster General’s bi monthly reports on the tank inventories of the German military. Unfortunately the German archives appears to be incomplete on this, so there is going to be some holes in the information, but as luck have it, one of the complete reports is from 15th of June 1944, and we can continue until November 1944. The Germans had allocated 35% of their tanks to the Eastern front between the two by June 15th, which was about 9 days after D-day. However, operation Bagration began on the 22nd of June 1944, and in the following months the Germans chose to maintain the number of tanks on the eastern front, at the expense of dropping numbers of available tanks on the western front. By November the ratio of tanks had shifted from 1.8:1 on the eastern front to the western front, to 5 tanks on the eastern front per tank on the western front. A pretty dramatic shift. This would change again in the next few weeks as a massive amount of tanks were transferred to the western front for the German Ardennes offensive. And I could do a separate answer on that. But for France the answer is clear, the Germans still massive prioritized the eastern front, even after D-day and as time went on this emphasis only increased. But while I have my research open, I can share some more data with you. The German Federal Archives, have details which includes operational and in repair states for the vehicles. I don’t think this is particularly conclusive, but perhaps it is interesting to some the slight difference in tank availability between the eastern and the western fronts at certain times. More interestingly perhaps, is that in November in general, the German availability had gone from 82–86% of tanks operational, to 73–74%. I anticipate some questions so I shall answer them for everyone in general. What exactly does the western front and eastern front include? The Western Front in this case is quite specifically the German Oberbefehlshaber West (OB West), which includes France, Netherlands, Belgium, Luxembourg and reserves in Western Germany. It does not include Italy, which is called OB Southwest. It was a separate theater, along with South East (Yugoslavia - included on the eastern front ) and Denmark-Norway. Finally you have the 4 Army groups of the Eastern front, North, Center, South and A. Army Group A was located around Hungary. How does this take into account tank losses and transfers? The data includes transfers, but this is quite unreliable, because the transfers are merely plans to send things, and they changed quite often. For example, on the 15th of September 617 tanks were planned to transfer to the western front, while 575 were planned for the east, but just 2 weeks later this plan was changed to 374 tanks for the west and 830 tanks to the east. In some data points, there is hand written correction made as well, as less tanks were produced than anticipated and adjustments had to be made. So in reality, the amount of tanks actually arriving, was rarely what was planned, so this data is not as useful as actual counts in the field. What you should consider is that the Germans were taking massive losses in tanks on both the eastern and the western front, the number of tanks on the eastern front, actually didn’t drop despite the entire Army Group center basically getting annihilated, while the tanks on the western front dropped significantly. This indicates that reinforcements were prioritized to the east. Does this take into account StuGs, SP Artillery or Tank Destroyers? This data counts StuGs as tanks, I cannot be bothered to make some differentiation between assault guns and tanks as separate categories. SP Artillery and Tank Destroyers are not counted, that includes things like the Hetzer, which arguably is kinda a StuG. I do have data on this, it follows the same trend. I don’t know why this was counted in completely separate reports by the Germans, but it was, and the data is more incomplete and for different dates as well. Do you have data on specific tank type deployments? Yes, ask and I will see what I can do. I might post some expanded data over time on my blog Critical Thinking here on Quora later.

There is a cognitive bias which sounds fairly similar to Mark Twain’s quote, which is called anchoring. This cognitive bias makes it so that a person is more likely to believe what they already know to be true. This applies to everyone, whether western or not. You also have belief bias and confirmation bias, both of which are psychological states, which makes people prefer to look for evidence which confirms their beliefs, or rationalize away contradictory evidence. In short, there are cognitive biases, which would make Mark Twain’s quote make sense, though it’s better to understand how this work, rather than a common off hand proverb. Question: What factors contributed to the effectiveness of the Red Army during World War II, despite their lack of equipment and training compared to the Axis forces?
Answer: The Red Army did not lack neither training or equipment relative to the Axis forces. Before we talk about the actual strengths, let us talk about the area in which they were weak. They lacked experience, and Germany did not. The German high command were generally experienced officers from WW1, at by the time of the Soviet invasion, German officers and indeed most of their standing army, had at least actual combat experience. Most German officers had 2 years of command experience in real military campaigns in Poland, Denmark, Norway, Netherlands, Belgium, France and Yugoslavia. Some even had additional experience from Spain. In 4 days in 1944, the Soviets moved 2 entire Army groups 220km from Vitebsk to Minsk, this included winning several medium sized Urban battles, bigger than the battle of Caen which took 2 months. The average speed was 55km per day. In contrast, the majority of Soviet officers were relatively new, though the few who were experienced also tended to do relatively well, for example Zhukov had gained experience fighting the Japanese and famously was no push over. The state of the Soviet officer corps, experience and such is a larger topic than just “purges happened”, you can always request I answer a question about this in detail. The effectiveness of the Red Army however came from a combination of multiple things. The first one was combat equipment. The Red Army was probably the most appropriately equipped military by the end of WW2. Let me just clarify, that the US military had the best access to resources, they could essentially get what they wanted, it’s just that they lacked the experience to design or request what they actually needed in many cases. The Soviets had the opposite problem, they often knew exactly what they needed, and WW2 was a struggle to produce enough of that. An example being they had the most automatic hand weapons of any army, with about 8 million sub machine guns produced during the war. They also had the highest concentration of artillery, the most mobile artillery and the most heavy tanks. Another significant factor, is the Soviet logistics, which were exceptionally good. This isn’t just a matter of having trucks, indeed crossing swamps is not greatly aided by trucks, no matter their quality. Soviet logistics were often horse based, as was German. The Soviets were however, very good at calculating correctly the necessary allocation, which meant their offensives were very well planned logistically, and executed very expertly. During operation Bagration, Soviet armies advanced on average 15km per day (55km per day in the opening period). Consider that during about the same time, The US Third Army under George Patton, advanced from Avranches to Argentan, which is 97 kilometers, in 2 weeks. That is an average of 6.93 km per day. The Soviets advanced more than twice as fast with predominantly horses, than Pattons fully mechanized group could manage, against 4 times denser German forces in Belarus which is characterized by dense forests and swamps. This is ridiculously fast for an opposed advance. In my opinion, the appropriate equipment, and the ability to logistically employ it at the exact necessary ratios across the front, is what made the Red Army in the later part of WW2 so effective. But of course there are endless aspects to this.

Question: What are the three shades of propaganda in psychological warfare?
Answer: The shades of propaganda refers to how overt the sender is. White propaganda, is propaganda in which the sender is obvious and does not try to hide themselves. This is most commonly seen as posters, music and leaflets. For example, below is a screenshot of Russian leaflets dropped in propaganda shells, which distributes instructions for surrender over an area. It is clearly Russian as it is watermarked, the video itself is also white propaganda, as it has the symbols of the Russian government clearly identifying the sender. Grey propaganda, is propaganda where the sender is unclear, thereby making it difficult to gauge the motivation and purpose of the propaganda. The most common form of this is through sponsored content, traditionally by funding movies with the message the sender wants, while hiding behind profit incentives to disguise their true propaganda motives. In the current age, this is still done, but it is heavily supplanted by grey internet campaigns, examples of this include censoring or promoting content on platforms such as Quora, Youtube, Google, Twitter etc. It also includes the editing of Wikipedia, or posting direct content on any social media platform pretending to be neutral or public figures. I believe the UK is the only ones who admit to directly manipulating like this through their Grey/Black propaganda unit 77th Brigade. Black propaganda, is propaganda in which the sender disguising themselves as an enemy in order to discredit them by making overt propaganda under a false name. This is often aimed at very gullible people, and tends to be very crude. For example, writing “We the Jews will molest all your daughters” in graffiti on a wall, then taking a picture of it and uploading it to social media, as if this message came from Jews, is about as brain dead simple as it gets. More sophisticated ones would be to make recruitment campaigns on behalf of the enemy which suck, or potentially create false documents then leak it as if it came from the enemy. Notice, that while I give examples, the actual methods of how to make propaganda work is not directly linked to the shade of propaganda, though some methods are more suited for some shades than others. Propaganda can be truthful, misleading or outright lies, but the shade of propaganda is about the honesty of the sender, and should be viewed independently from the message and method.

Question: Did the Soviet Union use de Havilland Mosquito during WWII? How about its performance compared with Petylyakov Pe-2?
Answer: The Soviet Union operated a single de Havilland Mosquito for testing purposes. The Mosquito arrived in early 1944. The Soviets were impressed at the ingenuity of wooden construction methods of the Mosquito, they thought that the Mosquito woodwork was equivalent to the Soviets, which was considered a praise as many Soviet planes were already build with wood. Performance wise they considered the Mosquito superior to the Pe-2 and Tu-2 planes. The Mosquito was able to carry a larger bomb load, at a greater range, and it was noted to have better flight characteristics at high altitude than the Pe-2. However, longitudinal instability and weaker rudders compared to Soviet aircraft, meant the plane was more difficult to control, particularly for newer pilots. Indeed the test mosquito seen above, crashed on landing at the institute of air research in the USSR, despite being flown by a very experienced test pilot who had received training in Scotland. Soviet analysis indicated that the performance advantage of the Mosquito did not come from radical design, as much as very high quality in materials and manufacturing. The Soviets were impressed with the plane and did consider making it under license, but they decided against it for the following reasons. As such, it just didn’t make sense to start production of a plane, that would be far worse than it’s original specs due to inferior wood and likely poorer engines as well, and only to have them be produced in the last few months of the war. The Soviets were overall impressed with it though, and did consider it better performing than the Pe-2 and Tu-2.

This is a long winded way, of saying that actually quite a lot of different fates awaited those in the Red Army. Name: Carl Hamilton
Question: After its defeat at Stalingrad in early 1943, why did Germany attack the salient at Kursk? Would it have been a better strategy to stay on the defensive to slow the Soviet advance on the Russian Front?
Answer: Germany were not in World War 2 to stalemate, they were in it to win it. During 1941 and 1942 Germany had successfully cut off Soviet salients, and destroyed the contents. While the 1942 summer offensive was not as successful the initial attacks in 1941, experience seemed to indicate that the Soviets were not very good at defensive tactics above the divisional level, and that the path for making large gains was the wholesome destruction of a large concentration of Soviet troops. Had the Germans won Kursk they might have destroyed 5 Soviet armies. As you can see, the Kursk salient was ripe for such an attempt geographically. This was the last chance Germany had at finishing their original plan, to destroy the Red Army in the field before advancing. However, in the meantime the Soviets had totally revamped their defensive tactics, and now operated with strong points, defense in depth up to 8 kilometers for divisions, with corp level defensive sectors, and a sophisticated fortification system. Additionally, the Germans estimated the Soviets were exhausted, and completely discounted the Soviet concentration at Orel, which would launch a major counter offensive into the side of the German forces. If the Germans had not attacked, the Orel offensive would have happened anyway, and probably with very similar results. Germany was defeated in 1943, they just didn’t know it yet.

Name: Carl Hamilton
Question: Has Russia ever fought Poland without Germany? And if they did how did it go?
Answer: Russia and Poland has fought many times. The result ultimately was the total destruction of Poland, until it was revived after World War 1. If you want to go with Russia proper against Poland, then we can start from 1568 with the Livonian war, though the Polish did little fighting, as Russia mostly fought against Scandinavia and Lithuania. From my count they have had 20 wars between them which did not include Germany proper, including 1 as the Soviet Union. “Prayer of the Bar Confederation before the battle of Lanckorona" Painting by Artur Grottger Of these Russia won 13 of the wars, including the one which saw the first partition of Poland, which did not actually result of German intervention though Prussia and Austria received territory, but resulted as the consequence of Poland declaring war on Russia and losing in the war of the Bar Confederation (1768-1772). Likewise the second partition of Poland came as a result of failed reforms in Poland, which angered the magnates of Poland. They formed the Targowica Confederation in opposition to the Sejim and asked for Catherine the Great of Russia to intervene in the conflict on their side. This became the second partition of Poland. Just 2 years after, Tadeusz Kościuszko tried to reverse the course by attacking the partitioning powers, primarily Russia, which resulted in the removal of Poland from the map as they predictably also lost the third time. Though you can discount this one if you think Prussia and Germany is the same thing. Either way, there were more Polish victories in the early conflicts, by the but from 1654 Russia won every single war with Poland, except the Soviet-Polish war, but they reversed that defeat 20 years later. In short, the wars with Poland in the past 350 years, have always gone well for Russia. .

Name: Carl Hamilton
Question: Are war games a good way to prepare for an actual war?
Answer: Yes, war games are an excellent tool for training for war. War games when done right, are able to simulate very accurately many decisions made by officers at all kinds of level. They can simulate technology, economy, intelligence, imperfect orders, delay, command structures, political objectives and team work between officers. And this is probably exactly why war games are played by military officers. I wrote a PhD proposal to introduce war games as a form of teaching and studying international relations to students at universities in Denmark, unfortunately no one was interested in this. But I would maintain it remains a great combination of game theory and simulation with human elements. We know from WW2, that wargamers could in real time simulate combat scenarios like those faced by British convoys, and anticipate the moves of German submarines and then radio back solutions to British destroyers. Do not underestimate the power of simulating scenarios before trying them in real life.

Name: Carl Hamilton
Question: During WWII, if Germans had attacked the Kursk salient in May 1943 before the Soviets had fortified the area, would it have been successful?
Answer: If the Germans had attacked earlier there would have been fewer Soviet fortifications. There would also have been fewer Germans. There would have been far fewer German tanks, and practically no Panthers. The terrain would still have been muddy, and it’s not like the Soviets didn’t have any fortifications at all. The Germans would still have been hit by a massive counter attack, and unlike in the real scenario, they would also have been fighting against the mud season of the area getting stuck horribly. Attacking sooner would not really have yielded many advantages to the Germans, which is why they didn’t. Despite all the memes about Hitler making every decision, the German military was aware that such an offensive would likely have failed.

Name: Carl Hamilton
Question: In World War 2, what’s were each allied power version of Stalingrad?
Answer: There is no battle in World War 2 for the western allied powers which comes even remotely close to Stalingrad in terms of scale, destruction or strategic significance in a single battle. The entire Normandy campaign which included USA, Canada, Free France and Great Britain caused 290,000 Axis casualties, including 23,000 dead, split between 4 countries. Stalingrad caused at minimum 800,000 Axis casualties, including 500,000 dead. You can fit the Normandy campaign inside Stalingrad in terms of actually dead Axis soldiers 22 times, and this was not split between several countries. In terms of losses, the 534,216 dead (796.634 if you include Caucasus) Soviet soldiers at Stalingrad is more than the 405,399 the US lost on all fronts in the entire war. Stalingrad isn’t just the single greatest battle in WW2, it is the greatest battle in all of human history. We should be very glad that Stalingrad was in fact such a singular moment in history, and that this was not the average battle. That the other allies never had to be in a similar situation was their incredibly good fortune.

Question: Are rumours that the Russians are planning another incursion further north near Sumy in Ukraine true? Will the Ukrainians prepare for this with defences or is it that they like surprises and will ignore the warnings as they did near Kharkov?
Answer: It seems a distinct possibility that the Russians will indeed go for Sumy at some point, several things point to this. Question: How can I apply Marxism in the study of international organizations?
Answer: If you know Marxism, it should be fairly simple. The most obvious application is to critique this organizations based on their class relationships and world systems theory. World systems theory explains things like which countries benefit from trade and which do not, by putting them into the categories of core countries and periphery countries, where value generally flows in the direction of core countries. We can ask, where are organizations like the IMF, World Bank and the UN headquarters located. Is this a coincidence? Who does it benefit that operations are taking place there? We can ask, the people who run these organizations what background do they have? Are they economists and lawyers? Are they over-represented by geography? The last one I can answer, yes they are. The UN for example has roughly 40% of it’s administrative staff being West European or American. We can ask, what kind of policy the international institutions lead, and who they benefit. Does it benefit the wealthy or the poor? Critique of structures is at the heart of Marxist theory, and international relations is no exception to that. Question: Which countries were allies of the Soviet Union during the Great Patriotic War?
Answer: In theory most of the world at the end of the war. The green are the allies of WW2, the bright green are those who entered the war after Pearl Habour, but not necessarily right after, like Argentina who only did so in 1945. The actually important allies of the Soviet Union was of course primarily The United States of America, and the United Kingdom, who provided the most direct military contribution and material support in the war for the Soviets. But there were other allies, notably Mongolia who despite not directly engaged in the war, provided significant support for the Soviets, particularly in the form of an extraordinary amount of horses, half a million approximately, to equip Soviet logistics and cavalry units. On top of this, Mongolian volunteers managed to fund the equipment of a tank brigade and an aircraft squadron. The population of Mongolia in 1941 was around 750,000. This meant that in practice every single Mongolian adult donated a horse to the war against Nazism. Today such a horse is probably 1000 to 3000 dollars. But considering this is per capita it’s quite a bit. Per capita the value of this was more than US lend-lease to the Soviets. And that is not even considering the cultural significance horses played in Mongolia at this time. I highlight this because I think Mongolia deserves recognition of how big of contribution this was compared to their population. Mongolia was indeed a very good ally to the Soviet Union.

Name: Carl Hamilton
Question: From Aug. 23, 1939 to June 21, 1941, could the USSR and Germany have been considered temporary allies? Since they signed the non-aggression pact, both invaded Poland, & provided each other with raw materials?
Answer: No, even if you go by the loosest definition of an alliance being when countries work together towards a mutual goal, rather than an official treaty declaring a military partnership in defensive or offensive wars. Neither was the case, though I can understand the confusion as this is a thing that is brought up very often, generally casually and almost always with no understanding of the meeting of the word or situation, this has caused a lot of people to say in casual context that it was an alliance. The Molotov-Ribbentrop pact, was one of many negotiations prior to the German active war phase, this was however not an alliance. It stipulated spheres of influence, though contrary to the above illustration, it did not stipulate an actual division, and further negotiations took place later. The Soviet invasion of Poland in 1939, was not requested nor coordinated with the Germans prior to the fighting, though of course some did take place to avoid a confrontation during the actual operations. The technical term for this is not alliance, but co-belligerent. They did not work together towards a common goal, they merely attacked the same country. Afterwards the Soviets and Germans did indeed trade. The phrasing “provided materials to each other” is a bit of a crazy one, you mean trade. Trade doesn’t make you an ally. America is trading with Russia right now, but I think you’d be hard pressed to think they are allies. 6% of Israel’s exports have traditionally been to Palestine, and they exported to Egypt and Turkey as well. Go tell them they are allies because they provide each other raw materials. Tell me how it goes. The reality of the Soviet German situation in 1939, was that Germany desperately did not want the USSR to enter the war either on the side of Poland or later with England and France, but needed to secure it’s western borders before fighting the USSR. What the USSR wanted was to avoid a fight where the UK and France would sit back and let the Soviets take all the losses of a massive war, and so they wanted to prepare for war with Germany and post pone it as long as possible, they figured that once they brought their industry to bear they would be able to beat Germany, and they figured that Germany fighting France would take at least 3–4 years. The problem was that the Soviets were completely wrong about how long France would hold, as was everyone else at the time. But there were no illusions in the USSR about a war with Germany, the Soviet intelligence service was aware of German invasion plans for the USSR from 1938, and the pact was made specifically to improve the strategic situation of the USSR, while reacquiring lands which had belonged to the Russian Empire without interference from Germany.

Name: Carl Hamilton
Question: In WWII, what was more dangerous- being in a U-boat during the Battle of the Atlantic, flying an Allied bomber over Germany, or fighting in the German-Soviet war?
Answer: German submarines had appalling casualty rates, out of the 40,900 submariners roughly 28,000 lost their lives in World War 2. And I dare say it wasn’t in very pleasant conditions either. Not that dying violently is generally a pleasant thing, but I do think that being in an underwater box with a 68.5% baseline chance of dying is pretty far up there in terms of psychological strains. In the British air force, out of the 125,000 aircrew who served in British bombers, 57,205 were killed in action. Resulting in a death rate of 46%, which is also an astronomical rate of loss. The American air forces in Europe suffered 26,000 deaths, out of 115,332 aircrew who served. This is a loss rate of 22.5%. Which is still a quite high loss rate but much less than the British. You might wonder why the British losses were that much higher. The answer is likely that the British undertook nighttime bombing in an attempt to reduce losses, but they actually suffered very high losses, not just some combat, but also from accidents which had a high rate. Nearly, half of all the US bombers lost were due to non-combat incidents. The British were likely even more. Additionally, it should be noted that since both countries had expanded their air force significantly, almost everyone in both were complete rookies with very little understanding of what they were doing. The US went from a core of 16,000 troops in the air force, to over 2.4 million in a matter of a few years, and in 1941 when they launched the Doolittle raid 100% of co pilots had graduated flight school less than 12 months ago. If we look at the ground forces of Germany and the Soviet Union, it is also pretty appalling. 25.1% of all Soviet troops in WW2 died in combat units. This is 29.1% for Germany, and 34.9% if we look only at the Waffen-SS. However, this comparison is a bit misleading, because for the German Soviets it is by branch, but for the bombers and submarines, it is a specific role inside a branch. For example US air force deaths were only 2.5% if you go by the entire branch. The front line forces of the Soviet Union in 1941, were a group larger than the entire US and British air forces combined. And they suffered 62% deaths in the first 3 months of the German invasion. In the next 3 months the Soviet ground forces would 33% deaths. And mind you this is of the entire branch strength lost, not just infantrymen for example. If you fought in the German 6th Army, your chance of dying was 98.1%. So under the specific conditions of the question, the most dangerous role was German submariners, followed by British bombers, then German ground forces. But if you go by operational units, there were instances of large combat units on the eastern front where your death was almost guaranteed on both sides.

Name: Carl Hamilton
Question: Why did Stalin choose not to attack Germany when it was weak and had no allies before the start of World War II?
Answer: The Soviet Union did not border Germany, so in order to attack Germany the Soviet Union would need allies to allow troops through and aid in a war. The reality however, was that the rest of Europe didn’t think Nazism was much of a problem, until it specifically attacked them. Had people worked with the Soviet Union they would have attacked Germany in 1937 in defense of Czechoslovakia. What follows is a long breakdown of the efforts of the Soviets to destroy Nazi Germany before WW2. Nerville Chamberlain with Hitler in 29th of September 1938 Of course there were warning cries, for example the French minister Louis Barthou, actually worked hard to make a military alliance with the USSR, but was assassinated in 1934. His successor Pierre Laval had to be forced by his own government, to finish setting up the Franco-Soviet Treaty of Mutual Assistance, after Germany had announced rearmament in 1935. His counter part in the USSR was Maxim Litvinov, the Soviet foreign minister, who strongly pursued improving relations with the rest, and making a large international anti-fascist alliance. Almost immediately after the French-Soviet treaty, the Soviets also guaranteed Czechoslovak independence, with the Czechoslovak–Soviet Treaty of Mutual Assistance, essentially forming an entente of defensive alliances. Germany used this as an excuse to re-militarize the Rhineland, saying they felt threatened by the new Soviet alliance with France. The French-Soviet alliance thanks to Pierre Laval was however practically useless, because of the conditions of the treaty. The treaty for example required the British to approve its actions, and the French refused to improve the situation with plans on how to coordinate military actions in case of war. By 1936 this treaty was understood as de-facto dead. And both Britain and France switched decisively to Nazi appeasement. From 1935 Litvinov was increasingly trying to take more extreme measures to contain the growing fascism in central Europe. The USSR had officially been supportive of the idea of national union based on ethnicity and identity, for example a unification of Germany and Austria. But since the Nazi take over Litvinov saw the threat of this becoming reality under Nazism, and pushed for something as fringe as a restoration of the Habsburg dynasty to Austria in an attempt to keep out the Germans. Actually Litvinov was teased by the American envoys in the USSR, who asked him where Marx or Lenin made justification for the restoration of a monarchy. Litvinov replied with “any procedure was justified which tended to maintain peace in Europe and peace for the Soviet Union."* In 1936, the Austrians noted that the Soviets had completely stopped badmouthing them, no longer calling them fascists, imperialists or vassals. And instead was pushing for collective security with Czechoslovakia. Unfortunately, Soviet public opposition did little to prevent the Anschluss from happening in 1938. The Soviets foresaw a great war erupting in Europe. Apart from building a massive armaments program which would ultimately save the USSR itself, it also attempted to a stronger alliance with Czechoslovakia, France and Great Britain, while trying to tie down potential German ally Japan by supplying China with materials. However, there was a major problem. While the Soviets in 1937–1938, had resources for massive expeditionary force of around 1 million soldiers, promised for Czechoslovakia, they had no border with it. The USSR needed to either be able to station a big army in France indefinitely, which they rejected outright, or go gain land access through either Romania or Poland to Czechoslovakia. Romania at this time was also fiercely anti-communist and partially influenced by the soon-to-be-in-power, fascist Iron Guard, and any negotiation with them would be fruitless. This left just Poland. In 1938 Poland had given Lithuania an ultimatum to give land to Poland (rarely mentioned in modern history books), Lithuania still upset that the Polish had stolen Vilnius, the Lithuanian capitol, during Soviet peace negotiations in 1921 still had no diplomatic relations. The Soviet Union essentially told Poland to withdraw their ultimatum or face immediately military action by the USSR. This worked, but the Polish land grabbing ambitions were not over, and their relationship with the USSR was terrible. In March 1938, the Czech ambassador to the USSR asked for assurance that the Soviet security guarantees of 1935 with Czechoslovakia still held, the Soviet Union said there could be no doubt that it did, but that it was the French they should be asking this, not the Soviets, as the French appeared set on working with Hitler. Litvinov in the mean time was trying to expand the security infrastructure to include Great Britain. But like the French, Great Britain was far more concerned about repressing poor people than fighting fascism, both countries made it illegal for volunteers to go to Spain to fight fascism, though many did anyway. Likewise France and Great Britain did nothing to prevent the Italian slaughter in Ethiopia taking place right next to their own colonies. Later that year, tensions increased around the German minority in Czechoslovakia. The Soviets were unable once again to secure any transit through Poland, who said they would actively resist any attempt to rescue Czechoslovakia from a German invasion. However, the Polish had also previously indicated they would be willing to help an attack on Germany provided the French committed to it. Rather than helping in solving the differences of Poland and the USSR, the French and British decided to betray the Czechoslovakians, and held the Munich conference in which they sold the Sudetenland part of the country to the Nazis. They invited the fascist Italians to this conference, but not the Soviets or even the Czechoslovakians. After Britain and France had sold even their own ally by treaty to the Nazis, the Soviets were extremely pessimistic, about any alliance with the western countries. In 1939 the remaining part of Czechoslovakia was annexed by Germany, and a last desperate attempt at an anti German alliance was made with Britain and France, who again did nothing to stop Germany. Litvinov who had spend nearly 10 years in futile attempts at approaching the west to make a European collective security alliance, fell out of favor. He was replaced with Vyacheslav Molotov in May of 1939. Molotov, very briefly carried on the negotiations, but was convinced that Britain and France, was in fact hoping for Germany and the USSR to destroy each other in a war. The Soviets had acquired intelligence of plans to invade the Soviet Union in 1938, and began serious preparations for it’s defense. Part of this was to create a larger buffer zone, and buy time, as they did not feel they were ready for an all our war with Germany on their own. This resulted in first the treaty with Germany dividing Poland, and later annexation of the Baltic and Bessarabia territories. The most strategically vulnerable position was considered to be Leningrad, and the USSR demanded a territory exchange with Finland to improve this. When Finland refused the Soviet fabricated an incident that provided them with a Casus Belli to take it by force. Having accomplished this by 1940, the Soviet Union began constructing the Molotov defense line. Seen below. The USSR estimated it would be ready by 1943, and thought that a German-French war would last at least several years considering the length of WW1. As you probably know, the Soviets were completely surprised and panicked when France gave up after just some weeks. There is little doubt that if the west had actually worked with Litvinov the Soviets would have treasured a two front assault on Germany any time after 1935. Instead Molotov’s defense by expansion prevailed, but this was after nearly 9 years of failed negotiations. Answer is based on the following references: *Alfred Low, 1980, The Soviet Union, the Austrian Communist Party, and the Anschluss Question, 1918-1938 Jonathan Haslam, 1979, The Soviet Union and the Czechoslovakian Crisis of 1938 Ian Kershaw, 2015, To Hell and Back - Europe 1914–1949 (I highly recommend this book in general) Michael Jabara Carley, 1993 End of the 'Low, Dishonest Decade': Failure of the Anglo-Franco-Soviet Alliance in 1939
