Name: Carl Hamilton
Question: If the Allies had not defeated the U-boats in May 1943, could the Soviets have continued advancing after their victory at Stalingrad without the lend lease supplies getting through?
Answer: The vast majority of lend-lease to the Soviets came through the Pacific ocean under Soviet flag, or through Iran. The lend-lease which passed the Atlantic on its way to Murmansk was the smallest amount. The defeating of German submarines had almost no impact on lend-lease to the Soviets, this was for the benefit of the United Kingdom and not much else. Convoys to Murmansk had a loss rate of less than 5%, so 95% survival chance was pretty good. Additionally, the Soviet offensives at Stalingrad and beyond never relied on lend-lease. Lend-lease made up a percentage of Soviet equipment. The most significant single item, was trucks, which by 1945, made up 32.8% of the used equipment in the war. Other categories were less significant, such as tanks which was less than 10% and food which was less than 1% of Soviet stocks. This should be considered in the context that most lend-lease was delivered after the battle of Kursk, so by the time of Stalingrad and Kursk, the Soviet Union was not receiving nearly as much lend-lease as they did later. Soviet offensives might not have been as fast in 1944 and 1945 as they were with lend-lease, but they would probably have happened anyway. Jonathan House and David Glantz estimated that without lend-lease the war might have dragged on another year, but the Soviets would likely have won anyway, but at a greater cost of course.

Name: Carl Hamilton
Question: Are Russian tanks really as bad as people say, or is it a Western-centric view on Tank warfare vs how the Russians see Tank Warfare? Is it corruption and lack of supplies that have hindered their tanks or just the tanks themselves?
Answer: Russian tanks are not as bad as they are portrayed in the west no. There is a prevalent idea that Russian tanks are easy to destroy, while western tanks are hard to destroy. This is not the case. What is true is that Russian style tanks when the ammo is detonated can explode catastrophically, which is far less likely in western tanks due to blowout panels. Some people choose to imagine this means that western crews are always okay when the tank is penetrated. This is also incorrect. But let’s talk a little about how the Russians and the west sees tank warfare. Russian tanks are primary designed for breakthrough and exploitation, western tanks are primarily designed for anti-tank duty. Until very recently, western tanks were not equipped with HE-FRAG rounds at all, which is the primary ammunition for dealing with infantry. In contrast, Soviet tanks and now Russian tanks have always considered the HE-FRAG round to be the primary ordnance of the tank. Russians see tank warfare as integral in providing fire-support for combined arms groups, and exploiting breakthroughs. In the current conflict, exploitation has not been possible, due to the NATO support Ukraine is getting in the form of electronic intelligence, surveillance and supply lines from factories which cannot be touched. If Russia will be able to use tanks in their intended role of exploitation again remains to be seen, but the reality of modern combat might make this impossible with the Soviet style tanks. However, this is no different for the western tanks all of which proved very easy to destroy with simple drones and old land mines. If we actually go by the established narrative in the west, it doesn’t actually look that good. As you may remember, in the beginning of this war, when most of the Russian tanks were lost, we heard a lot about the super weapons of Javelins, N-LAWs and Bayraktars and other such weapons. These weapons are highly modern and extremely expensive. All of them created after the T-72, T-80 and T-90 tanks were made. So essentially newer anti tank weapons from the west destroyed older Soviet tanks. This is to be expected surely? Contrast this with the destroyed Abrams, Leopards and Challengers. Most of which were taken out by FPV drones or mines. The T-72 is indeed vulnerable to a javelin, the Leopard 2 was proven vulnerable to a toy drone with an RPG-7 warhead from the 1970s duct taped to it. Indeed most of them did not blow up catastrophically, but they are destroyed none the less. Western tanks have a good reputation, because people are very impressed by first world militaries beating up under-equipped and exhausted third world countries without modern weapons. Ukraine is the first time these western tanks have actually encountered a professional military with modernish weapons, and they have completely failed to live up to their hype, instead performing no better than Ukraine’s T-64 tanks really. I am of course not saying that Russian tanks are phenomenal, but they were designed to fight this kind of war, and losses were expected in their inception. This is less true for western tanks, which on the other hand has been lauded as nearly indestructible, and was claimed to be able to sweep aside Russian defenses when they encountered them. This turned out to be a pure fantasy, and the reality is that both western and eastern tanks are equally destroyed by drones, mines and missiles, and are otherwise fairly similar in capabilities.

Name: Carl Hamilton
Question: Russia has reached the eastern outskirts of Chasiv Yar. Will the city fall into Russian hands or will the Ukrainians be able to hold it?
Answer: I am late to the party on answering this one. The Russians arrived near Chasiv Yar, and has since crossed the canal running through the town, which was the best defensive terrain feature the AFU could rely on. The other major strong points in Chasiv Yar were hit with high yield glide bombs, such as the ODAB-1500, a 1.5 ton thermobaric bomb. The above image is from a drone flying around Bohdanivka over 5km away from the industrial part of Chasiv Yar where this bomb landed. By my estimation of the relative effectiveness of a 1.5t thermobaric weapon, this bomb killed everyone within a 300m radius. Likewise at least 40 other 500 kilogram bombs were dropped with glide vehicles to take out strong points. The reality of the situation is that few sturdy defenses exist in the city now. There is no counter to this situation at the moment. Fixed positions will get bombed, the bigger and more elaborate they are, the bigger the bomb they will receive. The popular answers to this question, seem to focus on a couple of fantasies. The first one is that Chasiv Yar was supposed to be taken before May 9th. There is no indication of this other than a wish to say the city was held on this day and somehow that makes losing it at a later day okay. The other fantasy is that a couple of F-16s are going to change this situation. I sincerely doubt Ukraine is going to take their minimal training F-16 pilots and fly them to a high altitude to launch Air to Air missiles at maximum range in a vain attempt at intercepting the bombers dropping these glide bombs at a range of 60km or so from the front. This would put the F-16s into a very easily targeted position for Russia’s AA batteries. Based on this there is some hope that the city will hold for up to 6 months. I rarely make predictions, but I would be willing to bet a large sum of money that Chasiv Yar will not last 6 months, F-16 or not. Additionally, the Russians seem on the verge of taking the remaining area east of the canal south of the city. Once that is done, they do not have to actually take Chasiv Yar, in order to continue advancing south west towards a link-up with the forces that broke through Avdiivka. It seems to me this is the most likely action for the Russians to take currently.

Name: Carl Hamilton
Question: Was the Soviet Union just as much an aggressor in World War II invading the Baltic states as Germany was invading Poland and Czechoslovakia etc?
Answer: Do you count any aggression as being literally Nazi Germany? In that case sure why not. The Soviet Union did indeed enter the Baltic states, as well as eastern Poland, Finland and Romania. Now if that is all you care about, you can stop reading here, that happened, and the rest of this answer is not for you. Personally, I think the idea that the Soviet Union is Nazi Germany, is immoral, and it is factually incorrect, so I would instead offer some context to these events and then you can judge if everyone is still Hitler once the history is understood. Soviet Parade in Chisinau, 1940 after the Soviet annexation. We shall answer this question in detail by asking 3 important questions, Why do nations attack other nations? Are all wars of aggression equally cruel? What was the historical context of the territories taken by the Soviet Union? Why do nations attack others? This is a pretty important question in international relations theory. There are many answers, but none of them are “for no reason”. Germany had a reason to attack all the countries they did, that reason was either ideological, due to Hitlers idea of imposing Lebensraum, or strategic like in the case of Denmark and Norway; to control metal ore. The Soviets likewise has reasons, which we will get back to. But we should first establish the fact, that nations attack each other, this ridiculous idea of western democracies not attacking people for cynical reasons is horseshit to be honest. At this time, Britain, France and the USA all controlled vast empires. They did not acquire this land by asking people, but by a century of vicious and brutal violence and aggression. Realist theory states, that if a country sees a benefit in taking over an area, and they have the capability to do so, they probably will. And this exactly what happened. International law is for agreements between powerful countries, no one cares about international law for the weak nations of Africa, Asia or Americas at this time, I just want everyone to fully understand that. It should be noted, that it is also commonly agreed that some reasons for war are entirely legitimate and almost certain to occur. For example, revanchism, which states that countries will attempt to regain territory lost in moments of weakness such as losing a war. We will unsurprisingly get back to this. Are all wars of aggression equally cruel? Nations can be cruel indeed, but that doesn’t mean every nation has a culture of cruelty. Nazi Germany had one, it was in their ideology, and throughout history there certainly have been others. The Soviet aggression was however not to eliminate the population, however much some people want to equate them with each other. When the Soviets occupied Bessarabia, they did not kill the Romanian soldiers, and actually very few people died. Less than a hundred by some accounts. Soviet repression in the territory afterwards, was not worse there than other places in the Soviet Union either. Contrast this to when Romania reacquired the territory in 1941, and themselves and allowed the murder of 130,000 Jewish people, as well as an unknown additional number of Romas, Russians and Ukrainians. The Romanians did far worse things to what they considered their own territory in WW2 than the Soviets did. Likewise, the Germans killed 5.7 million Polish people, while it is claimed the Soviets in and after WW2 killed 150,000. That’s a pretty massive difference. So the answer is that no, not all acts of aggression are in fact the same, and it is difficult to compete with the Nazis in cruelty. What was the historical context of the territories taken by the Soviet Union? I have mentioned Romania and Bessarabia before so let us start with this. This territory is today called Moldavia, and it was given to the Russian Empire in 1812 by the Ottoman Empire after the Ottomans declared war on Russia. Russia did not start this war, and gained this territory as compensation. Following the Crimean War, the principalities of Wallachia and Moldavia were united as a vassal of the Ottomans, and gained full independence in 1877 when they fought together with the Russians. Afterwards Romania traded Northern Dobruja, for southern Bessarabia, thus recognizing all of Bessarabia as Russian. During WW1 Romania signed a treaty with the entente promising to give Romania Transylvania from Austro-Hungary if they won, which they did. After WW1 Russia was in a civil war, and Romania already having grown quite in size, decided to invade Moldavia and take it with military force. You’ll notice that the wiki article calls this an intervention, but to talk about an earlier point, thousands died when Romania did this, entering the territory of another state is an invasion whether they have a civil war or not and Romania simply land-grabbed this under the nose of the Russians. 20 years later, the Soviets took it back. A fairly similar story is the case for Poland. Poland being revived from the dead as a nation after WW1, also got involved in the Russian civil war, and with the Soviet forces occupied all over the place, were able to beat them and obtain the Peace of Riga in 1921. This ceded a significant portion of Lithuania, Ukraine and Belarus to Poland. 18 years later the Soviets took it all back. I am not going to go into the history of Polish territorial claims from the 1700s and earlier, I am also not lobbying for Sweden to become part of the Danish kalmar union. The Baltic countries were all Russian territories which essentially rebelled during the civil war. And rebellion is honestly a pretty big word as well. The 20,000 professional German soldiers in Estonia probably had a pretty big role in the outcome of that conflict as well. A similar story is true for Lithuania and Latvia. 1920 they all signed peace treaties with the Soviets which gained them their territory. 20 years later the Soviets took it back. Finally we have Finland which was a duchy in the Russian Empire, during the Russian civil war, this territory also declared its independence, and again with the help of over 14,000 German professional soldiers. They also got into a civil war of their own, as socialism was actually quite popular in Finland. This was peacefully solved by executing and starving to death their left wing political opponents. In 1920 a treaty was signed where Finland returned the occupied Repola and Porajarvi territories, in exchange for Petsamo. Petsamo would of course be taken back by the Soviets 20 years later. The reality of the historical context is that all of the Soviet aggressiveness in 1939–1940, were without a doubt a response to these countries fighting with the Soviets when they were on their knees in 1920. They thought that they could do anything they wanted since the Soviets were weak, and many people expected them to collapse. Instead the Soviets regained military power, and when they had it, they simply retook the land they lost and considered theirs. This is not Nazi Germany. Nazi Germany had no claim or casusbelli for invading Denmark, Netherlands, Yugoslavia or the USSR itself. And their goal was extermination and imposition of the “master race” not regaining lost land. This is the concept of Revanchism. It is not unique to this situation, and history is full of re-conquest. If you think it is petty to reconquer land lost 20 years ago, or that somehow makes the Soviets particularly aggressive, I will remind you that Spain was almost entirely lost to the Muslims in 720, and Spain continued to re-conquer their lost lands for the next *checks notes* 772 years, ending in 1492 with the fall of Granada. Spain then promptly kicked out the Muslims, who had been living there for nearly 800 years, in fact longer than the gothic ancestors of Spain had been living in Spain. And this is considered an entirely legitimate state and history today, and is never compared to Nazi Germany. I hope this was at least interesting, sorry for the lack of pictures on this one, but I couldn’t really think of any good illustrations other than a whole bunch of maps.

Name: Carl Hamilton
Question: Where do you think the Russian summer offensive would be concentrated on and what are the odds of success?
Answer: There are many possibilities for what the Russian summer offensive could entail. Now, let’s take the most optimistic prediction route first. The Russian summer offensive won’t happen. Sure, it is possible that over the coming weeks, Russia will get so bogged down that they have no ability to launch another offensive in the summer. Though I sincerely doubt it. Let’s instead speak of what is going on now. It should be noted that there is currently an offensive ongoing, the Donetsk offensive, which has the aim of clearing the area around Donetsk and ultimately the entire oblast. This offensive is not a possibility, it is already happening. Several areas has already been taken by the Russians including part of Chasov Yar west of Bakhmut and the strategic town of Ocheretyne north west of Avdiivka. These are the main vectors of the current Russian advance though not the only ones. ISW is thinking that the focus of a breakthrough here will be attacking the Kramatorsk line, a series of heavily fortified cities. It’s possible, but I think it’s mostly optimistic wishful thinking. Between Chasov Yar and Ocheretyne, there are no big cities or heavily fortified positions. To me it seems likely that the immediate Russian goal would be to attempt to encircle a large area around the cities near Toretsk and Niu-York. This would create a big hole in the Ukrainian line, which the Russian might try to exploit and circumvent the Kramatorsk line by going around the south west of it. Controlling all of Doetnsk is a key goal of Russia for political reasons. But the real prize would be Kharkiv and Odesa. Odesa is unlikely due to the nature of a major assault crossing over a river like the Dniper, but Russia has created a Dniper flotilla, and it seems like this is eventually going to be something they will try either way. But more likely would be to try and take Kharkiv. Now Kharkiv is not best taken by assaulting it, but by surrounding it. Destroying Kharkiv would eliminate the reason for taking it in the first place. It is a heavily populated and industrialized area, destroying this will make it just a big ruin which is not extremely beneficial. So, if Russia was to take Kharkiv, they would likely go around it and try to cut it off forcing a siege. They could do this with a small encirclement, in the Kharkiv oblast, or they could try something more ambitious by going through Sumy and encircling the region by controlling the major supply lines. If Russia does launch a summer offensive which is separate from the current Donetsk offensive. Then to me it seems most likely to take place in or in support of a Kharkiv offensive, but it is entirely possible they will simply built on their current success. As for how likely their success is? I think they will achieve some success. The AFU is not in a great state right now, and Russia introduction of high caliber thermobaric air bombs with glide kits, has essentially solved the problem of heavily fortified trenches. Ukrainian earth works are no longer the obstacle they used to be, and this is already proving to be quite a change for the Russian ability to advance. But I do not think the Russian success is going to drastically increase the tempo of advance or collapse the Ukrainian front all at once like some people are suggesting, I do however find it more likely to succeed than the extremely optimistic predictions that Russia just won’t do anything, which is mostly based on childish cartoons than the reality of the current operational state.

Question: Was RDX/TNT 60/40 (cyclotol) mixture explosive material filling used for a German WW2 5cm mortar shell? Is this true?
Answer: As far as I am aware, the German mortar shells and most other grenades, were filled entirely with TNT and no RDX. Some german explosives used amatol. This is often 60% TNT and 40% Ammonium-nitrate, and likely this is what you are thinking of. Cyclotol is an American explosive which is specialized, and used in some American nuclear weapons. It is pretty unlikely any German weapon ever used this.

Question: Could we expect to see Russian sabotage against European weapons manufacturers such as the artillery factory in the Chezh Republic?
Answer: Without a doubt. European weapon manufacturers are making weapons which are used against Russia. For all intends and purposes they are at war with Russia, even if we pretend like NATO at large is not, though France is working on changing that. Name: Carl Hamilton
Question: Is Russia close to running short of artillery pieces? UKR reports destroying over 10k
Answer: No, they are not close to running short of artillery pieces. First of all, Russia has certainly not lost 10k artillery pieces. If we go by Oryx the actual number is around 1,000 so only 10% of what you say Ukraine is claiming, and this includes 120mm mortars which are usually counted separately from tube and rocket artillery. The general staff report of Ukraine is actually counting 13,000 artillery losses including rocket launchers. An impressive number considering it’s more than twice as much artillery has Russia actually fielded. The International Institute for Strategic Studies has a slightly different view. Yes, Russia did suffer a reduction in available artillery, however, between 2023 and 2024, the production of artillery exceeded the losses and in 2024, the Russians have increased their artillery availability, and done so largely with newer and better systems. The IISS defense analyst Yohann Michel stated in February, that at the stockpiles that Russia had available, they would be able to maintain their current level for another 2–3 years. But not only does Russia have massive numbers of equipment remaining, they have increased their production significantly. Rather than depleting their artillery this year, Russia is likely to reach a level of artillery throw weight which actually exceeds their pre-war capabilities.

Question: Is it ethical to browse the dark web for academic research?
Answer: You cannot easily browse the dark web at all, because of the lack of effective cataloguing tools there. But there is without a doubt a legitimate use for the dark web in academic research. The most obvious one being access to Wikileaks, which has a dark web portal, allowing you to read a ton of diplomatic and intelligence files. These are a valid and even very important source for historical research, international relations research as well as politics. Additionally, some researchers may be researching sensitive political issues which requires encrypted communications and forums, and choose to communicate with their informants or colleagues through these channels to avoid reprisals from organizations or governments who doesn’t want a topic researched. For example corruption.

Name: Carl Hamilton
Question: In wwii, during the battle of stalingrad, could the soviets have destroyed both the German 6th army and the rest of army group south? What prevented that, and did the red army have that capability at that point in the war?
Answer: They did have this capability and the original plan Called “Operation Saturn” had exactly the goal of reaching Rostov on Don, which would have cut off all the German forces in the south. However, this plan hinged on the quickly surrender or defeat of the German forces in the Stalingrad pocket, which was estimated at 80,000 troops. It turned out it was over 250,000 troops, and the fighting would continue not just in December but through January as well. This meant that operation Saturn was cancelled as significant Soviet forces were tied up in cleaning and containing the encirclement, additionally Mannstein launched a rescue attempt to relieve the pocket. This further exhausted the Soviet striking forces in the area. The Soviets still had pretty significant forces available, but the plan was deemed too risky with events not unfolding exactly as expected. Having suffered serious defeats in the previous years, the Soviets were wary not to over extend. Finally, the Soviets did not have enough trucks to launch deep offensive of the length which was required for to reach Rostov on Don without doing start stops, this meant they would need to follow the railroads which made their path predictable and therefore easier to ambush. This was to be a decisive victory, and launching a risky grand offensive under these conditions was not something the Soviet general had a stomach for, despite the poor state of German forces meant it was technically possible. Instead the Soviets opted for a smaller offensive, called Little Saturn, seen on the map above. This offensive aimed at eliminating the weaker Axis allies near Stalingrad, namely the 3rd Romanian army and the 8th Italian army. It was partially successful in this, knocking out about 100,000 troops. It was followed up by the Voronezh–Kharkov offensive, which was hugely successful knocking out 250,000 troops more for just 37,000 losses. This resulted in the elimination of the Hungarian and Italian armies on the eastern front more or less. These offensives were not as risky, but ultimately destroyed nearly as many Axis troops as the Stalingrad offensive itself, and did so with minimal casualties. It’s a very over looked scenario, that panned out pretty well and it was almost certainly the right choice to use the resources like so, rather than trying to cut off the southern German army group.

Name: Carl Hamilton
Question: What is Marxism theory, objectives, characteristics, similarities, and differences?
Answer: Marxist theory is a category of theories which uses material classes as units of analysis. The main premise of Marxism is that the ruling class and the working class have opposing interests, and that much of politics is the struggle between these interests if not all. For example, a worker’s interest is to get paid as much as possible, an employer’s interest is to pay the worker as little as possible to maximize their profit. In relation to this basis theory Marxism has the following goals: Marxism is characterized by an emphasis on achieving political objectives through solidarity and science. Within science there are a few common themes in Marxism as well: Marxism share some similarities with feminism, which often also uses the critical approach, but while Marxism tends to criticize based on material and political assumptions, feminism criticizes exclusively on gender assumptions. Marxism shares many similarities with classical liberal economic theory actually, David Ricardo’s and Adam Smith’s theories are incorporated in Marxism, the difference often being that Marxism doesn’t think that a liberal market is a good thing even if it works within the premise. Marxism differs radically from theories that uses the idea of artfulness to achieve material goals. Religion is an obvious one, but perhaps interesting is the idea that warfare is considered an art form in the west, but it was considered a science in the USSR and China. It differs from much earlier philosophy in the sense that the idea is not personal improvement or contemplation on the nature of the world, but recognition of the situation with the specific goal of changing it not accepting it.

Question: After two years of fighting, what is Ukraine's ability in making its own weapons and ammunition?
Answer: Ukraine’s weapons production ability is close to zero. Not quite zero, but it is essentially working through artisans. What does this mean? It means that the production is being carried out manually and mostly in smaller machine shops. Big factories obviously do not survive long in Ukraine right now, and this severely limits the scale of any production. There are those who would post a picture of a couple of guys in a basement making mortar shells saying this is a booming production. But this is an outright lie and fantasy. This is what a booming production looks like: RDM Danel factory SA Not a couple of people using manual tools in a basement. I don’t know how that isn’t obvious, but apparently it is not. Ukraine is doing pretty well with what they have, but if they were actually booming in military production, they wouldn’t be completely reliant on foreign deliveries now would they. And they are. The reason why Zelensky has been pointing out that without western shells Ukrainian artillery is silent, is because Ukraine is incapable of any relevant production of shells above mortar caliber. Hiding this fact doesn’t help Ukraine, it’s just silly.

Question: What are the strange, polyhedrally shaped Russian tanks, that have been observed spearheading recent successful Russian attacks in krasnohorivka and ocheretino, while artillery strikes and fpv drones bounce off their structure?
Answer: If you mean these: They are some sort of phased array jamming device, which seems be attachable to all kinds of things not just tanks. There is also a variant which some people call the nipple, which is often put on top of tanks. Either version serves the purpose of disrupting radio controlled munitions, including drones. You might also be referring to the turtle armor, which some pundits call it. This is a field modification, which adds stand off armor to tanks and other vehicles. Yeah it looks stupid, but 1m+ stand off distance reduces the effectiveness of HEAT charges by over 60%. This means that shaped charge FPV drones likely are close to harmless against the armor, provided they don’t hit something very thin behind it.

Name: Carl Hamilton
Question: Why did the “ancient” Roman Republic, and later the Roman Empire, fail to improve their weapons and military tactics in any way at all?
Answer: They did not fail to improve their military tactics or equipment. They improved both quite consistently over time. With some major reforms here and there. For example during the empire the plumbata was introduced, which was a highly effective throwing projectile cheaper to make than javelins and able to be carried in greater numbers while serving much the same purpose. Also, the Roman republic itself had two very noticeable military reforms, the first major reform happened around 315 BC, when Rome replaced the hoplite fighting formations with the manipular system. Which introduced the 4 core components of the legion, namely the velites (javelineers) hastati (light infantry) principes (heavy infantry) and triarii (veterans). The Marian reform of 107 BC, got rid of a lot of the unnecessary logistical support for legions, demanding that legionaries carried much of their own equipment, as well as making them professional soldiers instead of citizen soldiers. The hastati and principes were essentially merged as a standardized legionary, while the triarii was kept only in spirit as evocatus, voluntary veterans who signed up for extra service after their contract was up. During the Republican period equipment also changed quite a bit, from primitive bronze plates attached to the chest in the early period, to steel chainmail later in the period. In the Imperial period there was also a time when segmented plate armor was popular but it fell out of favor again. Shields and helmets changed, and in the late imperial period, the Roman army was embracing specialist units from non-citizens and shifting to have a heavier focus on cavalry units themselves.

Name: Carl Hamilton
Question: What were the most significant battles of World War II for Germany, the Soviet Union, and the United Kingdom/United States?
Answer: It’s difficult to list every important battle for all of these nations, so I will instead limit it to what I consider the most important victory per nation. For the United Kingdom: The Battle of El-Alamein: Britain saves it’s African and Middle Eastern colonies and reverses the situation in the African theater. Essentially the British Empire lives on, it was also crucial in setting up the conditions for the later invasion of Italy. For the Soviet Union: The Battle of Stalingrad: It reversed the situation on the eastern front, destroyed a German army for the first time in the entire war, saved the Soviet Union’s Caucasus fuel resources, knocked out Hungary, Romania and Italy from the eastern front in practice, and marked the beginning of Soviet strategic initiative which they would never lose again. For the United States: The Battle of Midway: Perhaps some would also say Coral Sea, but definitively US naval supremacy was established at Midway, it was in question for a little bit, due to the innovative and well organized Japanese fleet, but the destruction of the Japanese carriers and the success of US naval intelligence definitively sealed the fate of the pacific. For Germany: The Battle for France: Germany’s greatest success in WW2, the operational success of defeating France so totally and so quickly should not be underestimated. France’s GDP was greater than that of Japan, their knocking out so quickly surprised practically everyone, and to do so with such few losses, was quite a feat.

Name: Carl Hamilton
Question: Can you recommend a good first novel for someone who has never read science fiction or fantasy before?
Answer: Yes if want science fiction you should read Frank Herbert’s Dune, Huxley’s Brave New World or George Orwell’s 1984. If you want fantasy, I highly recommend starting with Brandon Sanderson’s Mistborn, Ursula K Le Quin’s A Wizard of Earthsea or J.K Rowling’s Harry Potter. Mistborn Art These are all massively popular books which are popular for a reason. They are in fact not terribly difficult to understand, and all of them have heavy elements of fantasy or science fiction, without them actually being necessary for the plot. This is quite different from Lord of the Rings, which some might consider missing on the above list of recommendations, but LOTR is fundamentally about fantasy entirely. And honestly, it’s a fairly long an obtuse book series, which isn’t as action packed or obvious as the movies are. Also A song of Ice and Fire is another great book series, however its low fantasy setting is not a great example of fantasy in general. For an intermediate book series in fantasy, I would recommend The First Law by Joe Ambercrombie, or maybe The Stormlight Archive by Brandon Sanderson. A lot of people also seem to like the Wheel of Time, by Robert Jordan. I found this to be quite drawn out and boring to be honest. For an intermediate book series in science fiction, I would recommend The Expanse which is in fact also highly realistic. Or if you want to mix Fantasy and Science Fiction, dare I say Warhammer 40k?

Name: Carl Hamilton
Question: Why is the M2 Browning still used currently? How good is it?
Answer: M2 Browning, a 12.7mm heavy machine gun, is still in use essentially because no one has made a replacement for it yet. The M2 was originally introduced in 1933, which makes this gun over 90 years old. Indeed it appears that it might be replaced in the conceptional role by a Lapua Magnum 338, at least according to Garand Thumb who were looking at the newest version of the potential future machine gun. The M2 itself, is honestly not that great. Yeah it’s good if you just don’t compare it to other 12.7mm machine guns, and you’ll hear a lot of people talk about how powerful it is. Again, yes compared to like a 7.62mm machine gun. But the direct analogue to the M2 is the Dshk, and I won’t argue the Dshk is better, it probably isn’t, but this hardly matters. The Dshk is from 1938 and it was replaced by the NSV in 1971 inside the USSR. Additionally the 12.7mm Kord also is in use in Russia and affiliated countries. The eastern 12.7mm guns have some pretty significant advantages over the M2. Firstly the NSV is 41 kilogram with a tripod, while the M2HB is 58 kilogram with a tripod. The Kord with a bipod weighs only 32 kg, and due to it’s recoil compensation can be fired with just that. The Kord has about the same rate of fire as the M2HB while the NSV has a higher rate of fire. If you really want more firepower, there are is also the KPVT, a 14.5mm machine gun, roughly 50% more powerful than a 12.7mm. The M2 is honestly an old bulky design, and the Americans are well aware of this, and have been for quite some time. It was supposed to be replaced in by the M85C in the 1980s, but it was deemed too unreliable. Then from 1990 they tried to replace it with the XM312, but it was cancelled in 2004, because it was too unreliable. Then from 2009 it was supposed to be replaced by the XM806 but it was cancelled in 2012 because it was delayed and complicated. XM806 In short, the US military has been trying to get rid of the M2HB for nearly 40 years, but the sheer incompetence of General Dynamics to create a new 12.7mm gun, has prevented this. And it seems like at this point they may just adopt a more easily controlled long range round like the Lapua Magnum.

Name: Carl Hamilton
Question: Did knights carry two swords during battle? If not, why?
Answer: No, they did not, because on the battlefield two swords offers no advantage. You always want to be using both your hands for what ever you do for fighting, but there are so many better options. Rather than using two weapons which are fairly poor at penetrating armour, and doesn’t have that much reach, you could instead be using one weapon which has far better reach and penetrates armour much better, such as a poleaxe. A knight might use two swords in a non-battlefield setting, such as a duel, indeed In Japanese swordsmanship there is an established fighting style for two swords in duels. Though carrying two swords is even more inconvenient than one, and a more typical and practical combination would be a buckler or dagger to supplement a one handed sword. If you ever found yourself in a situation where you had no other options than an empty hand or another sword, yes go for it, but this is extremely rare and likely not intentional.

Name: Carl Hamilton
Question: What weapons proved effective in the war in Ukraine?
Answer: The most underestimated weapon before the war, was the humble FPV drone. This was considered to be an insurgent and improvised weapon, mostly famous for it’s use by islamist fundamentalists in Syria such as ISIS. The AFU had put their money into TB-2 Bayraktar drones after their success against Armenia. However, the TB-2 is largely a failure in the conflict. While much successful footage came out initially, the reality is that practically 100% of TB-2s were destroyed, and quite early as well. On the contrary, the cheap FPV drones which became popularized by Chechen veterans from Syria, quickly evolved from dropping small grenades, to carrying full size RPG warheads and being supplied at an industrial level. Already in December 2022, western analysts were raising alarm over the success of these inexpensive weapons. The most successful one is the more expensive Lancet type drone which is in fact a purpose build military kamikaze drone. Unlike the FPV drone it has a serious and multipurpose warhead, and the newer versions have AI assistance and a range of over 45km. So far, there has been 1,195 Lancet hits confirmed through video evidence as counted by lostarmour, including 262 tank hits. 114 confirmed hits from the helicopter launched LMUR. 28 confirmed hits from KUB-BLA. But this pales in comparison to the fact, that the Russian forces have also conducted at least 3,945 hits with smaller FPV drones of which there is video evidence, about half of these are on vehicles crews leaving their disabled tanks, infantry or defensive positions. These hit counts do not include grenades dropped from drones. It should also be noted that the AFU use FPV drones, but I was unable to find a comprehensive list of hits and video evidence from them. Also famously they use naval kamikaze drones to strike Russian ships and shore targets. I think this venue of weaponry is the one that has been proved to work the most in practice during this conflict. Though we will likely see an electronic counter to them, something which is already emerging.

Name: Carl Hamilton
Question: Do you personally believe that the war in Ukraine is about NATO's eastward expansion or Putin's grand plan to recreate the Russian empire?
Answer: I personally believe in the theories of international politics. The premise here is a false dichotomy. You are presenting two choices as if reality must be one of these options. This is incorrect. The reality of international politics is neither that countries generally act because of a single reason nor that their politics are designed by a single person and for no reason. What I think should be understood more broadly outside of political science, is that the event was predicted. It was predicted by John Mearsheimer’s theory of offensive realism. Now a lot of people go around saying that Putin is an irrational actor, especially if they watch Vaush on youtube. However, generally speaking irrational actors do not last long in power, if you think any powerful long standing leader is irrational, the problem is simply your own ability to analyze. You are confounded by reality, and rather than adapting your view to explain reality, you simply reject it as unexplainable. This is a religious view, not a scientific view, and doing this makes someone no better than the Catholic church saying that astronomical scientists were heretics for representing models they thought were irrational. The policy of Russia, is not about conjuring up the Russian Empire from history, nor is it about recreating the Soviet Union. Russian politics are security maximizing offensive realism. That means they position themselves to gain influence over their regional sphere, in order to protect from the maneuvering of other great powers. In this case USA and its allies. Whether Ukraine joined NATO or not, wouldn’t change the threat perceived in Russia. Now you may say, but NATO isn’t a threat. It doesn’t even matter, no matter how many times you tell yourself this, great power maneuvering is perceived as a threat by other great powers. This is how the system works, it doesn’t make special rules for NATO or the USA. Whether you agree with the perception in Russia, doesn’t change that perception, and it is no different if other countries were substituted. Disregarding the actual scientific predictions regarding the actions before the war, is probably one of the lead causes of the conflict to begin with. There is a miscalculation, that the USA is an undisputed hegemon or unitary superpower on a global scale. This is no longer true. There was a very brief period in human history where the US could act globally as it saw fit and without consequences. Many people think they live in this period of history, I would personally think that this period of history is over, definitively. The problem of policy now, is that people refuse to acknowledge this, and increasingly this will lead to responses from other countries, who has the power to challenge decisions made in the west. If the reality of global security policy and other non-western nations regional interests are not considered, we will simply have more conflicts, and I think that is to a large extent what Ukraine is about.

Question: Why do many people who firmly believed that Ukraine could win the war against Russia start to think that Ukraine may lose?
Answer: I would wager that in all honesty a lot of those people never believed in Ukrainian victory to begin with. Unfortunately, a lot of journalism and social media writing is more activism than information. By that I mean, they have been writing about Ukrainian victory for the purpose of supporting Ukraine, not because they thought this was actually a likely outcome. I’ll give you an example: Here you have David Axe, the main military analyst of Forbes, and one of the most cited journalists in the west when covering the technical aspects of the war in Ukraine. It’s my firm opinion that David Axe does not care about reality even a little bit, his posts are entirely activism. Before the 2023 Ukrainian offensive he wrote about how the Challenger 2 would absolutely roll over the Russians. This did not happen, what happened was that the Challenger 2 armed brigade fought for a couple of days, lost challengers without any effect and was pulled off the line entirely. About 1 year after the first article David Axe wrote instead: So what changed? Did the chief military analyst write the first article without knowing the specs of the challenger 2? Of course not. Nothing changed, all of the problems of the challenger 2 was known to David Axe. He didn’t write the first article because he thought this was a great tank, he wrote it as activism to increase morale in Ukraine. Now there is a lot of articles coming in about the looming terrible situation for Ukraine. It turns out the material we send was bad, Ukraine is actually in dire need of manpower (though no one is yet really considering where all the manpower they used to have went), and as it turns out Russian electronic warfare is effective and there is zero indication that they are running out of any equipment despite over 400 articles written about them running out of everything from time to missiles. Now why are the new articles mentioning this? Did all the western media drop their activism? Did they cut ties with the intelligence community, stop being owned by billionaires or political groups with vested interests? Of course not! This is still activism! So the first narrative was one of dismissive superiority. Essentially we (the western people (white people)) are superior to the Russians (Asiatic hordes) they are not only incompetent and immoral, they are also totally lacking all material because their system is inherently inferior to ours, so they will collapse and lose shortly, please support this cause. Okay that didn’t work, so people are getting slightly disillusioned with the idea that we are doing really well and they are doing really badly. Well what do we do then? We move on to the next type of narrative which tends to work historically. It is called the slippery slope, and while it’s a fallacy, that doesn’t stop it from being pretty effective. The premise is that if A then also B, in this case if Ukraine falls Russia might just attack NATO and our 4000+ nuclear weapons. The second part of this narrative is that Ukraine desperately needs our support. They are losing because they don’t have the right material and the don’t enough of it. And they very much need it now. Is this narrative chosen by coincidence? Of course not. If it is not yet obvious, this is the realm of journalism putting pressure on politicians to increase support, and in the case of America it is democrats putting pressure on republicans to allow the US to continue funding Ukraine, by creating a sense of global emergency like the future of NATO hinges on Ukraine (it does not). I believe that the US will eventually resume major shipments to Ukraine, and you will see that the media narrative will suddenly go straight back to talking about how every piece of material we send is a wonder weapon that surely will defeat Russia this year. My guess would be that our next wonder weapon narrative will be about small drones like the Russian Lancet, delivered in numbers to Ukraine which will make up for their lack of manpower. But who knows really.

Question: Are you surprised that the Danish Navy has suffered from equipment challenges without them being resolved or even fully addressed?
Answer: Not at all, it is exactly what I expect. In Denmark there once was a great story of when we introduced anti-ship missiles in the Danish navy. The US made harpoon missile was introduced in Denmark very quickly after it’s inception. In 1982 however, a Danish warship accidentally fired a harpoon missile at summer house in southern Denmark, and the Harpoon became known as the oopsie-missile in Denmark. What happened was that the Harpoon missile misfired though the Captain of Peder-Skram frigate, was initially made into a scapegoat. It was later revealed that the harpoon missiles were highly unreliable, and could be fired even without being armed. Denmark cannot afford to develop most of the equipment in our ships, and as such, we rely on foreign suppliers, who are just there to make a quick buck, often it is not even possible to get them to update things, because some of these companies no longer even exists, like McDonnell Douglas. Denmark is not a serious war country, though we have competent people in the military, we are constantly the subject of corporate schemes to unload equipment for a profit. For example, we replaced our 1950s MG3 machine-gun with the 1950s M60 machine gun, because corporations convinced our politicians and military officials that it was more modern now it has plastic furniture. So no I am not surprised when things don’t work in our military, that’s pretty much what I expect half the time.

Name: Carl Hamilton
Question: What are the best sources to learn military tactics and strategy battles?
Answer: What you have to understand is that military tactics and strategy is not a universal thing. Each country formulates their own ideas, codes, systems, training and theories of what tactics and strategies work in given situations. This is called doctrine. So this changes over time and over geography. Throughout history, certain countries and organizations have been recognized as more influential in the development of broad tactics and strategy, and some concepts are recognized by almost all doctrines. These are usually basic concepts. You can read the classic Sun Tzu’s Art of War, if you are a complete novice in the topic of military tactics and strategy. If you are more interesting the basics of contemporary strategy, you could read another classic called On War by Clausewitz. Personally, I am most well versed in Soviet tactics and strategy, albeit from a western point of view, though I think this is relatively accurate. There are also a plethora of people who will tell you isolated aspects of tactics which they acquired in their own experience as soldiers here on Quora and other places. This is of course good first hand experience, but you have to be careful with personal accounts, as people often can’t see the forest for trees, and becomes so stuck in their particular tactic, that they often claim it is the only thing that works. Finally you have all the theories which are written on specific topics, and simulations which range from academic experiments to video games, which can in fact serve to illustrate many real life tactics, such as DCS, which can teach you quite a bit about air combat.

Question: Are there examples before Industrialization of armies significantly impacting the course of a war by deliberately targeting their enemy's supplies? Was pre-modern artillery and warships or cavalry, skirmishers and guerilla tactics more effective?
Answer: Pre-modern war tactics were not more effective, generally more primitive things are rarely ever more effective than more advanced things, however did they use guerilla tactics and target enemy supplies as a grand level strategy? They certainly did. Quintus Fabius Maximus Verrucosus was the Dictator of Rome elected as war time leader to defeat Hannibal, after he has crossed the Alps and defeated the Romans decisively at both Trebia and Trasimene in 218 - 217 BC. Quintus Fabius devised the plan to engage the Carthaginian general by avoiding his main army. Instead attacking his supply lines and harassing him. Sadly for Rome, this approach was time consuming and not very “glorious”, so Quintus Fabius was kicked out of office, and replaced by a new leader Gaius Terentius Varro who proceeded to gather the Roman army and then get absolutely destroyed at the Battle of Cannae. The Romans learned that the Fabian strategy of avoidance and supply cutting was the correct one, and Quintus Fabius was elected consul several times and recognized even in his time as a military genius, despite winning no large field battles at all. During the middle ages avoidance and other forms of strategic combat was very serious business, to the point in fact that pitched battles were actually quite rare. The Vikings in particular force fed much of Europe the reality of high mobility warfare, as the Vikings raided much of Europe practically all of western Europe had to come up with new defensive strategies, which is one of the reasons for the many fortifications in England and France. Additionally, the Christian armies were often out numbered and unable to defeat the large and well organized Muslim armies during the Jihad period, and by the 10th century, the primary tactic was one of continues skirmishing and avoidance, trying to cut supplies and not engage the main armies of the caliphate. The crusades were markedly different exactly because the Christian armies had the strategic initiative. The Byzantine military experience made the foundation of the military treatise De velitatione bellica, which deals with the Byzantine guerilla warfare and foundations of military intelligence and reconnaissance. I’ll put a link to this entire work in the comments.

Name: Carl Hamilton
Question: Is the T-64 a better tank than the T-72?
Answer: No the T-64 is of course not better than the T-72 in general. What you could say is that the T-64B was better than the T-72 Ural for that period. The T-72A and the T-64B were fairly equivalent, while the T-72B from 1985 is without a doubt far superior to the T-64B version at the time. The most modern versions of the T-72B3 are without about miles a better then any T-64 variant. In terms of safety, there are essentially no difference. The T-64 and T-72 both have the hull mounted autoloader, so in terms of tendency to explode catastrophically when hit, they are about even. In terms of actually not being penetrated though the T-72B and forward has a massive advantage over the T-64 models, which uses some kind of laminate composite armor, while the T-72B turret uses bulging reactive plates, common thought of as chobham or special armor in the west. Both are able to mount explosive reactive armor over their standard armor as well. During Soviet testing it was also found that the T-72B’s components were the most reliable of any Soviet tanks, lasting on average 3 times longer than T-80B components and 1.75 times longer than T-64B components, meaning that the T-72 requires almost half as much maintenance as the T-64. The T-72B and forward can use the missiles Svir and Invar, while the T-64 uses the older Kobra tank guided missile. The T-64A was around 38 t while the T-72 was 47 ton. I can’t rightly say how heavy the T-64B was, but it seems reasonable that the T-64B might have some mobility advantages over the T-72 by being lighter. However, as stated the T-72B3 is heavily modernized and has far superior electronics, gun, ammunition, engine, optics and armour over the T-64B of any variant. The T-64 was likely the most advanced tank in the world by a very good margin in the 1960s and much of the 1970s, but by modern standards it is subpar and a modernization program for it to the extend of the T-72 has not been launched. The Soviets discontinued the tank in 1987, while keeping the T-72B in production, that was no mistake.

Name: Carl Hamilton
Question: What's the difference between RTS and 4X games?
Answer: RTS is a traditional strategy game genre, which was pioneered by Westwood Studio’s Dune 2, Command and Conquer series, and Blizzard’s Warcraft & Starcraft games. This game genre is usually characterized by the player building bases, establishing an economy around resource extraction to build an army and defeat the enemy player. Some more modern games in the genre deviate a bit from the purist RTS, such as Homeworld and Company of Heroes which minimize base building, while games like Supreme Commander minimize unit control. Some games completely eliminate the economy aspect to focus entirely on unit control, but they are RTT games, Real Time Tactics. Such games include Men of War and Wargame/Warno. 4X games are a type of grand strategy, where the actual fighting is extremely simplified in order to focus on very large scale strategy usually involving a nation state. 4X specifically is based around the idea of empty space which allows the player to colonize. The original pioneering game is Civilizations. In 4X games you typically start with one initial location under you control, whether it is a city of a planet, from there you must colonize and control territory, by exploring, expanding, exploiting and exterminating your opponents. Hence 4X. Stellaris is another good example of this set in space. In general these games are different from other grand strategy, because politics are very unimportant, as every nation starts off on equal footing, it is usually a race to grab as many resources as possible, while other grand strategy like Europa Universalis has the player starting off as a nation in a historical context, and their relationships to greater or even powers is very important, emphasizing good international politics in the gameplay.

Name: Carl Hamilton
Question: During WWII, did Germany commit more troops and resources in its attempt to capture Moscow in 1941-42 or later at Stalingrad in 1942-43?
Answer: The battle of Moscow was greater in scope, the German committed 6 armies to the capture of Moscow, while only 2 armies were involved in the attempt to capture Stalingrad. Though at Stalingrad the Germans were supported by 4 armies which were not German. There were almost 2 million German involved in the attack on Moscow, compared to about half a million in Stalingrad. It should be noted of course that the battle inside of the Stalingrad area, were some of the most intensified battles in human history. While there were more Germans at Moscow, they did occupy a much wider area, and were not compressed in the same way as at Stalingrad. Additionally, there was a lot of stagnation on the Moscow front, with the line remaining relatively stable for another year after the initial battle of Moscow ended, with constant fighting as well. The battle of Moscow did turn into the Rzhev operation, and the scale is difficult to actually calculate in earnest, as the Soviets and Germans are not in agreement on when which operation starts, and due to their lengths many units were moved around. So it is far more difficult to actually determine this precisely, than it is at Stalingrad.

Name: Carl Hamilton
Question: How would the original M1 Abrams fair in combat vs. its Soviet Russian contemporaries?
Answer: The original M1 Abrams is not the version which exists in the minds of most when they talk about this famous vehicle. The one most people are familiar with is the M1A1 or M1A2 which are not the original versions of the tank. The M1 differed from later versions quite significantly due to its lack of a 120mm gun and thinner armor that also lacked no depleted uranium. In terms of armor the original M1 Abrams had roughly a 350mm RHAe frontal arc protection, as opposed to the M1A1 with a 400mm and the M1A2 with a 600mm RHAe vs kinetic penetrators. Substantially more against HEAT. The Soviet contemporary would be the T-80B. The T-80B had a frontal arc protection of 500 RHAe, significantly better than the original M1. In terms of weaponry, the M1 had the L7 105mm rifled cannon, which was obsolete by the 1980s, which was entirely acknowledged by the USA who were trying to procure 120mm guns for the M1 but they were not ready when the M1 was, so the first 120mm gun armed Abrams were not fielded until 1985. The T-80B had a 125mm gun, with significantly more power than 105mm gun. The M735 was the standard APFSDS round for the US 105mm gun armed tanks in the 1980s, it began production in 1978 a year before the M1 and was designed for the M1 and M60A3 tanks to increase their effectiveness. According to US tests the M735 which was the standard, was completely inadequate for penetrating the T-80B, even the newer M833 which was not available to the M1 initially was inadequate. While the Soviet 125mm gun with the ammunition the American were aware of, was deemed able to destroy the M1 and even M1A1 from the front. Hence why later M1s were given DU armor. You can observe the chart below. In terms of mobility the T-80B and the M1 Abrams were both excellent. In terms of day time optics both had very good magnification. In terms of night time optics the M1 had a significantly better suite, with it’s thermal optics, though it’s nothing like what you see today. The T-80 also had one extra trick up it’s sleeve, the ability to fire Kobra ATGMs allowing it to engage like an anti tank guided missile launcher, at a range of at least 4km, twice what is considered the effective kinetic engagement range at the time which is 2km. In short: the Soviet contemporary had significant armor and firepower advantages over the initial M1 Abrams. Of course either tank could destroy each other under the right circumstances, but the M1 would have essentially no real protection from the front, which is a massive disadvantage.

Question: The general consensus on Quora, from the beginning of the russo-ukrainian war is that Ukraine is causing unsustainable losses and winning it's war against Russia. Why then are some NATO countries calling for deployment of their soldiers in Ukraine?
Answer: There is no consensus on Quora, which is a social media platform at best. People have been airing all kinds of predictions since before the conflict even started. The vast majority of posts regarding this quite serious topic is made on the premise of memes, and usually with the goal of writing posts as activism rather than any reasonable or informed opinion. People like speculating, people like reading sensationalist headlines, people like reading and hearing about imminent victory and the superiority of their favorite football team. Name: Carl Hamilton
Question: How could the Germans destroy the T-34 tanks at the beginning of the war when none of their weapons could penetrate them from the front?
Answer: When Germany invaded the USSR in 1941, the Soviets had just 900 medium tanks, most of which were T-34s, and just 500 KV-1s. Of the 20,500 Soviet tanks lost in 1941, just 11% were medium tanks, and many of these were not lost because they were destroyed. Likewise even in 1942, of the 15,100 tanks the Soviets lost, just 43.7% of the losses were T-34s. In the vast majority of cases, the Germans had a very hard time dealing with the T-34s in the beginning of the war, luckily for them they were very rare actually. If they did have the misfortune of facing them, there were a few options though. From the German manual above, it says that all tank mounted guns were ineffective, but a frontal penetration is possible in isolated cases. More reliable would be the 88mm flak gun, or the 105 howitzer which could be deployed in direct fire modes. The numbers is the range of possible penetration, the left column is the turret the right is the hull. This is of course for the earliest model turret, not the improved turret from 1942. Perhaps a quite sober fact is that once the T-34 became the main tank of the Soviet army, they won all strategic operations on the eastern front. The introduction of Tigers and Panthers did not turn the war in favor of the Germans, and even at a heavy cost the T-34 was still on the winning side at Kursk in 1943, which was the first time that T-34s made up the majority of tanks in a major armored operation.

Name: Carl Hamilton
Question: Right before Germany invaded Poland in 1939, it staged a false flag attack (Gleiwitz Incident). Why didn't the Germans do something similar to this when they later attacked the Soviet Union in 1941 during Operation Barbarossa?
Answer: The incident was one of a series of false flag actions which the Nazis carried out, they mainly did this to avoid direct confrontation and justify their actions to the more unintelligent parts of Europe. For much of this time, the western powers of UK and France were content with playing along largely, because they did not want a new war with Germany. Even during the invasion of Poland in 1939, there was not much sentiment for a real war with Germany, hence the 8 month period after the invasion being called “The Phony War” as the western allied did practically nothing to help their friends in Poland. However, by 1941, the war had started in earnest, Nazi Germany could no longer pretend that they were not going to have a serious war with the UK as they were already deeply engaged in one, and they didn’t care about deception or public opinion at this point anymore. Additionally, no justification for invading the USSR was needed, as the Germans saw Jews and communists as the same thing, and being one was guilt enough for extermination, as such the mere existence of the USSR was enough justification, no other pretenses were required.

Question: How would a Japanese Samurai Yari spear unit fare against a Greek phalanx?
Answer: When ever the question is, “How would older military people fare against newer ones?” the answer is almost always going to be the more modern people would win. Because you see, everything former civilizations are capable of more modern ones are capable of as well, plus things which would be mind blowing to older civilizations. So a Greek phalanx, is essentially a hoplite unit, since you specifically didn’t say Macedonian phalanx. Greek hoplites were poorly trained, with terrible bronze armor at best, poorly made bronze shields and relatively crude iron weapons on a good day. Samurai from the height of the Sengoku Jidai period, fought far more often than Greek hoplites ever did, they were trained from birth to be warriors without exception, they wore sophisticated steel armor that covered most of the entire body, they used relatively good quality steel for all their weapons. Additionally, the samurai used advanced formations and tactics, while the Greek hoplite phalanx was simply people standing in a line most of the time, with the Thebans completely blowing everyone’s mind by not standing in a straight line. This is baby steps compared to the complicated battalion maneuvers common on Samurai battlefields. Finally, the hoplites would be supported in reality, by light cavalry, stone slingers and javelin throwers. The Samurai yaris would be supported by very talented archers, heavy lancer cavalry, horse archers, actual pike formations and you know musketeers. In fact the hoplite commander going out in front of his formation for a ritual challenge to the enemy would probably be surprised by the yari samurai getting out his pistol side arm and just blowing his head off. I know, I know. The Spartans were ultra human badasses who scared everyone. Yeah everyone in 300 bc Greece. But you know 1600–1900 years of evolution in warfare is kinda a big deal. Question: What were the reasons for Germany's defeat to Russia in World War II, despite having better equipment and military strategy? Was Russia's success due to their fighting skills and familiarity with the land?
Answer: This is question despite being auto-generated that touches on the very core of how World War 2 is explained in popular history. The phrasing itself is very noteworthy, because the AI who generated this question does so on the basis of what others write, and it asks how Germany was defeated, not how the Soviets won. Do you think the fact the WW2 eastern front history is primarily told from the point of view of Nazis, might have significantly skewed the way the war is perceived? Hint: Yes. If the Germans had superior equipment, superior strategy, their army was more experienced, and in 1941 even outnumbered the Soviets quite a bit on the front, then why didn’t they win? Well it must be because of the 3 things that Manstein and the other Nazi war criminals all agree on. The Weather, the number of Soviets and Hitler sabotaging himself. In reality, this is of course outright lies. Let’s talk about why these things are not the reason first. So with that out of the way, the better question is, how did the Soviets win? The answer is plain and boring. The Soviets approached war scientifically, they started WW2 with a bad theory and an incomplete procurement and training system. Throughout the war the Soviets introduced excellent military equipment, which in general was far better than the German, they introduced a new military doctrine specifically made to counter what the Germans were doing. Their officers gradually became more experienced, until the experienced Germans had no advantages anymore. And they correctly saw the strategic path to victory through attrition and by correctly exploiting weaknesses in the Axis lines. This is the simple version of course, but really that is all there is to it, we can talk about equipment and strategy in details in the comments. Additionally if you are interested I wrote about the massive problems the Soviets had to outcome in 1941–1942 in terms of doctrine here: Soviet Military Doctrine and the Officer Purge Soviet Military Doctrine Part 2 - Learning How to Defend A small point on World War 2 Resource Efficiency

Question: How did the Soviet Union take Eastern Europe so easily?
Answer: The USSR did not take eastern Europe all that easily. 1.44 million Soviets died in liberating eastern Europe from Nazism in the last 12 months of world war 2, that is combat casualties strictly, not missing or non-combat related deaths. That is still about twice as many dead soldiers as all the US and UK military losses for the entire war. I wouldn’t say that was an easy thing. After defeating the vast majority of the German military, the Soviets were in control of eastern Europe. In the political front of course the allies made their own spheres of influence following WW2, but largely agreeing on them and actually enforcing them are two different things. All of the big three moved to secure their own spheres of the world following WW2. The Soviets focused on solidifying their control of eastern Europe, which initially meant supporting communist parties in elections, however, with the escalation of the cold war, and the establishment of NATO the Soviets imposed more direct control in Poland, Czechoslovakia and Romania. As Hungary and East Germany were considered occupied axis territory, these were essentially always under direct Soviet control. But as you might be aware, Soviet control of eastern Europe was also not so simple even after this. A violent revolt in Hungary in 1956, an ideological one in Czechoslovakia in 1968, civil disobedience in Poland, particularly in the 1980s, as well as Ceaușescu basically doing his own very crazy thing in Romania. As with all spheres of influence, it required maintenance and a high degree of active operations, as the western countries were constantly trying to undermine the stability of eastern Europe, much in the same way the Soviets did in the west. But as the USSR was a very powerful country they did maintain control and quite a high degree of it, compared to the more subtle economic control favored in the west.

Question: Did the Nazis know that the Red Army would stop behind the Vistula River and let them easily suppress the uprising of the Polish people? Did they receive any messages from red army officials about them not interfering?
Answer: No, they didn’t know that, chiefly because they didn’t. They were largely stopped at the Vistula river, but they didn’t see the river and just stop. The reality is that the Soviets engaged the German army on the outskirts of Warsaw several times, but were defeated. Additionally the Soviets actually crossed the Vistula and attempted to set up a beach head on the other side, but again the Soviets were forced to abandon the beach head due to intense pressure from the Germany army. The forces which reached Warsaw were those assigned on the Brest-Lublin offensive. The offensive was named as such because these were the strategic objectives of the offensive. From the 18th of July a serious push was launched westward from Soviet positions in southern Belarus and Northern Ukraine. The objective was reached in this offensive by the 28th of July when Chuikovs elite 8th Guard Army took Brest, while Konstantin Rokossovsky (A Polish commander in the Red Army) had taken Lublin on the 24th of July. The Warsaw uprising started on the 1st of August just 2 days after this offensive had reached it’s objectives in Lublin and Brest. Elements of the Belarussian front were already tentatively moving towards Warsaw, in an attempt to cut off the Germany Army group center’s retreat. However, if you get out your map, you’ll notice that the 8th Army in Brest was 180 kilometers away from Warsaw, and the first Polish Army and Rokossovsky were 130 kilometers away from Warsaw. The first units to arrive near Warsaw were from the much weaker 47th Army, which did not have sufficient armor. On the 29th of July the Soviet broadcasted a radio message to the Polish encouraging them to resist the Germans in general. The Soviets were hoping to catch the retreating Germans between the 47th Army to the north, Chuikov and Rokossovsky’s armies to the south, and a Polish uprising to the west, encircling the remnants of Army Group Center. However, the southern Armies could not move the 130–180 kilometers in just a couple of days through enemy terrain. The first Soviet elements rushed to Warsaw and arrived on the day of the uprising but was nastily surprised by the fact that rather than a panicked retreat of Army group center, the Soviet forces ran into 4 fresh German armored divisions, which engaged them east of Warsaw in the Battle of Radzymin/Wolomin. The Soviets lost this battle. When the Soviets elite units from the 8th Guards and 1st Polish Army arrived, they immediately engaged the German troops as well, and fought in the Battle of Studzianki south of Warsaw, between the 9th and 16th of August. While this battle was a resounding victory for the Soviets, other places on the front didn’t fare so well, and battle for Sandomierz to the south lasted an entire month until the 29th of August. The idea that they just stopped is simply false. This is a fantasy created to fit a political narrative, while the reality is that for the entire of August 1944, the Red Army fought multiple battles along the Vistula and Warsaw, the problem was that they didn’t win them all, in reality you cannot advance through an enemy you have not beaten. An additional note is that the Warsaw uprising was not coordinated with the Soviets, because the London backed resistance wished to control Warsaw on their own. The idea that the Soviet broadcast had anything to do with the initiation of the uprising is false. This uprising was a part of a series of uprisings under Operation Tempest, and this operation had already led to several towns being liberated by Polish militias. However, the drawback of this was that after this had happened in multiple Polish towns, the Germans had caught on, and were prepared for the same happening in Warsaw. For some reason this particular aspect is rarely ever mentioned.

Question: What is the ratio of aircraft shot down in the eastern front between Luftwaffe (German AF) and VVS (Sovyet AF)?
Answer: According to G.F. Krivosheev, the Soviets had 41,000 combat-aircraft losses in combat. Soviet recording keeping was quite precise on this. Unfortunately the same can’t be said about German record keeping. Germany produced over 34,000 BF-109s in WW2, and over 20,000 FW-190s. German records only accounts for 7,369 lost between 1941 and 1944. According to Dan Zamansky, between 1941 and 1943 the German air force had 21,888 combat losses in total, with 24,914 losses being possible, what ever this means. Of these 9,912 were on the eastern front, with an additional, 12,034 being “possible”. Now, if we isolate 1942 and 1943, we might get an idea of the exchange rate, as in 1941, many aircraft were simply destroyed on the ground in the opening stages and skew the numbers a bit, as they were not shot down in the air. Soviet combat air losses were 7,800 in 1942 and 11,200 in 1943. German air losses in the east were 3,693 in 1942 and 3,698 in 1943. German possible losses in the east were 4,587 in 1942 and 4,332 in 1943. The German possible losses are not non-combat or such things, but where the state of the aircraft is unclear. Most of the original German war time documents are actually lost. The German figure therefore includes aircraft in which a loss report was made, but the degree of damage not mentioned, this could be due to the pilot dying and so nothing was written, but it is not actually entirely clear. Consider then that the high number is 8,280 German aircraft lost in 1942, giving a 1.06:1 ratio in favor of the Soviets, while 8,030 German aircraft lost in 1943, giving a 1.39:1 ratio in favor of the Germans. The numbers are not totally unreasonable, but they do not make much sense. The Soviets were without a doubt throwing far more aircraft and of better models at the Germans in 1943 than in 1942, but this resulted in fewer German losses and more Soviet ones. There are unknown variables, and incomplete records at play, but I hope this information is at least somewhat useful.
