Question: What year were the first MBTs (Main Battle Tanks) deployed? How do they differ from modern MBTs?
Answer: Main Battle Tank (MBT) is not actually a real classification of tank. The MBT of a country is quite simply the main tank they use hence the name. This is almost always a medium tank and for most of the cold war literature it was referred to as such in the west. When the Soviets built the T-72 and T-64 tanks they were also designed under the name medium tank, because it was designated by mass. The Soviet themselves switched to classifying tanks as Main Tank and Special Tank, while in general, the idea of Main Battle Tank was formalized by the 1990 convention: “Treaty on Conventional Armed Forces in Europe”, aimed at reducing the presence of weapons. Certain island dwellers are entirely convinced the Centurion was the first MBT. This convention defined it as an Armored Fighting Vehicle (AFV), which has By this definition a T-34 or M3 Lee could be considered a main battle tank. The Chieftain which people often point to as being the first MBT was designed under the name of Medium Gun Tank No. 2. The designation o MBT was simply added retroactively, as well as for the centurion. In reality the MBT designation doesn’t tell you anything about a tank’s capabilities.

Name: Carl Hamilton
Question: Were there any American tanks used in the Battle of Kursk?
Answer: Indeed there was. The battle of Kursk saw vast amounts of Soviet tank reserves being used, which included all kinds of tanks in irregular formations. This included foreign tanks such as the M3 Lee tanks seen above, which was used by some units in the 6th Guards Army. Some M3 Stuart light tanks might also have participated in Kursk. The Soviets were not particularly happy with either of these tanks, the M3 Stuart used high octane aviation fuel, which meant they required a separate fuel supply from all other tanks, additionally it was very poorly armored and armed even compared to the worst Soviet tanks like the T-26. The M3 Lee was better received but the design was very bad as well, with the main gun being fixed in the hull. The M4 Sherman which the Soviets loved had not be delivered yet. It should be noted that British Churchill tanks also participated in Kursk as part of the 5th Guards Tank Army, where they fought against the elite SS Panzer corps. Due to mobility issues the Soviets were not entirely happy with the Churchill, however, the defensive aspects of the tank cannot be denied, and the Churchills were put where the fighting was toughest, and many of them survived the battle. Valentines and Matilda tanks also equipped some units of the Red Army, The Valentine Mk II with it’s 57mm gun, was very well equipped for anti tank fighting for a light tank. The Soviets compared the Valentines to M3 Stuats and T-60/T-70 Soviet light tanks, and fought that the Valentine was pretty well armored, and very well armed, as well has having pretty good off road mobility despite narrow tracks. It was therefore appreciated and used by many Soviet units even quite late in the war, as replacement for other light tanks, including at Kursk.

Question: Challenger II tanks are having a problem with mud in Ukraine. It has been reported, but are Russian tanks any better at it?
Answer: Yes, because Russian tanks are lighter. The reason the Challenger II has so much trouble is because of the ground pressure. The Challenger 2 is simply so heavy that it can sink into even the smallest amount of soft ground. And while it is true that Russian tanks like all tanks can get stuck in mud, being heavier makes you worse at this. We can even quite simply calculate how much. The T-90M tank, is 48t, has track length which touches the ground of 4.280m and a track width of 0.580m This means it has a track surface area of 4,9648 m2 and if we divide the weight with this, we get that the T-90M has 9.668t per m2 ground pressure. The Challenger 2 tank, is 75t with add-on armor, has track length which touches the ground of 4.790m and a track width of 0.650m This means it has a track surface area of 6.227 m2 and if we divide the weight with this, we get that the Challenger 2 has 12.044t per m2 ground pressure. That is 25% higher than the T-90M. Additionally, the T-90M has 1130hp for it’s 48t, giving a ratio of 23.5 hp/t. The Challenger 2 has 1200hp for it’s 75t, giving a ratio of 16 hp/t. In both ground pressure and hp/t the Challenger 2 is vastly inferior to even the heaviest Russian or Soviet tanks on the field right now, it is a very fat tank, and this contributes to how easy it is getting stuck in mud. The Soviet T-64 that Ukraine uses has a ground pressure closer to 8t per m2, and this is what Ukrainian tankers are used to driving around the fields in.

Question: What are some good historical fictional novels about Samurai?
Answer: Well, the most famous in the west is probably Shogun, by James Clavell which is a fictionalized version of the struggle between Tokugawa Ieyesu and the western alliance near the end of the Japanese warring states period. It is seen from the point of view of a British navigator (pilot) of a privateer vessel chasing the Portuguese to east Asia by going through the pacific. If you have never read much about Samurai, this is a pretty good introduction to the subject, though it is not overly historically accurate, it is entertaining, it is also made into a TV series twice, both of which are pretty great to be honest. The 2024 Shogun TV series I can also recommend Cloud of Sparrows by Takashi Matsuoka. Again it includes foreign characters which are a great bridge into understanding the culture of samurai. It is far more accurate, and portrays many more aspects of society than Shogun, it also includes both the end and beginning of the Edo period as settings which is quite interesting, it has a good plot and is very well written. I recommend these books over purely Japanese books on the subject for the reason that they are difficult to get into from foreigners, and I suspect you are not Japanese if asking here. Additionally, most people interested in samurai are probably less interested in the day to day life of feudal Japan in general, and more about what made samurai interesting, which are the highlights of these two books.

Name: Carl Hamilton
Question: Why is the Axis defeat at Stalingrad (1942/43) viewed as the turning point of WWII? Operation Bagration (1944) caused more German casualties, Army Group Center was destroyed, and the Soviets pushed the Germans out of Russia completely.
Answer: It is viewed as the turning point because it was in the sense that after Stalingrad Germany no longer had the initiative on the eastern front, and everything they did from there on was merely a reacting to the Soviets who had the control. You could also view it thusly: Moscow proved Germany could be stopped, Stalingrad proved Germany could be defeated, Kursk proved Germany could no longer attack, definitively putting them on the defensive for the rest of the war. Bagration was the largest and most complete victory for the Soviets without a doubt, but at that point the Soviets were in a much better position. The Soviets won the battle of Stalingrad, despite the desperate nature of the battle. Despite the defeats in Ukraine in the same year. Despite the low manpower and resources available to the Soviets in November 1942. This is the time when the Soviets overcame these difficulties. They managed to apply a heavy economy or force, concentrate and build up a critical mass, confuse and surprise the enemy, use effective intelligence and destroy a large part of his forces. But it was a massively costly victory, and not a total one either, as the Soviets failed to destroy the German Caucasus army. It did however knock out most of the axis support that Germany had, from Italy, Hungary and Romania, which was a crucial step in reducing their presence on the eastern front. While Bagration was indeed more impressive, it was a more comfortable situation, where Soviet superiority over German forces was essentially undisputed. Not that it was not hard fought, but Stalingrad was the most intense single operation in history in terms of manpower and equipment lost, and set up the remainder of the eastern front.

Name: Carl Hamilton
Question: How significant is the reported advance of the Freedom of Russia Legion, the Russian Volunteer Corps, and the Sibir Battalion into Kursk and Belgorod Oblasts?
Answer: This advance is a PR stunt and not really an advance at all. Essentially it consists of a skirmish that didn’t go so well for the AFU at the border checkpoint, it is also not the first fight there. It was followed by a fake claim that AFU troops were deep inside Russian territory, supported by a video of a couple of soldiers on an empty street. Unfortunately for this footage is from the Ukrainian village of Ryzhevka, in the Sumy region, which itself was occupied by the Russians in 2022 and similarly used for propaganda purposes. In the border crossing attempt, which was filmed almost in its entirety, two Ukrainian T-64BV tanks fired at an empty building and two random objects, before being disabled by a mine and later destroyed by Chechen national guard unit with a grenade from a drone. By my estimation this T-64BV managed to cross about 50m over the check point, the crew can be seen running back across the border after it was tracked. The second tank did not cross the border, but instead retreated upon seeing the first tank on fire. There were no Russian troops present at the border check point, instead the border troops being Chechen, watched the whole thing from the air and naturally put it on tiktok immediately. This advance was a small scale attempt to generate support for the Ukrainian course, and maybe also put some pressure on the Russian public during their election time. But being caught faking the location is a PR nightmare, though many will simply deny it, one can just look at google earth images from the location I mentioned it see for themselves. It is important for Ukraine to generate some victories in order to persuade western backers who are not delivering the promised aid, but I think this was a very silly way of going about it, and probably will adversely affect the course more than anything else.

Name: Carl Hamilton
Question: In WWII, from mid 1941-late 1943, 40% of USSR was under German occupation. During this time, or later in 1944-1945, did the Soviet Union experience a personnel shortage? It seemed like no matter how big their losses were, it was never an issue.
Answer: If you mean amount of population, then it is true that about 40% of the USSR was under German occupation. To be precise, 79,972,000 of the Soviet population was in fact under occupation in November 1942, which was the largest amount to live under occupation. Of course this included those who died, and those who were in hiding like partisans. Soviet Partisans made up a large contribution in the effort against German occupation. Considering that the total Soviet population in 1941 was roughly 190 million people, about 41% of the Soviet population was actually under occupation in November 1942. To make matters worse, many of the remaining population were not useful productive people. And I don’t mean that as in their system was bad. I mean refugees without adequate housing and a lack of infrastructure to take care of them were not able to significantly contribute industrially. But perhaps even more important, the Soviet Union was a country that had essentially just solved the medical and agricultural barriers to population explosion, as such it was a very young country. What do I mean by that? Of the about 190 million Soviet citizens in 1941, 72 million of them were below the working age, i.e. children. And 17 million were retired. That means roughly 47% of the entire population were too old or too young to actually work. There were 52 million working age men in the USSR in 1941, and during world war war 2, roughly 36 million people would serve in the Red Army, while several million were women, we can estimate about half of every single able bodied man in 4 years served at least some time in the Red Army. While the massive young generation allowed people to mature into conscription age and working age, this wasn’t just a small problem. It was a gigantic problem of proportions that very few countries have ever faced and survived. The reason why it might feel like that it wasn’t an issue, is because there are many driven narratives which very much likes to talk of the USSR was merely a blob of people, in that way you will never learn how they solved problems. There are many political reasons for this, but I think that’s a talk for another time. We can go into a few more details about the manpower shortages of the USSR in WW2. Disregarding the officer purge and the loss of troops in 1941, there was already a shortage in comparison to the plans of the USSR. In 1937, the Soviet army was in many ways a territorial militia, with a small but extremely modern and mechanized core made up of 49 rifle divisions, with 35 territorials militia divisions. A pretty high ratio of local militias to infantry divisions. By december 1940, the Red Army was mobilizing and had reached 152 rifle divisions, and increase of 3 fold in 3 years, this is not counting of course the 26 cavalry divisions, 9 mechanized corps, 18 tank divisions, 12 airborne divisions and 10 motorized divisions. To in 1938 the Red Army was 1.5 million strong, by December 1940 it was 4.2 million strong. As the Soviets knew the Germans would invade and earlier than expected after the surrender of France, they were absolutely pushing the panic button and would enlist another 1.1 million men in the spring of 1941, to reach and army of 5.3 million by June 1941. This was a problem for the Soviet work force, even before they start losing them. And not only did all of these hundreds of knew divisions need enlisted man power. They all needed officers. Officers who in the very best case had been trained from 1937, but in reality many of which has been trained only in the last 2 years. Additionally they needed reserves. And while the soviets managed to build an impressive reserve, they simply could not train officers fast enough for the needs of the army. Furthermore, who makes the best officers? Stupid people with bad math and reading skills? No. Educated people with good understanding of many sciences make the better officers, unfortunately they also make better skilled workers, scientists and engineers. This answer is already long, but I hope you can appreciate that manpower shortage is not just a simple question of if there technically exist people in your country, it is also a matter of time and many other factors. Without a doubt, and just read some non-English/German book on the subject and you will soon discover just how big the problems the USSR actually had to overcome was, including in terms of manpower resources.

Name: Carl Hamilton
Question: What is wrong with the American Abrams tank, and why are the Ukrainians losing them?
Answer: There are some things wrong with the Abrams tank, despite the endless optimism. Reading most other answers, one would think that the Abrams was perfectly suited for modern operations in Ukraine against drones, despite being designed for fighting in Germany in 1980s against other tanks. There are in fact flaws to the design, the tank has strengths and weaknesses. The most and most obvious thing that’s wrong with the Abrams, is that it is too heavy. It is a really heavy tank, and due to excessive eating it has only gained weight since 1980. The tank was designed originally at 55t, due to attempts at adding more armor to the tank and other upgrades, the M1A2 Sepv3 is estimated to sit at around 73t. The engine compartment has not gotten bigger. Even the older models without DU armor are heavy vehicles. And it has many disadvantages, firstly it does not fit on to the common 50t railroad flat bed cars, which is a logistical problem. Secondly, it does not do well with heavily muddied areas because its ground pressure is massive. Thirdly, it is unable to cross some bridges due to weight limits. Fourthly, the weight means that components of the Abrams require more maintenance and is under more stress than on lighter tanks. Finally, the heavy tank is difficult to tow for other tanks, meaning only a few specialized recovery vehicles can do it. All this weight unfortunately, has not gone where it is needed most, which is the top. Despite around 15t of additional protective upgrades, none of the M1 Abrams ever received anything to make them more difficult to destroy from the top. This means the original M1 Abrams and the newest M1 Abrams are equally vulnerable to drones, DPICM and other top attack weapons. The already excessive weight might also be one of the reasons why no one has added additional armor to the top in the form of cages. The M1 is not a bad tank, but it has design flaws, it was not build to do what it is doing now, it could be better, in fact a drastically different design would be a better option than just adding more weight on this tank. There are several other comparative disadvantageous of the Abrams to some of its competitors, but I think this is enough to point out why it might not feel so hot right now. It’s probably quite a challenge to fight from the front in a tank duel, but what does it matter if it is getting stuck in mud due to its weight, getting destroyed by cheap drones or getting tracked by artillery before it ever gets in range of other tanks?

Name: Carl Hamilton
Question: Did Russia give away any T-34 tanks to Britain during World War II?
Answer: Yes, the Soviet Union gave away a T-34 and a KV-1 to both the UK and the US. Reports from both countries circulate the internet including a Soviet view of the western allied analysis. The T-34 was given to these countries in order to help them understand the stage of Soviet armor development and give inspiration for both countries to create effective medium tanks. However, by the time the T-34 arrived in the US, the Sherman was already well under way and little was gained from the T-34, though the KV-1 was rather influential on western design, as the US did not have a heavy tank program yet. The Pershing tank in particular share a striking amount of similarities to the KV-1, which you can read about here Copy or Not? #5: Soviet Tanks vs Western Tanks. The british who did not have a successful medium tank at this point responded quite differently, they very much considered producing the Soviet T-34 but with a 17 pounder cannon, which would have been an interesting concept, though the turret was pretty cramped even with the smaller F-34. They also considered making CS version of the KV-1 with a 150mm howitzer. Which you can read about here: Bovington: T-34 and KV-1 impressions Now the reason why the British didn’t do this after all, was because the US essentially promised to arm the entire British army, and delivered I think about 17,000 Sherman tanks in WW2 to the British, which is more than they could have produced themselves anyway. So there was no need for a British T-34 after all. But as many of you know, they didn’t abandon the idea of putting a 17 pounder in a medium tank, and applied this to the Sherman instead of the T-34 in the famous firefly variant.

Question: How did the Poles treated Germans and Russians in their territories acquired as a result of ww1? There are some claims that the actions led to Nazi-Soviet pack to invade and divide Poland and the Katyn massacre.
Answer: According to realist international relations theory, the treatment of Germans or Russians would not greatly affect the decision to invade a country. Indeed I would say this is also the case here. Poland also did not acquire the territory due to World War 1, but due to the Polish intervention in the Russian-civil war, as the Polish attacked the Red Army, after it took control of Vilnius following the withdrawal of German forces from the area. Poland fared surprisingly well in the Soviet-Polish war and ended up with a considerable part of Belarus under occupation as well as parts of Ukraine. Due to the ongoing Russian civil war, the Soviets were essentially forced to sign a peace treaty on these unfavorable terms, which satisfied no one really, as the Polish had hoped for a great realm connected to both the Baltic and black sea, while the Soviets had hoped for total control of the former Russian Empire. At this point a future conflict was guaranteed. In 1939 the Soviets recaptured the territory of Belarus and Ukraine from Poland as well as some minor additions. The reason for this was not due to how people were treated in these areas, but because the Soviets did not want part of Ukraine or Belarus in foreign hands. Likewise, the treatment of Germans in Poland was completely irrelevant to the Germans. After WW1 some territories of historical Germany was given to Poland and Germany wanted these territories back, additionally as part of the Nazi ideology the Poles were considered sub-human and ideal slave labor, as such the plan was to also exploit the remaining part of Poland for the benefit of Germans until they no longer needed them at which point the plan was to exterminate the remaining Poles to allow for a great German Empire, which of course also included much of the USSR. The Katyn massacre and other acts of repression from the Soviets were not carried out as a form of revenge either. This was due to the Soviets wanting to attain control over the areas quickly, and this was done through repressing those who were class enemies in the Soviet view, as well as eliminating those which the Soviets considered could form the cadre of a Polish resistance or alternative government. As such, officers, government officials and civil servants were cynically targeted to prevent such a revolutionary core from forming. It had very little to do with ethnicity, and quite a lot to do with expediency of establishing the Soviet control. Not that the Polish government was as popular in Belarus as modern Polish historians try to revise history to show, George Sanford(2005) in his book Katyn and the Soviet Massacre of 1940, notes that following the German invasion local militias in western Belarus spontaneously started fighting with the Polish army, killing as many as 2,500 Polish soldiers and border guards. On the contrary no spontaneous militias were formed to fight the Soviets. Though all of this Pales in the comparison of the brutality that the Germans showed in their advance, killing at least 6,000 civilians in the bombing of Warsaw the following assault on Warsaw killed an additional 18,000 civilians, due to casual brutality of the Nazis around 200,000 civilians were killed by the Germans in the invasion roughly 5,700 per day.

Name: Carl Hamilton
Question: Why do people say that Germany should have built more Panzer IVs instead of heavier and heavier designs to stop the masses of tanks of the Allies in WWII while NATO also built ever heavier tanks during the Cold War to counter the Soviet tank masses?
Answer: Building more Panzer IVs would not have altered the outcome of World War 2, but people often say this to point out how flawed the German heavy tank program actually was. The truth is however, that the Panzer IV building programs were also flawed. The entire German war machine was high inefficient and suffered from lack of early mobilization and massive resource waste as well as outdated production methods. The heavy tanks were not designed really to stop masses of other tanks, but simply to survive at all against the common AT weapons of the time. AMX-30 had just 80mm of armor which is pretty bad for a 1960s tank. During the cold war NATO did not really opt for a heavy tank design approach. In the 1960s the French and Germans in fact opted for light tanks exclusively, mainly the Leopard 1 and the AMX-30, while Britain and America went for conventional medium tanks in the Centurion, Chieftain and M48 and M60 Patton tanks. Again, these tanks were not made to counter Soviet tanks. Initially Soviet technology was drastically underestimated leading to generations of western tanks were had pretty low capability. The centurion in reality was not at all adequate compared to it’s competition. When Hungarians in 1956 drove a T-54A (not even the newest version at the time) tank into the British embassy, the British took a look and panicked just a little, as it turned out the British 84mm and American 90mm guns were not really able to reliably penetrate the front of the T-54. This facilitated the adoption of the reliable 105mm L7 cannon, specifically made as a tank destroyer cannon against the T-54. Of course, at the time the L7 was being introduced the Soviets were almost finished developing their next generation tanks the T-62 and T-64. These tanks caused the next series of western development namely the Challenger, Leopard 2 and Abrams tanks. Throughout the cold war, the west was practically always reacting to Soviet tank developments and according to the US department of defense, in terms of quality the Soviets were basically always ahead at least a little. Now you’ll always see people say things like this was designed for being outnumbered 3 to 1. That’s a statement that in historians in technical terms call “bullshit”. No one designs, plans or hopes to be outnumbered 3 to 1. No one. Being outnumbered was simply a product of the vast amount of resources the Soviets were able to concentrate in a highly centralized production structure. The answer to masses of Soviet tanks was never “better western tanks”. It was nuclear weapons. Let’s not kid ourselves. The US had nuclear mines dug into the ground in west Germany, and they absolutely planned on using them in case of a Soviet invasion. It wasn’t until the late 1970s that the idea of defeating a Soviet armored attack without nuclear weapons was seriously considered, and this in turn resulted in a host of new anti tank weapons including I-TOW, Abrams, Hellfire, A-10, AGM-65 and others.

Question: Which Russian tank has the strongest armor: T-80 or T-72B3? What makes its armor superior to other models?
Answer: This is actually a fairly complicated question, and there isn’t an obvious answer. Now originally the T-80 had better armor than the T-72, by a fair bit even. But in 1985 the T-72B was introduced which incorporated NERA special armour, which is the same as is used in Abrams and Challenger tanks. With the T-80U in the same year the armor of the T-80 was upgraded to also include NERA elements, but instead of having air caps, they have cellular polymer armour. Exactly how this works, is actually still not understood in the public domain in the west even after 30 years since the fall of the USSR. I suspect, that the T-80 being the premium tank, got the better version of NERA, and thus always had the better protection. What the actual levels of protection are from the front right now is also not known. What has happened to the armor of the T-72B3 and the T-80BVM is hard to say, but it seems very likely that since 1985 the internal armour technology has moved forward. Truth of the matter is that any modern tank in service has secret armor, and while nationalists online always claim their tank is made of particularly magical elements, we just don’t know actually.

Question: Does the submachine gun still play a role in close quarter battle tactics, or has it been eclipsed by other weapons?
Answer: At least in active military use the submachine gun is essentially obsolete. Some remain in service as personal defense weapons, but it’s very rare on a global scale. The vast majority of rear line troops who previously would have been given submachine guns are now given carbines with intermediate cartridges. The most common carbines for self defense includes the M4 and AKS-74U.

Question: Why did the soviets not field more advanced tanks such as the T-64, T-72, T-80, etc during the Soviet-afghan war?
Answer: Because there was no need to, and because the units involved were not equipped with them. The Soviets commitment to Afghanistan was far smaller than what people generally tend to think. The Soviet force was made up mostly of the 40th Army plus some airborne units. The 40th army consisted of a category B (not full readiness) infantry division, and 2 category A (full strength) divisions, namely the 5th Guards Motor Rifle Division, and 103rd Airborne division. The airborne obviously were not equipped with MBTs, the category B divisions were equipped with T-55 or T-62 tanks, while the 5th Guards Motor Rifle Division were one of the first to be upgraded to the T-62M standard, it was also not equipped with the T-72, T-64 or T-80. The 201st and 68th category B infantry divisions also joined the area for operations, as well as some smaller independent brigades and air units. But that was it. The total force committed including all air support was only 115,000 at any one time, less than half the amount of troops committed to Ukraine on the first day, and that was the peak of manpower there. The USSR saw it mostly as a lower priority ground war and occupation, with some modern air units, though many were still equipped with the aging Su-17, while those in Europe were Su-22M+, Su-24 or Su-25 aircraft. Likewise, the T-62 was thought to be just fine for fighting insurgents who didn’t have any advanced tanks or anti tank weapons. The T-64s, T-72s and T-80s were reserved for fighting against NATO because they were a serious opponent in this field. Out of it’s military the Soviet Union committed about 3% of it to fighting in Afghanistan, in contrast to the 1 low medium priority army deployed in Afghanistan, the Soviet forces in Germany alone amounted to 5 elite category A armies with extra reinforcement plus an entire air army and dedicated strategic short range support units. That is why you never saw any of the Soviet advanced tanks in Afghanistan, it wasn’t necessary and it wasn’t a high priority location.

Question: In January 1943, the Soviets offered the Germans still encircled in the Stalingrad pocket generous surrender terms. If they had accepted the offer, did the Red Army really intend on keeping those terms?
Answer: Absolutely, and the Germans did accept by the way. The Red Army intended and generally did kept the terms they offered, after all they were not Germans. The majority of German POWs survived, even in Soviet captivity, with a mortality rate up to 35.8% as opposed the Soviet POWs in captivity in Germany, of which nearly 60% died, which is the majority. Many people argue that the Soviets killed the POWs at Stalingrad based on a quick skim of the Wikipedia page for it. However, there are some flaws in this argument. This is from the book Hitler: The Pathology of Evil by Victor, George (2009), which happens to be the only book source on Wikipedia related to the number of POWs taken at Stalingrad which is said to be 91,000. However, the first obvious problem is that it doesn’t actually say that. The other source is a British tabloid paper, without any references, so not exactly a credible source. The second thing to notice here is that the most credible statement on the page I have shown you, is the direct quote from Paulus saying they have at least 18,000 wounded who are not receiving any medical care. These people died, if anyone is in doubt. Because getting shot and then not receiving medical care will do that, even if it isn’t instant. Additionally, we know that many Soldiers continued to fight even after Paulus had surrendered, according to Wiki this number was at least 11,000, but again no source, so who know how many it really was. Either way, it took a month to clear out the remaining soldiers afterwards, so it was not few. So 91,000 Germans, 18,000 were almost certainly going to die due to their untreated wounds, 11,000 at least were still fighting and would be killed, were they counted as the surrendered? Then we come to the surviveability of malnutrition and exhausted soldiers on a march in freezing temperatures. No doubt many of the surviving soldiers were too weak to truly survive such a trip, even without being seriously wounded. Many died to to the rampant sickness inside the German ranks near the end of Stalingrad, particularly typhus. 1945–1946 there was a Soviet wide famine, and guess who was not prioritized for feeding, shockingly it was the Nazis. That’s not really cruel or murder, Nazi POWs obviously should not be fed before the civilian population in general. The German POWs ultimately returned in the 1950s. This is all fairly important context for the idea that the Soviets simply killed the Germans. Some 5,000 or so Germans returned to Germany from Stalingrad, but usually when this is mentioned the context is not given. I am not even sure that all of the 91,000 pows were actually German, there could easily have been Romanian or Italian troops in the city by the time of surrender, as some units were pushed aside on the outskirts of Stalingrad. Obviously those troops would not return to Germany. In short, the calculations which usually figure into the debate on this, are pretty poor on the internet. They lack context, and the veracity of the numbers and the surrounding variables are pretty poorly argued usually. Fact of the matter is that German POWs were nearly twice as likely to survive WW2 as Soviet ones were, and many of the German deaths were their own doing, by continuing to fight and have wounded without treatment, their burning of Ukraine’s food also causing the famine which in turn also killed more German POWs. Final note, the 91,000 figure is a bit of a mystery, it seems that others reference The Second World War: Ambitions to Nemesis by Bradley Lightbody, (2004, p. 152), however Lightbody, does not have a source for this number at all. Though he does have a bibliography which includes Ian Kershaw (great historian) and Antony Beevor (less great). The numbers might honestly be available in the Soviet archives, if anyone cares to look them up on Istmat, but I think I have chased this number long enough for a Quora post.

Name: Carl Hamilton
Question: Why is critical thinking a necessity in our society?
Answer: Critical thinking is extremely important for the progress of society and always has been. You live in a chaotic torrent of information, and much if not most of it is simply not true. Critical thinking allows to you evaluate information, judging it based on the arguments it presents in order to make points. You should be able to sift out the facts from the fiction. Understand the meaning of those facts. Question what you know and make questions to find out what you don’t know. Analyze problems related to it. Evaluate the information. Create solutions to problems. Whether it is about how to get a particular nail into a wall of a particular material, or whether the politicians are making policy based on your interests and feasibility, you must be able to understand the world around you. Without critical thinking, you are bound to merely repeat what others tell you, meaning you have no agency of your own, and merely act out what designs others have for you. A society like this is stagnant, unproductive and probably unpleasant to live in.

Name: Carl Hamilton
Question: Why are many people so incurious about the world and about how we know what we know?
Answer: I do not think it is fully understood entirely. In order to really get to the bottom of this a pretty exceptional study would have to be conducted with a very large survey base, which I am not aware of being done, and so I wouldn’t say there is one conclusive result, however there are perspectives and known variables. Firstly, it’s important to point out, that most people have some curiosity, with a small exception, that curiosity is just topical. Most people sadly do not care about history, real politics or science for example, unless it’s that small part which they work with. On the other hand, 90% or so of people are fairly curious about other people’s bodies, and this is essentially because it promotes the continued existence of our race. Then we can talk a bit about social factors. If you have primary socialization (how you are raised) which rewards curiosity, likely you will get more. Children of academics are provably significantly more likely to take an interest in science and culture, because their parents teach that this is a beneficial thing at an early age. Secondary socialization (other influences during growing up) can also affect this in less predictable ways. Next you have cultural factors. Some societies appreciate intellectualism more than others, and promote learning or specializing in various things. Japan for example has considerable cultural traits which promote highly specialized hobbies, while Europe tends to promote more rounded approaches to cultural activities. A large part of this is to what degree the society considers it prestigious, with a down turn in the value of intellectual degrees in the western world, there is likely to be a link in a down turn of interest in pursuits of related endeavors. There is also psychological aspects to consider, what you might consider to be a lack of curiosity, can simply be a cognitive tendency called anchoring. Essentially, you have already found the truth, and any additional and particularly contradictory information is rejected, or at least resisted. This is extremely common, and extreme anchoring is a trait in some mental conditions as well. People simply think they already know, so why be more curious? Politically of course, this is related to apathy, a society where you feel as if there is nothing you can do about it, will promote apathy, and apathy leads to a lack of curiosity. Everything is the same, nothing matter, you can’t change anything, why bother? Finally I would like to highlight the fact, that many people simply do not have time to be curious. The fact of the matter is that the majority of the human race, lives in highly stressful environments, where the majority of time has to be spent on carving out a living at all. Question: Is Russia's ''accusation of NATO troops are actually manning and directly overseeing Ukraine's advanced anti-air defense systems which were provided by the West'' true?
Answer: Quite likely yes, and it should not be surprising to anyone really. Think back on similar historical situations, such as the Vietnam war or the Korean War. The Soviet Union send people to support the Northern side in both wars, and denied they did so in both cases. In the Vietnam war China also send people who even joined in front line operations, and quite a few as well. In Korea Soviet pilots engaged American ones in jet fights. In Vietnam Soviet soldiers helped man and teach the use of anti aircraft systems. So the exact situation that Russia is saying is happening in Ukraine, has already happened in history before with the roles reversed. Now, often when people talk about Vietnam and people mention Soviet volunteers, you see people laugh and say “yeah right, volunteers”. Volunteers historically has generally shown an overt involvement of governments in various proxy wars. One of the few exceptions being the international brigades in the Spanish civil war, but the volunteers of Germany, Italy and the Soviet Union were all there on behalf of their governments. So if we can accept that volunteers are very often a cover for actual government operations, then acknowledge what is going on in Ukraine, 30,000 people were officially part of the Ukrainian foreign legion just a couple of weeks into the war. These included people like Trevor Cadieu, a Canadian high ranking general. If a Russian high ranking general was a volunteer in a war against America, not a single US news-outlet would believe the story of him being a personal volunteer acting alone. Since then no official count has been made on how many volunteers are in the Ukrainian forces, but still enough to man several front line battalions after 2 years. Wouldn’t it just be the most weird coincidence if among the many thousands of NATO veterans who happens to serve in the Ukrainian forces, were a whole bunch of technical specialist with previous experience on the exact AA systems delivered to Ukraine? This is not such a stretch, Russia has provided no evidence, but the US also didn’t provide evidence for Vietnam, yet it was true, and i am pretty sure it is no different now than it was then.

Question: Is anarchism the worst political ideology?
Answer: In my opinion anarchism barely qualifies as a political ideology at all. Anarchism is the absence of rulers and governance. Some also define this as the absense of a state, and consider a state to be an entity which has the legal monopoly of violence over a territory. We’ll get back to that in a moment. The first problem with anarchy is that it unlike most ideologies, does it not offer an ideal method of governance. It says governance itself is the problem, then throws all organizational achievement on the floor and says it will sort itself out better like that. Anarchy in it’s very definition has already been tried by basically everyone, and without outside interference. It is called the early stone age. Every human tribe originated in anarchy, no states, no police, no government, no rulers. Just tribes going around, having a life expectancy of around 25, and generally suffering and dying. The first state in the creation of mankind as the dominant species in the world, was to step away from this, and create organization of humankind which went beyond a tribe, and with a unified ruling system that could direct efforts beyond what a small group of people could believe in. This system pretty much conquered the entire world, and the few places it didn’t never really progressed beyond the stone age. The modern society is ridiculously complicated and rely on a massive amounts of systems of authority and ruling. Getting rid of this system would result in the collapse of life as is known to basically everyone, because global trade systems and networks are unimaginable without international cooperation, which more or less requires nations. Finally, if we just stick to the very basic idea, that anarchism is supposed to remove the monopoly of violence over a territory, the implications here alone are enough to see why this is such a silly idea. Right the police doesn’t have a monopoly of violence, now everyone has equal access to employ violence. Congratulations all disputes that cannot be solved by talking about it, is now solved by whoever is the most ruthless and well armed. I am constantly amused at the idea that people watched the movie Mad Max Fury Road, and thought. “You know what, that’s the world I consider most ideal.” The de facto outcome of any state of anarchy, is that people will organize into states as fast as possible, and those who do not do this, will quickly be dominated by those who do. Not saying there is anything wrong with anarchists or anarchists making criticism of any system of government, corporations, economy etc. But if anarchism is just a criticism of authority and not a real desire to live in a chaotic world of lawless barbarism, which is what anarchy is, then it’s not an ideology. Freedom is not a system or way of life, you are always going to be a slave to things like, needing food, and quite quickly to other necessities of reality itself. Personal freedom to do anything, is not possible.

Question: Is Ukraine repeating the mistake they made in Bakhmut by trying to hold onto Avdeevka?
Answer: There is little choice due to the nature of what is mechanically possible for Ukraine. Let me explain to you the defensive tactics of Ukraine as I see it, and you will see why Avdiivka and indeed many other cities like Bakhmut are defended the way that they are. Fresh Ukrainian Soldiers prepare to counter-attack near the Avdiivka Coke Plant. To quote Zelensky during the battle of Bakhmut, if they simply retreat from the city, the immediate result will simply be a repeat at another city. This is certainly true, if for no other reason than the fact that Ukraine has chosen to build their defensive lines in cities and use them as strong points. But the fact remains that simply giving up Avdiivka will not improve the situation much, as they will simply have to do the same kind of operation in another city. Ukraine has opted for a tactic known as flexible defense, but they cannot carry this out in practice. Flexible defense essentially is based around the idea of having many small obstacles and firing positions, which are not obvious concrete bunkers. Instead a network of temporary positions, with concrete bunkers mainly serving as bombardment shelters. This is very difficult to attack without big losses in a conventional war of the past, for example the Finnish initially used it to great success in 1939 against the Soviets. However, there are two major problems with it. Firstly, this kind of fortification is labour intensive, each unit digs multiple firing positions, and they still prefer to have concrete dugouts for bombardments. This means that it can take months or even years to make an effective network. Avdiivka is one such network which has been fortified for 8 years non-stop. Secondly, without mechanization this is essentially a form of static fortification network. How do you get out of a fortification network if the enemy is about to take it? Basically you don’t if you cannot be driven away. Walking out of a trench in full view of the enemy is very risky to put it mildly. Does it work for some? Yes, sure, but a lot of Ukrainian troops die in every retreat, because the moment you are not in a trench, you are food for rocket artillery and other unpleasant things. You have to understand, that the vast majority of Ukrainian troops are leg infantry with a few civilian cars for transport if they are lucky. Only a few brigades are actually armed with armored troop carriers. Remains of an AFU platoon near Avdiivka attempts to escape a position moments before they are hit by mortars, as seen from a Russian observation drone. So, the troops stuck in Avdiivka are essentially fighting to the end or to a local surrender. Abandoning Avdiivka would result in the troops there being cut down on the way out, only to repeat the process in a town, with worse fortifications another place. Essentially, the entire line of contact is a build up area, with very strong and long time trenches build by the Ukrainians, a combination of positions with low manpower ready to jump out and fire some rockets at advancing Russians, while acting as forward observers in general for artillery. If their positions are being stormed, they have very little chance of actually escaping, but they can sell their lives costly, and this is in fact the actual tactic of Ukraine. If this line of defense eventually is broken through in depth, Ukrainian leg infantry will be fighting in the open, without trenches, without bunkers, against an enemy currently throwing at least 10 times the amount of artillery their way. As such Ukraine is not making a mistake in Avdiivka, they are selling the lives of their soldiers as dearly as they can for now. The only mistake is potentially the leg infantry assaults without artillery, tank or air cover they are doing, in desperate attempts to hold unto the defense network, in my opinion such wave attacks are more costly than even the best defenses warrant.

Question: How does the British Warrior Armoured Fighting Vehicle compare to other country's vehicles and equipment in the same class?

Neither of these armors will stand up to dedicated anti tank weapons or any modern quality, but it should be noted that both also have some armour upgrades which will allow them to potentially survive some low yield shaped charges. Warrior Hull UFP: LOS 115mm RHAe (38mm@70d) Warrior Hull LFP: LOS 67mm RHAe (41mm@70d) BMP-3 Hull UFP: LOS 105mm RHAe (18mm@80d) BMP-3 Hull LFP: LOS 69mm RHAe (60mm@30d) Armament: The difference in this category is huge, the warrior comes with a 30mm cannon and a 7.62mm machine gun, that is all. While the Warrior can be outfitted with a Milan missile it is not standard, it is not nearly as good as the Agona/Bastion missiles of the BMP-3, nor can you reloaded it from the safety of the vehicle. Additionally, the 100mm gun offers much more distance and firepower against soft targets than the warrior can deliver. 30mm RARDEN clip for loading the gun. Even if we just focus on the 30mm cannons that both vehicles have, the warrior is poorly armed. The L21A1 cannon that the warrior is outfitted with, is a very primitive gun, that requires 3 round stripper clips to fire. That means the gun is not fully automatic, and I invite you to go on youtube and see just how phenomenally slow this gun is. In contrast, the 30mm cannon on the BMP-3 is a duel chain fed autocannon with at least 300rpm, the gunner never have to stop shooting to load another 3 rounds, and can be used as an AA gun at close range, additionally on the BMP-3 the gunner can switch between HE and AP with a button. Basically every other IFV that isn’t British, uses a similar autocannon with a high rate of fire and automatic loading. The Warrior is the worst armed IFV I know of still being in use. Weight: Warrior: 25t BMP-3: 19t Engine and Speed Warrior: 550hp = 22 hp/t, 75km/h top road speed BMP-3: 500hp = 27 hp/t, 72km/h top road speed Troop Capacity: Warrior: 3 crew + 10 passengers BMP-3: 3 crew + 9 passengers Note that both are intended to carry 7 soldiers in a squad. Question: Is the legend of Rurik, called to rule the Russian land, a Germanic falsification? It is simply a modified legend about Hengist and Horsa who were called to ruled over the English land.
Answer: Romanticized Rurik The legend of Rurik is not a Germanic anything, it is based on the earliest surviving written codices from the Rus states. The Primary Chronicle as it is called, was probably written sometime in the 12th century, and covers an area from around the 9th century forward. It has as such nothing to do with Germans. It is equivalent to the primary sources: The Anglo-Saxon Chronicle and The Royal Frankish Annals. These sources are not entirely reliable and often a bit contradictory, but there are incredibly few written sources from this period, so we tend to take what we can. There is however a general consensus that Rurik was indeed the founder of the Rurik dynasty that ruled many of the Rus princely states, including Novgorod and Kiev. Rurik himself was likely a Swedish Viking and Varangian mercenary serving in Byzantium before becoming a warlord and ruler.

Question: Why did Russia have a larger number of heavy tanks compared to Germany, even though Germany had renowned tank designers such as Krupp and Porsche?
Answer: The Soviet heavy tank program, was far more mature and thought out than the German one. The Germans genuinely thought bigger was better, and had no logical limitations on their development of their heavy tanks. In contrast the Soviet heavy tanks were mass producible and reliable. In fact, by German standards Soviet heavy tanks were not heavy tanks at all. The IS-2 at 46 tons, was only slightly heavier than the Panther at 44.5 tons. While the Tiger was 57 tons and the King Tiger 70 ton. Indeed in terms of weight there was more difference between a IS-2 and a King Tiger than an IS-2 and a T-34–85 (31 tons). The Soviet mass produced just 2 types of heavy tanks during the war, the KV-1 and the IS-2, though there were of course variants built on the chassis. The KV-1 was built from 1939 to 1943, and so the Soviets already had a head start. By the time the first Tiger tank rolled off the line the Soviet had already produced almost 3,900 KV-1 tanks, which is more than all the heavy tanks the Germans would produce in WW2. In the first year of war the Soviets still managed to produce over 1,000 KV-1 heavy tanks, and they continued to refine this production capability, focusing on doubling their output by streamlining the tank rather than making any core changes to it, the majority of changes were the thickness of armor. In contrast, German heavy tank produced peaked in 1944 with about 600 Tiger 1s and 400 Tiger 2s made. Making both at the same time itself was a silly idea, while the Soviets completely switched production in 1943 to make the new IS chassis, which allowed them to produce no less than 4,760 heavy tanks in 1944 alone, including 2,200 IS-2 and 2,500 ISU-152 and ISU-122. The reason for the few German tanks was not a lack of resources, but insistence on ineffective production methods, and many models. For example the German engineers made adjustments to the design of the Tiger for every 12 tanks or so made. Just the major overhauls of the design happened frequently, for example the core design was slightly changed 15th of August 1942 and again on the 15th of October 1942, then again on the first of December in 1942. They couldn’t go 2 months without a change to the design so major that it needed a designation. In summary, the Soviets produced heavy tanks earlier, and understood how to make long serial runs of production. The German had a chaotic and unorganized production run resulting in many stops in production to make adjustments, and were never able to output anything close to what the Soviets did, even if they had more time it would not have mattered.

Question: Why is the Henschel HS-129 tank buster that had better armour protection not famous like Ju-37 Panzerknacker or Il-2 Shturmovik?
Answer: The HS-129 was not a good tank buster. A lot of the fandom the plane has built is based entirely around the fact it had a big gun, namely the 75mm Pak-40. However, in reality, only a very low number had this gun, the majority of those build had 30mm auto cannons. Which were never effective at destroying tanks like the T-34. The addition of the Pak-40 to some planes, made it very poor at flying, and while having fire power is great, not being able to fly well is not, and the plane never caught on in this configuration. The Ju-87/37 is mostly famous for it’s noise, and because it was more or less the only of its kind when it was used in Poland and France in 1939–1940. Not because this was actually the best dive bomber in WW2. The US made helldiver probably deserves that honour. While the IL-2 was probably one of the only planes that could claim effective anti tank weapons. Firing an actual anti tank gun out of plane while flying and shaking, especially due to poor flight performance, is frankly a terrible idea for trying to hit something, even a tank. This should be obvious by the fact that no one else did this after World War 2. What they did do after World War 2, was using anti tank cluster bombs for tank busting. Because if you are not going to have great accuracy, dropping a hundred anti tank warheads over an area is pretty effective, especially if they are concentrated. And this is exactly what the IL-2 did, hence why it unlike the other two planes actually had a chance at destroying tanks, other places than on imaginary after action reports.

Question: The Americans usually called in artillery strikes. How did the Soviets and the British typically overcome German machine gun nests with overlapping fields of fire?
Answer: If by Americans using artillery you mean heavy howitzer fire, this is likely not the case. The Americans might have called in mortars, and their widespread us of portable radios made on-call artillery at all levels a possibility. As for the Soviets, they did not have the widespread use of radios, so using artillery on surprise machine guns they encountered would not have been a viable option for everyone. Instead the Soviets made excellent use of combined arms tactics, particularly in the late war. The Su-76 for example was a self propelled gun that was designed to provide support to infantry formations. During an assault the assaulting infantry were basically always reinforced with support equipment, at least since Stalingrad. The support equipment usually included a tank, or something like an Su-76, but in some cases like assaults against heavily fortified positions, could also go all the way up to the heavy 152mm SPG ISU-152. The Soviets favored direct fire, because it enabled the gunners to correct their own shots, though it was riskier than indirect fire, the vehicles like ISU-152 and Su-76 were armored against what they were expected to face. The British like the Americans likely relied on mortars and had them on call, and in some cases might have had 25 pounder guns, which are roughly equivalent in firepower to the Su-76 or ZiS-3 towed cannon. It should also be noted that infantry tactics in all the armies did not require heavy support elements. Infantry at the squad level were tried to fight machine gun positions through basic fire and maneuver infantry tactics, in which one element distracts the machine gun with suppressive fire while the other move into a position in which they could use grenade to destroy it.

Name: Carl Hamilton
Question: What makes a tank design revolutionary, rather than evolutionary?
Answer: Whether it is a tank or another military product, an evolutionary design represents the refinement of a technology, without introducing anything particularly new. A revolutionary design, on the other hand fundamentally changes one or multiple aspects of a technology, and forms a new period of design philosophy, on which all new evolutionary design aspects must compare. For example, if we look at the T-34 in WW2, it pretty much embodied what the Soviets at the time wanted in a tank. A good gun, sloped steel armor, good mobility and reasonable armor. If we look at the next 20 years of Soviet armor development what changed? Tanks got slightly heavier, and got slightly more steel armor, they had slightly better guns. Suddenly you got the T-64 which completely changes how tanks are designed. For 1t more weight, you more than double the armor which is no longer steel, and you’re able to fit a much more powerful and even new type of gun. If you look at the feature diagram of base models (without ERA) below it will be very obvious when the revolutionary design change occurred. After a revolutionary design change, it is also typical for the Soviets at least, to retroactively fit as much of the technology to older designs as practical, such as laser range finders, electronic fire controls, composite armor etc. It should also be noted that many of the features of the T-64 was then adopted by other countries as well, verbatim in the case of countries like China and France, and partially in the case of USA and Germany. These countries had to make tanks which were at least as capable in the same areas, as the T-64 after it was discovered what it could actually do. Primarily this meant adopting the smoothbore cannon and composite armor. And while many countries claim that their particular version of composite armor, or their particular version of a smoothbore cannon is better than others, these are small evolutionary changes, not new paradigms. The vast majority of tanks in the world still operate with the T-64 feature package as the standard, with improvements. The next generation of revolutionary tanks, will like by the T-14 and the NATO equivalent that is currently in the making armed with a 130mm cannon. The firepower will not be the revolutionary aspect. The new change that the next generation of tanks will have, will be in the form of full compartmentalization of the crew, a sophisticated electronic warfare suite, and possibly some drone and anti drone technology.

Question: What type of body armor did the Soviet Union use during World War II?
Answer: The Soviets used an all steel torso vest, which was generally carried by assault engineer troops. The most common version was then SN-42 which was 2mm thick. This vest offered protection against shrapnel, melee attacks and pistol caliber bullets. At long range it might also offer protection against rifle rounds, but something like a K98 would have no trouble shooting through at normal angles. Due to the vest being made of steel though, it probably offered more significant protection against bullets coming in at odd angles, than soft body armour does today.

Question: With the recent conflicts in Europe and the Middle East (in the early 2020s), is there a trend, a necessity to whitewash the crimes of the Nazis during WWII?
Answer: There is, as we say in history, a battle for the memory of WW2 and Nazis. This battle did not begin recently, it has been ongoing ever since WW2 ended. This is true both in Europe and the Middle East. The tendency to whitewash or the tendency to expose has gone up and down in Europe, while in the Middle East it has remained fairly steady. When you say “European conflicts” I am guessing you mean Ukraine. Ukraine has indeed had a tendency to whitewash the OUN in particular, the Ukrainian Nazi auxiliaries from WW2. However, this is not due to a recent conflict. In fact this tendency is strong associated with nationalism in general, and began practically on the day the USSR fell apart. OUN leader, Stepan Bandera, was indeed made into a national hero in Ukraine, where he was officially awarded the title post-humously. However, this happened in 2010 and the decision was Viktor Yushchenko’s, not Zelensky’s. Additionally, it would be unfair to not point out that such whitewashing has happened many other places in Europe too. I personally witnessed people quite happily celebrating the Arrow Cross organization in Budapest last time i visited, on the middle of the main stream leading to the parliament, with no one batting an eye. Likewise in my own country, the complicity of Danes in Nazi atrocities is generally not acknowledged at all, vile SS Nazi and known murderer Søren Kam, escaped Justice his entire life, with no serious efforts even made to have him prosecuted until 2006, despite his identity and crimes being known since the 1970s. As for the middle east, anti-semitism has been omnipresent for quite a long time, much longer than the current conflict. The white washing of Nazis was essential for many middle eastern countries for various reasons. First of all, the fact that millions of innocent Jews were murdered for their ethnicity, is not able to coincide with the idea that Jews are colonizers and collectively responsible for many problems all over the middle east, as as been the narrative promoted by many of the dictatorships that until recently ruled much of the Arab speaking world. For example, al-Liwaa al-Islami, the ruling party of Egypt’s official newspaper, published in 2004 an article called "The Lie About the Burning of the jews" by Dr. Rif'at Sayyed Ahmad. In 2006, Lebanese New TV employed this strategy. The channel broadcast a show where it was stated that Holocaust scholar Raul Hilberg had said only 50,000 jews had died in WW2, which of course Raul Hilberg never said. The holocaust has also been outright denied by the official Syrian government news paper, Syria Times, in 2000, and by al-Manar in 1999. Which I believe is owned by Hezbollah operating out of Lebanon. Hamas on the other hand, has the official view, that the holocaust was organized by the Jews themselves in order to make Jews move to Palestine, this was stated in al-Risala in 2003. Now that isn’t to say that everyone in the middle east have been trying to whitewash Nazis or deny holocaust, in 2006 the recent comments and groups attempting to do just this, outraged Kuwaiti Journalist Khaled al-Janfawi who said: Holding a conference devoted to Holocaust denial reflects a lack of cultural and human sensitivity which may exacerbate hatred among human beings. [...] We Muslims need to display human, cultural, and moral sensitivity in order to be a positive force in a humane world that no longer tolerates ethnic and religious conflict. We must stay away from anything that generates conflict among human beings. [...] Holding a Holocaust [denial] conference in Iran is adding fuel to the fire. [...] Some of the participants were agitators, and [others] were [individuals] involved in racist discrimination against [minorities] other than the Jews, such as the African -Americans in the U.S Likewise, intellectuals in Tunesia, Morroco and Algeria expressed similar views and disgust at the historical revisionism. The most outrageous examples apart from Iran, are those countries who had previously fought with Israel militarily. Which is not really surprising. Much of the whitewashing of Nazis are left overs of the Arab-Israeli wars. And while it is flaring up now, it is not because of a recent tendency to do this, but because of the long standing political context in the middle east, of viewing everything related to Jews to being about Israel in actuality. The tendencies to promote or fight whitewashing is a rather fluid thing, shaped by governments, media and historians, and not something the average person can really be blamed for. For this post I consulted the papers: Mikael Tossavainen, 2008, The Holocaust In Arab Public Discourse: Historicized Politics And Politicized History, JSTOR Gilbert Achcar, 2020, Holocaust Denial in Western and Arab Contexts, Journal of Palestine Studies

Question: Is WW1-style tunnel warfare and mining possible in Ukraine?
Answer: Yes, this is very possible, it has indeed already happened. In mid November 2023, Russians detonated a bomb underneath a concrete reinforced strong point south of Avdiivka. They had dug a 170m tunnel to place it, the above picture is from the subsequent assault on the position which opened up the Russian offensive on the southern part of Avdiivka, a battle which lasted until just a few days ago. It might be hard to tell, but you can see the massive crater which in the screenshot is currently full of a platoon of infantry assaulting the location. Underground concrete bunkers are exceedingly difficult to destroy with indirect fire, even direct hits from heavy artillery does little to them. So the usefulness of mine bombs, where you can place a large and precise bomb underneath heavily fortified strong points still exists, and it is indeed used. The alternative is to use large caliber thermobaric weapons, but it is possible we have not seen the last tunneling operation in this war.

Question: The T-64, T-72, T-80 and T-90 all have 125mm main guns, but are they basically the same and use the same ammo?
Answer: The 125mm series of guns installed on these tanks are similar, but they are not the same and do not perform the same. There are many minor improvements to the gun over it’s life, but we can talk about the two main variants. The 2A46 and the 2A46M. The 2A46 suffered from accuracy issues, which were largely addressed with the 2A46M. Firstly as seen from above, the barrel became seated on the thermal sleve with more points of contact, which reduced inconsistent performance when the barrel heated up. The 2A46 featured a recoil buffer on the lower right of the gun breach, which swayed the gun slightly during firing. This meant that the 2A46 had a tendency to fire slightly to the side of the aim point. Not a terrible amount at normal ranges, but enough to affect accuracy at long range. However, this was fixed on the 2A46M by making two recoil buffers spreading the recoil between and upper right and lower left recoil buffer. Additionally the 2A46M featured a new breech block, gun cradle, and a new barrel with an interrupted screw which permitted quick swapping the barrel out the front of the tank in field conditions, with 2 hours without the need for removing the turret or advanced machines. Essentially almost every part of the gun was in fact changed, and resulted in drastically higher accuracy, life span, and ease of maintenance. The actual improvements of the 2A46M-5 which is what is currently used on the T-72B3, T-80BVM and T-90 tanks, are not entirely known. Likely they are aimed at improving service life, but other features might be present. All 125mm guns are backwards compatible, but older guns might not be able to shoot the newest ammunition, but it wouldn’t matter much anyway, as the newest ammunition requires a newer auto loader anyway.

Question: What was Stalin's reasoning for allowing the Germans to advance deep into Russian territory during Operation Barbarossa before launching a counter-attack?
Answer: The Soviets launched counter attacks very often, and sadly usually quite hastily in 1941, they did not wait a minute to do. However, usually the Soviets were ill prepared, poorly coordinated and unaware of each other during counter attacks, the most serious of all the counter offensives launched in early 1941 was the Battle of Brody. During this battle of just 7 days, which actually started on June 23rd just 1 day after operation Barbarossa. The Soviets committed a massive armored counter attack to stop the German offensive on the border. Over 3,500 tanks were used, but there were many problems. Most of the Soviet tanks were outdated models of T-26 and BT tanks, which often lacked effective communication measures, effective cannons and had essentially no armor. The Soviets only had around 443 of the new T-34s and KV-1s, about half of the T-34s were still waiting on radios, and so only the KV-1 forces were able to effectively communicate during maneuvers, while essentially all German tanks had radios at this time. Additionally, the Soviet formation system was undergoing a reform at this time, and the commanders were unused to the unwieldy mechanized corps. The various mechanized corps were also given mission objectives, but were attacking from multiple directions without an established doctrine to coordinate these attacks. This led to situations where a Soviet task force known as Group Popel, effective cut off the led elements of the German attack of the 11th armored division. This should have led to the destruction of the German division, but instead other Soviet units ignored this breakthrough and got bogged down. The German forces which were outnumbered quite significantly in tanks, managed to achieve a numerical superiority again and again, by focusing all their units on individual Soviet corps and defeating them in detail. Where Soviet T-34s and KV-1s advanced, the Germans were broken but only for a while, these new tanks were suffering from a drastic shortage of 76mm ammunition as none of the corps has built up a wartime supply of the new ammunition types. This meant that other successes like those of the 10th Armored division, had initial success in destroying and trading well with German tanks, however, they had to retreat from what otherwise looked like a victory, due to simply running out of shells entirely. Some KV-1s were reported as firing nothing but machine gun ammunition. The completely ad-hoc planning and lack of ability to of some Soviet generals, led to completely unnecessary losses, such as the entire KV-1 component of the 22nd mechanized corp getting stuck in a swamp and losing their best equipment without a fight. In conclusion, the Soviets did counter attack, but the Red Army was not ready for this scale of warfare. This wasn’t simply because officer corps or because they were surprised. None of these factors were because they lacked officers or because they were actually surprised by the offensive, but because there was no time to plan this counter attack, there were still a level of doctrinal incompetence focusing on rapid attacks, and because the units were not yet equipped for this scale of operation. Later in WW2, the Soviets would spend considerable time planning attacks, and this initial combat quickly taught the Soviets that the most important category of production was not tanks, mortars, guns, rifles or trucks. But ammunition, and never again should Soviet units suffer from a lack of shells.

Question: Has the title Caeser been used in post-Roman times?
Answer: You bet it was, emperor in German is in fact Kaiser and this in fact is Caesar. The latin C is pronounced as K, and with a bit of different pronunciation it is quite obvious that Kaiser is the title of Caesar. It is made all the more obvious as the the Holy Roman Empire, which preceded modern Germany, considered itself the successor of Rome, and the Holy Roman emperor was the Kaiser, the new Caesar. So considering this, Kaiser Wilhelm II was indeed the last Caesar, barely 100 years ago since his rule ended. Also yes the Tsar title is also derived from Caesar, though it is not exactly the same word in the way Kaiser is.

The 25mm rounds were unable to penetrate the armour of the T-90M, which is also a predictable outcome, if small autocannons could do that, there would be no reason to carry 120mm guns on tanks. The crew of the T-90M survived, showing that despite being disabled the protection of the newest Russian tanks are quite good. Name: Carl Hamilton
Question: Is military air dominance important?
Answer: For America it is, because their military doctrine revolves around having it. If you follow the Soviet doctrine which much of military thinking outside NATO is based on, then air dominance is not important to have, indeed against a peer rival it is impossible to achieve. The Soviets and probably the Russians now, viewed air power as having the missions of front line support, deep interdiction or strategic delivery. In the case of front line support, the aircraft would operate within a protective umbrella of long range AA missiles, and focusing on deterring enemy CAS while providing their own CAS to the ground troops. Deep interdiction is the term of hitting critical infrastructure targets such as bridges and supply depots, which usually required your planes to fly deep into enemy territory, and thus was very dangerous. Strategic delivery usually meant the dropping of nuclear bombs, which was likely to be a one way trip. However, the Soviets arrived at the conclusion that the deep interdiction could be carried out by ballistic and cruise missiles, more recently it has also been carried out by drones. These missiles and drones are very difficult to defend against, and as such there is no need to achieve air superiority in order to destroy interdiction targets. Therefore it is no longer that important to achieve air superiority, it is more important to achieve a high degree of defensive platforms for interception, and have a high degree of missile production for delivery of attacks in depth.

Question: How did the Soviet Union pay Britain for war matériels in WW2?
Answer: In various ways, though there is an idea that the British didn’t ask for anything in return, like the materials were free. They were really not. In the very beginning of the material exchanges, the Soviet Union paid in gold, as Britain did not accept Soviet money exchanges, and wanted only gold in order to economically hurt the Soviet Union. Obviously, this policy was changed during the war, it was merely a left over of the economic warfare that occurred before the war. When the first Supply Protocol for aid to the Soviet Union was signed, the British contrary to popular belief in fact did ask for something in return, and we know exactly what it asked for. It was the following items: The Soviets were unable to fulfill the rifle request of the British, due to their own very high need of firearms in 1941. Some of these items are more note worthy than others. For example, while 1400 kg of platinum isn’t going to take up a lot of space, it’s quite value dense. The current value of platinum is 30,000 dollars per kilogram, so it would be worth about 42 million dollars today. A Valentine tank was produced for 10,000 pounds a piece, 355,743 pounds today, which is 453,180 USD. That means the platinum would be roughly worth 93 Valentine tanks, if we adjusted both for inflation without considering other factors. In 1941, the Soviets received 216 Valentine tanks and 145 Matildas, through 1942, they received another 959 Valentine tanks and 626 Matilda tanks. In inflation adjusted terms, the platinum alone would have paid for a significant portion of the first tank shipment. Though it is difficult to ascertain the exact value at the time due to use value of platinum being very high, and the market price being fixed. However, this isn’t really important, the point is merely that yes, the Soviets did send valuable items to the UK. I am not going to through every item, but one other of particular note is Timber. The requested amount was simply as much as the ships could carry back to England after the other items were satisfied. That is potentially millions of tons. You can put this into the context of the British wooden wonder plane Mosquito, which did use spruce in some areas, which happen to be a very common export timber type from Russia. The British surely found a use for all the timber they received either way. Finally of course, the Soviets paid for all of this in an invaluable currency: Blood. Every soldier who fought was a soldier the British didn’t have to field themselves, and between 1941–1944 this was very obviously a cheap deal for Britain. During a parliament session in 1946, prime minister Clement Atlee what was asked the total value of the materials received from Russia during WW2. He answered I could not give that without notice. Clement Atlee then proceeded to give a full account of what the British material to Russia was worth. Accounts was kept about how much was given by the allies, but it was not considered important to account for what was received, neither in blood nor timber sadly.
