Name: Carl Hamilton
Question: How do we increase the birth rate of a country?
Answer: We can answer this question, with the power of history and sociology. We have in fact one of the most interesting social experiments of all time available to us. It is called Germany. During the cold war, you had both west and east Germany, with the same culture, history, people, language etc. The difference was in policy, which is a thing we can affect, so if we want to affect birth rate, we must use policy. We see here the birth rate in east and west Germany during the cold war, we have an initial rise as reconstruction after WW2 completes, then in the 1960s the introduction of birth control pills and condoms very rapidly decreases the birthrate in both Germany’s, it is faster in east Germany due to a more open discussion of the issue, and earlier adoption of both, but the effect is still very similar. By the 1970s, women no longer needed to have children just because they had sex, which meant that childbirth was a choice, not an obligation. As such the birthrate became associated with the desire to have children, rather than necessity. Both Germany’s saw this very low birthrate as a bit of a problem, particularly economically as the labor availability for low end jobs was diminishing. West Germany and East Germany attempted to solve this in drastically different ways. The West German government figured that if you need cheap labour, why not just import it? Which resulted in the Gastarbeiter program. In which many foreign were invited to work in Germany, particularly from Turkey and later Yugoslavia. The East Germans on the other hand decided that having a child should not be a hindrance to someone’s life. As such the East Germans made a program which emphasized a woman’s choice, lack of social stigma for having an unwanted pregnancy, created kindergartens and other childcare programs, and gave public child support in forms of money to mothers. In short, they made it a secure choice to get a child, rather than a burden or scary event. They allowed and encouraged to employ mothers in jobs, while in the west it was strongly discouraged. In conclusion, if you want to raise birth rate, make a welfare state where women feel secure, and they will likely want to have children. Most women who say they don’t want to have children, is because they are scared it will affect their life, career or social status negatively. This is a problem that can be fixed, but it requires a sensible attitude, and frankly a sexist stance combined with a disregard for the financial security of average people, are the main reasons for declining birthrates. In countries where you have hyper competitive societies, you will have low birth rates, enter exhibit Korea and Japan. In case you are very curious about the comparison of west and east Germany’s attitude to this problem, I can recommend the anthropological and sociological study Why Women Have Better Sex Under Socialism. West and East Germany provided a unique insight into policy effect on this, and it is well worth to keep researching it.

Question: What's happened to the Abrams tanks supplied to Ukraine? They haven't been used, so have they all been destroyed, sunk into the mud or simply failed to work? The Challengers and Leopards were a disappointment but at least they got to the front line!
Answer: The Abrams were spotted moving to Kupyansk, expecting this to be a major Russian goal in 2024, the Abrams tanks were likely send here as a mobile reserve to counter a major Russian armored attack should it come. The Abrams, Leopard and Challenger 2 are designed for specific tasks, and if we can step away from the propaganda for a moment, they are not good tanks for fighting in prolonged combat in infantry support roles or offensives against dedicated enemies. These tanks were designed for conducting determined counter attacks against major Soviet tank offensives. They are in many ways tank destroyers. The reason the Chally 2 and Leopard 2 did not live up to the hype, is because people fail to recognize the mission they were designed for, and so have unrealistic expectations. I suspect, that the AFU keep their cool, and only deploy the Abrams tanks in a concentrated fist as part of an armored counter attack, they have a very high probability of inflicting a serious blow to a Russian armour unit. Not without losses, but for sure a high speed counter attack is what they were made for, and the result will no doubt be more impressive than if they decide to send a platoon of Abrams into a minefield, the result of which I can predict quite easily. Therefore, the Abrams is being held in reserve for now and likely will be for quite a while yet. Provided the Russians open an offensive in northern Ukraine or Kharkiv they might also rapidly be moved in this direction.

Name: Carl Hamilton
Question: How is Ukraine’s artillery so wonderfully accurate?
Answer: Well Ukraine’s artillery is so wonderfully accurate because the vast majority of it was made by the Soviet Union, who’s army was described as the “God of artillery” or an “artillery army with a lot of tanks”, which ever you prefer. Perhaps it’s important to highlight that there are many kinds of accuracy involved in artillery fire, there is targeting, correction, internal, external and terminal ballistics, not to mention wind effects and deterioration of equipment. A little bit like on a computer where you have a CPU, GPU, RAM disk writing speed etc, your accuracy on a gun can never be better than your worst component. This is your bottleneck. Ukrainian servicemen practice on the Msta-B Soviet 152mm howitzer. No matter what you do though, you cannot achieve accuracy beyond the physical limits of the shell. If you have a guided shell that can correct itself, then this is quite high, 1–10m accuracy depending on the circumstances for things like GPS and laser guided shells. For dumb shells, accuracy decreases with range no matter what you do. You cannot remove drift in the air entirely, even if your gun is point exactly at the target, it does not guarantee a hit. We have essentially arrived at the point where it is not so difficult to achieve maximum accuracy within what is possible with a system thanks to GIS and computer calculated fire solutions. So really any army with these basic tools are able to have wonderfully accurate artillery.

Question: What explains Nazi Germany’s inexcusable intelligence failure prior to Operation Barbarossa of not understanding the true size of the Red Army, both active and reserve?
Answer: German human intelligence was frankly pretty bad. The Nazis were able to use a lot of signal intelligence, and even air recon of the front of the Soviet Union, but their primary human intelligence came from a few nationalists in some of the western Soviet republics, like Roman Shukhevych who collaborated with the Nazis from February 1941. These agents however, were essentially outlaws in the USSR, and had no insight into higher placement of units. So the Germans actually had reasonably good intelligence on the Soviet front strength, but quite little intelligence on the interior of the USSR, indeed some of their best intelligence came from official visits. Another problem was that intelligence was not acted on despite being known. For example, German inspectors had visited Soviet aircraft factories as part of their non-aggression pact. They had reported that the Soviets were able to produce very high numbers of aircraft, and that their next generation of aircraft would be technically advanced. This information was in fact kept from Hitler, because it was thought that it wouldn’t matter. In the initial discussion for the invasion of 1940, the Germans estimated that the Soviets had just 50–75 divisions, and that they needed 80–100 divisions to beat the entire Red Army. Already by the second discussion round in August 1940, estimations of Soviet strength in Europe was increased to 96 divisions, and a figure of 150 total divisions. And the German requirement was raised to 147 divisions. Additionally, the Germans conducted a survey of economy, estimating that their initial push in Barbarossa, would occupy 75% of their armaments industry and 100% of their precision industry. This was a wild assumption that basically relied on the idea that people east of the Urals were too stupid to make optics or other factories. During the planning period in February 1941, chief of staff general Franz Halder, estimated that the Soviet Union could muster in total 155 divisions to oppose the German invasion. He made several other comments, he said Soviet artillery would be ineffective and that the best Soviet general was Semyon Timoshenko. No doubt, this was based on hear-say from the Finnish winter war, rather than actually good intelligence. The final estimation came in June 1941, when more aggressive recon flew over the Soviet border, and discovered not 96 divisions in the west, but 138 as well as 40 armored brigades. Originally, the Germans were asking for a divisional overmatch of 1.33 to 1. Then this was raised to a request of 1.53 to 1 in Germany’s favour. The Germans ultimately were able to bring up 152 divisions supported by 14 Romanian divisions. For a total of 166 divisions against the Soviet 138. A ratio of 1.2 to 1 in favor of the Germans. Considerably worse than their initial request. By the time Barbarossa was concluding the Soviets had not utilized 155 divisions like Halder had anticipated, but 220, considerably more than what was originally anticipated. Semyon Timoshenko was also a decent commander, but far from the Soviet best, he was merely the guy who was sent to Finland to solve the chaos and terrible organization of Kliment Voroshilov. Based on this fallacy the Germans had a completely wrong impression of the Soviet officer corps. So, in conclusion, the Nazis not only had an intelligence gathering failure, they also had a very poor reaction to emerging intelligence, and used fallacious thinking when making evaluations. When it turns out the enemy is about 40% stronger than you first anticipated you should probably revise your plans. They did not.

Question: Why didn't the Soviet Union accept the Marshall Plan? Did they have a counter offer?
Answer: The USSR rejected the Marshall Plan, because they felt it was an attempt to simply gain control over the devastated countries of Europe from the US side, as well as allow venues of infiltration into Soviet areas of influence. Which was largely correct. Often when talked about, it is left out that the Marshall plan did not come without conditions. They were as follows: If this isn’t obvious immediately, these are extremely favorable conditions for the US. As the US industry was in perfect conditions after world war 2; they could easily out compete most European companies, so the discrimination against US imports meant that US companies would dominate European markets for the foreseeable future, which is in fact exactly what happened. Encouraging reductions in public spending meant privatizing much of the public sector, which again meant that US companies could replace some functions of state in Europe, giving US influence in those areas. This was not achieved to the extent the US wanted. Increasing exports to the USA meant sending them resources, as I mentioned most European companies could not compete with the USA, so export was done in lower end less valuable products, which was then turned into high value products and send back to Europe. Currency convertibility meant in practice that everyone had to buy us dollars for trade, and settle every trade deal in dollars. Buying US dollars meant that the US came to control not just European trade but world trade through their control of currency. Additionally, 5% of the Marshall aid was secretly allocated to CIA fronts which used it under disguise to create convert action against the political enemies of the USA in Europe. It should be painfully obvious why all of these conditions would be totally unacceptable to the USSR. The USSR was also the most devastated country aside from Poland, and things like “relax rationing” would simply have created famine in the USSR, which was barely on the verge of it already as agricultural damage was being repaired. The deal was never intended for the USSR, and had there been a deal with the USA where they would honestly have helped the Soviet rebuild, who honestly needed it the most, they would simply not have passed the bill in the US congress.

Question: What are Putin's key political ideologies?
Answer: Putin does not have multiple ideologies, but I am guessing you mean what are some tenants of his ideology. This is quite a question, and as usual with political ones the answer is very varied. Recently some people invented a term called Putinism, which is more or less an attempt at making him out like Stalin or Lenin, and suggesting he has created a set ideology. Putin, unlike Stalin or Lenin have not written long thesis or books about ideology however. If Putin has not created his own ideology, perhaps the question is, what does he actually believe in? Obviously if we look at statements on Putin from the west recently, he is Napoleon, Hitler, Stalin, but this doesn’t actually say what his ideology really is, it just says that we don’t like him. Let’s go back in time to before we had an approved narrative on Putin and people were trying to figure out what he actually wanted. The following exerts are from “The differences between Putin's Russia and Yeltsin's” Prism Volume: 6 Issue: 7, 2000, Gorbachev tried to liberalize the Soviet totalitarian system. Yeltsin held on to power and thus prevented a communist comeback. Putin is trying to maintain a liberal society and, particularly, a market economy, and at the same time to restore state power which tottered during the anticommunist revolution. Notice here that the marked difference is that Putin is pro-liberal society and market economy. Perhaps one of the far more interesting statements in this article from 23 years ago, is about Oligarchs and who they are. Today essentially it seems that anyone who supports Putin is an Oligarch and that’s just what it means. That is not what was said in 2000. Under Putin the so-called problem of the oligarchs still remains, at least for the time being. The essence of this problem lies in the combination of property and power. The oligarchs acquired their huge fortunes by virtue of their closeness to Yeltsin, Gaidar, Chernomyrdin and Chubais. Then, by dint of their wealth and financial clout, the oligarchs began to play a decisive role–greater than that of the representative organs–in the domestic and foreign policy of the country’s leaders. Just as they did under Yeltsin, the oligarchs still exercise firm control over Putin’s policies with regard to the redistribution of property. Another difference in how things are viewed now compared to then is the regionalism. Today regions in Russia are highly integrated, which is alternatively portrayed as a racist aspect of Russian totalitarianism, and also at the same time that Russia is made up of radical enclaves like Chechnya who’s regional leader’s support for Putin is an authoritarian problem. In 2000 it was described quite differently. Thanks to the generally successful antiterrorist operation in Chechnya, Putin has managed to avoid the collapse of the Russian Federation. Putin’s attack on the autocracy of the regional leaders has also contributed to the neutralization of centrifugal tendencies in Russia. The article go on to make an overall evaluation of Putin: As a traditional Russian Westernizer, it should not be forgotten that Putin is a confirmed Germanophile; the new president will not erect a new iron curtain. I am certain that he has no interest in being hailed as a second Stalin. In contemporary Russia and in the contemporary world it is in principle no longer possible to recreate a totalitarian regime. Putin does not have the motivating ideology for this; he does not have his “crusaders.” It should be remembered that Russia is no longer a self-sufficient country; it constantly has to look over its shoulder at the West and relate its aspirations to the realities of democratic civilization. Stability will be maintained, but there will be no dictatorship. This is quite wildly different from what would be published now, but if we sum up the core beliefs outlined here for Putin in 2000, it is liberal society, market economy, a stable federation, anti regional autocracy, westernization and cooperative with the west. In short he has what I would call a classical liberal ideology, as opposed to the neo-liberal ideology which is dominant in the west. What isn’t talked much about here is Putin’s consolidation of power against the Oligarchs, there was a period where the Oligarchs exercised power over Putin and the Russian government as mentioned. Putin was locked in a power struggle with them for several years, and ultimately managed to reduce corruption and connections to Oligarchs by replacing a significant part of the Russian officials with his clique of former or current security agents, collectively called siloviks, such as Sergei Shoigu. This however of course has created a state apparatus which is heavily security oriented, which in all fairness is not so different from the Soviet Union’s priority arrangement, though their methods and scale is different. It is incredibly difficult to actually ascertain the real ideology of Putin. Partially because political scientists here are mostly concerned with international politics, in which they merely portray Russian interests as Putin’s interests, which is not how international politics works, and partially because domestic Russian politics are difficult to understand for foreigners (including me). The kind of explorative study into Putin’s ideology simply isn’t really done much. And while many are quick to put a label on him from communist-revivalist to fascist based on some chosen actions of the Russian state, this is not a helpful categorization. Many mistakes are made because we have simplistic and often silly views of what other people want or believe in, unfortunately I don’t really have the answer, as the security side of politics is my focus, but an ideology is made up of more than security policies.

Question: Which was the better Russian fighter during WW2, the LA-5 or the Yak9? I understand that there was a lot of rivalry between the two companies.
Answer: Initially the La-5 was the ace maker in the Soviet air force, along with the P-39 lend-lease aircraft. It was a big upgrade over the LaGG-3, which could not compete with the Bf-109 aircraft all that well. The La-5 had 2, 20mm guns while the Yak-9 had just 1, giving it a firepower edge over the Yak-9. The Yak-9 was itself an upgrade from the Yak-1 introduced earlier. And while the Yak-9 series was a decent aircraft, it never quite reached parity with the better Bf-109 air frames, even on the Yak-9U model. The Yak-9 and La-5 were introduced in the same year, and they were also further developed. By 1944, the Yak-3 and La-7 were available as the final evolution of Soviet fighter designs, the Soviets managed with these to achieve mechanical superiority over German aircraft, though it was quite late in the war. If you look at the top 10 Soviet aces of WW2, you can see the distribution of the aircraft they flew does not favour the Yak-9, not that this is a large or fantastic sample size, but I think it is an indicative hint. The Yak-9 was great for it’s versatility and numbers built, but I think the La-5 was a better performer in air to air combat. Name: Carl Hamilton
Question: Why were the Nazis so obsessed with creating new weapons even when what they had was good enough?
Answer: Depending on your meaning of “new weapons” there are quite good reasons for them to do so. WW2 was a highly technologically driven war, in which new capabilities were designed. Though in one aspect the Germans took a misstep. They did spend a lot of resources on trying to create ‘quality’ products over the west. In some ways it does make sense, you have less people than your opponents, so in order to even have a chance at winning, you need to concentrate force and out perform your opponents. The Nazis leaned heavily into this strategy, luckily for us, they were pretty shit at it. wasting tremendous amounts of resources on fiddling, unnecessary competition between companies, awful factory optimization, military driven requirements and unrealistic design goals. However, it is important for a nation in war to try and find solutions to battlefield problems, or introduce new problems for the enemy, hence there was a great need for producing new weapons. This is a research question, while the faults i mentioned earlier are largely engineering problems. Things like the jet fighter Me 262 was an attempt to solve the problem of lack of fuel, Avgas was difficult to make in the 1940s, particularly for Germany, because it required high octane. Jet fuel is a simple mix of kerosene and gasoline, which meant it was far easier to produce the fuel. Likewise, the German heavy tank was supposed to solve the problem of not being able to field as many tanks as the enemy, so making a tank that could fight while out numbered made sense theoretically. The STG-44 was supposed to give infantry squads the ability to provide their own covering fire, and act as an SMG for close range fighting if necessary. It would have solved the problem of having squads with rifles, LMGs and SMGs, all of which were specialized. The real problem was the idea of wonder weapons (wunderwaffe), which were thought to be so radically new or powerful that they would change the direction of the war. This obviously didn’t happen, because half of them were science fiction, and weapons like the V-2 and V-1 were impressive, but they carried far far less devastation than your average allied bomber raid.

Question: Has Putin significantly weakened Russia as a military power?
Answer: That is highly unlikely to be the case. There are a lot of posts about Russia declining militarily which are not based on any sensible theory, but merely on the idea that losing equipment means you lose military power. This is not true, and I will tell you why Russia’s military power has increased, as well as why equipment losses do not matter in the way people clearly think. The primary idea of Russia being weakened as a military power, is that losing troops and equipment means you become weaker. This is not the case unless you lose either to such an extent you cannot replace them. We know from history that this area is around 5% of the entire population (Germany lost 7.7% in WW2), yes at this point the manpower losses becomes a problem for your country. However, as of yet Russian losses has not reached 7 million in Ukraine even in the wildest dreams of the most optimistic claimants. Indeed even in the highest estimations of Russian losses, Russian conscription exceeds losses, which means that the military is growing. If you accept that the unsupported claims are likely exaggerations, we arrive at another conclusion, which is that the Russian military is increasingly veteran. They can afford to rotate their troops quite often, and have been building up a significant number of troops with experience while not keeping them in the front at all times. We can add to this that according to Mediazona’s confirmed losses list, that the highest amount of losses so far were taken by the penal units in the spring of 2023, and so the highest losses is over represented in the most expendable units, which is actually quite logical when you think about it. Now the other aspect is that of equipment. Russia has probably lost a vast amount of their pre-war stock, particularly older Soviet equipment, but does this really weaken Russia? I would argue not. Equipment is an expendable resource, it is worthless if it is not used, and it de-values with time. So old Soviet equipment is a resource that the Russians might as well use all they can of right now, because it will be truly worthless in the next major war. For post-war military power, I would not count Soviet equipment as really contributing towards Russian military power, so in essence this is free expenditure that cost the budget quite little, and serves to drain an enemy which cannot replace equipment at the same rate. In the mean time, Russian production of military equipment has increased drastically, and this is no secret, the American ISW, CSIS and IISS strategic analysis think tanks have already said so. And the new generation of equipment is specifically designed to operate in peer-adversary combat environments. All the new Russian equipment is based on peer combat experience, which means it is driven to practical functionality, and not theoretical or corporate schemes as is the case in peace time military-industrial complexes (including the Russian pre-war one). In short, Russia currently has a veteran military with a lot of peer combat experience, which very few nations has, it has an expanding military industry, and the ability to induct enough troops to increase the size of their military. This mean Russia militarily are likely stronger now overall, than they were in the beginning of the war. Please note, I am not saying the Russian military is stronger than NATO or a threat in earnest to the alliance, but the question is if it is stronger or weaker relative to itself previously. I think without a doubt, it is increasing in capabilities not decreasing, all the predictions of them running out of missiles or shells was based on the ludicrous assumption they just wouldn’t produce any more weapons than was in their stockpile.

Question: Why did Revolutions like those in France, Russia, Cuba, Iran, etc. come under attack from the 'Western powers/powers that be' when they occur?
Answer: There are two principle reasons why revolutions come under attack, and while in more modern scenarios people will often find complicated reasons to justify the same reactions, I find it merely a cover. To arrive at the essence of why, we can look at the French revolution for a more honest take that was not quite as covered in modern propaganda as political justifications are now. In 1791 almost immediately after the French revolution, the Declaration of Pillnitz, was issued by Leopold II of Austria and Holy Roman Emperor, as well as Frederick William II of Prussia. The statement read as follows: His Majesty the Emperor and His Majesty the King of Prussia (…) declare together that they regard the actual situation of His Majesty the King of France as a matter of communal interest for all sovereigns of Europe. They hope that that interest will be recognized by the powers whose assistance is called in, and that they won't refuse, together with aforementioned Majesties, the most efficacious means for enabling the French king to strengthen, in utmost liberty, the foundations of a monarchical government suiting to the rights of the sovereigns and favourable to the well-being of the French. In that case, aforementioned Majesties are determined to act promptly and unanimously, with the forces necessary for realizing the proposed and communal goal. In expectation, they will give the suitable orders to their troops so that they will be ready to commence activity. That is the entire reason for the beginning of what would become the Napoleonic wars. It’s quite simple. The Kings of Europe, particularly Austria and Prussia, did not like the idea of ordinary people deposing a king, no matter how bad he was. As such it was a matter of communal interest for all the “sovereigns of Europe”, as in the rulers. Simply put, the privileged ruling class never likes the idea of a revolution and want every one of them to fail. This is the domestic policy reason. The second simple reason, is the foreign policy one. If a revolution happens, likely the alliances of that country will be broken, trade deal nullified and everything up for re-consideration. If you are a foreign power gaining something from your relationship with that country, you are against that revolution, if you are a foreign power and an enemy or rival of that country you are for it. For example, if France had a revolution now, made by extreme right wing people trying to create the France proper by kicking out the “non French”, it would simply not be allowed by NATO, it would be considered undemocratic fascist junta and it would be destroyed by military force if necessary. Without a doubt. However, if Russia had a revolution, made by extreme right wing people trying to create Russia proper by removing the minority republics from Russia, it would be entirely different matter for NATO, it would be the collective will of the people, and Russia as a multi cultural empire was due to fracture into ethnic states, such a thing could be supported entirely naturally, for the sake of democracy. And that is essentially the two reasons for every support or opposition to any revolution in history.

Question: Would the Walther PPK be as popular today (or even still sold) if it wasn’t known as “The James Bond gun”?
Answer: The Walther PPK is one of the most influential pistols ever, the Smith and Wesson Model 10 defined the revolvers in the 20th century, Glock pretty much sets the standard now, but between these you had the Walther PPK. The Germans themselves made 5 million copies, the Soviets however took this gun and said “yeah that’s pretty much what we want” and made another 5 million at the Izhevsk plant alone. Quite a lot of additional pistols of the makarov type and walther PPK are likely made outside of the main factories, but at least 10 million were made combined, making it in the Top 3 most produced pistols in history. The Soviets did not really consider pistols an important military item, so when they wanted a new one they looked around and took one that worked really well then adapted it for their use, though in the case of the Makarov, they also carried over the 9x18mm cartridge, which was completely different from their own 7.62x25mm cartridge, made for the TT pistol (which itself was a copy of the FN Model 1903). I should also note that the 9mm makarov is slightly larger than the 9mm Ultra for the Walther PPK, so you can’t interchange the ammunition.

Question: Have communists usually outsmarted fascists because, among other things, fascists are easily hung up on racial differences, whereas communists more often use racial differences to their advantage?

Question: Are video games more or less forgiving today compared to 10 years ago?
Answer: Video Games are more forgiving now, and it’s not a bad thing. For example, Elden Ring is a quite hard game, developed by FromSoftware, and it is the successor to the Darksouls series, which is notoriously difficult. Elden Ring however, is markedly more forgiving than predecessors in the series for two reasons. The first one is that it being less linear allows you to build your character the way you want it pretty early on. This allows you to play the way you want much earlier than previous titles, it doesn’t actually make the game much easier, but it doesn’t force you to play in a way you don’t want, until you progress to the point where you get acquire your gear. This is part of a trend which allows players to solve problems through their own solutions rather than linear force, I don’t think that’s a bad thing. The other and perhaps far more widespread reason, is because controls and hardware has changed. Play any darksouls game on a PC and you’ll quickly realize the true challenge is trying control your character the way you actually want it, while enjoying the 30 fps you are locked to, or the terrible internet connection of the invading lagger teleporting across your screen. The reality is that technology has solved many previous issues, like low FPS, which means less sensitive input and less sensitive perception of action. You are quite likely to be able to afford a large monitor, able to play games at 2k or higher resolution, able to see details and play games at frame rates over 120. The connection most people play games on is no longer ADSL, but relatively lightning fast speeds. This makes games far more responsive and intuitive to look at than 10 years ago. FromSoftware only achieved technical excellence with recent titles, they’ve always been innovative and had great ideas, but it is really only now that their titles are working as intended. If you are feeling modern games are too forgiving, you can always play some Armored Core 6 or Escape from Tarkov, if you are feel like your life is lacking depression.

Question: Are tank guns as good as a 155mm howitzer?
Answer: Tank guns like the 125mm and 120mm standard smoothbore tank guns of the east and west, generate way more chamber pressure than most howitzer guns do which fire their shells at slower speeds generally speaking. For example the 155mm M777 howitzer fires shells at 827 m/s muzzle velocity. In comparison the 125mm tank guns, can fire APFSDS ammunition at up to 1,800 m/s. This means that tank barrels have to be able to withstand quite a lot of pressure. As such guns like the 125mm 2A46M has a service life of about 450 shots with APFSDS, up to 1,200 shots with full caliber ammunition, compare this with the 1,500–2,500 shots with the M777 howitzer before a barrel change is needed. In that sense howitzers are able to fire more rounds of a higher power. If you are asking if a 155mm howitzer is more powerful than a 120–125mm tank gun in terms of explosive power, the answer is yes they are.

Question: Why is nobody stopping Venezuela?
Answer: The short answer is that the people who would want to stop Venezuela are a little busy. Likely you are referring to what appears to be the imminent actual annexation of Guayana Esequiba. The people who would want to stop this is the western countries in general, and the US in particular. The reason for this is because of the oil fields in Guayana, if Venezuela annexes the area, they will gain control over the offshore oil, which is currently exploited by ExxonMobile and Hess American oil companies. The news recently have made it out like this is entirely about Venezuela wanting the oil and nothing else, but this is a largely a fabrication. The oil is certainly why America cares, but Venezuela is already one of the largest oil producers in the world, and the extra oil itself likely isn’t going to make much difference. In reality, this territorial claim was not made yesterday, or even when the oil was discovered in 2015. The territorial dispute originates from 1890. For decades at this time, Venezuela was bullied by colonial powers, who wanted this particular territory, not for oil, but in order to tax river exports from Venezuela. Basically, it was established that the disputed territory belonged to Britain so they could extort the local population. Consider for a moment British satirical magazines depicted Britain as a thief running away stealing the land in 1899. The Venezuelan government has continuously claimed this was wrong, and since 1962 officially disputed it using evidence that arbitration taking place in Paris 1899 was a mere cover for a territorial steal. They are right about this. Venezuela has quite patiently waited for international communities to process the very obvious case presented both in 1899 and in 1962. 124 years after the initial steal, and 61 years after the official dispute at the UN, there was no ultimate settlement. Venezuela’s patience quite understandably reached its limit, as the plan seemingly was to say that the territory belong to Guyanna so that western oil companies can continue taking the oil or just run the case so long that the area could be stripped of natural resources. Venezuela acted now, because the US is busy with support to Ukraine and Israel. What better time is there to assert the dispute than now?

Question: Is the claim that "Western Europe is rich thanks to its colonies" true?
Answer: Yes, to a large extent it is true, and it is rather obvious when you think about it. There is a certain amount of resources in the world and they cannot be used in two places at once. We can take Britain as an example. There are some things that the British just wouldn’t have been able to do historically if it wasn’t for their colonies. In 1937 the British Empire exported 340,587 long tons of bauxite, which is the primary source of aluminium. This was becoming a strategic resource and was a highly lucrative trade. How much of this originated from Britain? 0%. 300,707 long tons (88.2%) of the British exports came from the colony British Guiana. If the native population had reaped the benefits of exporting this material, they would have been incredibly wealthy, there were about 2 tons of bauxite per person living there in 1937. Question: Does everyone have a different sense of humor?
Answer: No not really, I know that it is always more comforting to think everyone is very unique, and many people complain that different generations have different sense of humor, but do they really? You can probably categorize most humor in quite few boxes for example: Surprise, taboo, timing, irony, wit, intertextuality and schadenfreude. I think most people enjoy all of these to some extent. What is different is the frame of reference and expectations that people have. This is different not just between generations (time) but also cultures (location). Millennials in the west tends to think that their humor was very random, allegedly many people thought that two llamas discussing the murder of a human, was particularly funny because they were wearing hats. LoL so random! This is however, not a particularly millennial exclusive thing, in fact doing and saying very random and out of place things, is merely a variation of surprise. Surprise has been considered the height of humor for quite a while, ever since Monty Python essentially. Before Monty Python, wit and intertextuality, was very common as a form of humor, if you ever want to remember such a time, I highly recommend watching “To be or not To be” from 1942, one of my all time favorite movies, and probably the best screwball comedy movie written.

Question: Did Ukraine underestimate Russia’s capabilities or is it the failure of Nato intelligence? What could explain the failure of the Ukrainian counter offensive?
Answer: The offensive was launched in a rushed manner and with a divorce from reality of warfare. Many people in the west and apparently also in Ukraine patted themselves on the back following the successful Ukrainian defensive in the spring of 2022, and the successful Ukrainian offensive in the from September to November in the same year, and many people were talking about various equipment doing wonders to the Russians, but what I really remember from this time was not wonder weapons, it was trucks and trucks and trucks of these bad boys: Mines. Apart from Ukraine using basically the entire arsenal of Soviet TM-62 anti tank mines they had, they were also supplied with mines from Estonia, Germany, France, Sweden, UK and the USA. Furthermore Ukraine heavily used anti-personnel mines, again many left overs from the Soviet Union, probably expending the entire arsenal of PFM-1 mines delivered by BM-27, which was a serious problem for the Russian forces. Additionally, if we remember the initial Russian invasion force was a little over 200,000 strong, the Ukrainian military was mobilized to a strength of nearly 600,000 within a few months, and according to Ukrainian authorities reached about 1 million in total strength by October, including many in the interior of course, not all on the front line. For most of the war, Ukraine has been fighting with a numerical superiority in the area of operation. The entire Russian armed forces in 2022 was 900,000 troops, of which 280,000 were the army, 31,000 in the marine infantry, and 45,000 in the VDV. Which means Russia committed about 55% of their combat troops to the invasion initially. However, by January 2023 the Russian army had increased to 550,000 troops, VDV increased to 50,000 troops, while the marine infantry decreased slightly to 30,000. Either way, the amount of combat troops in the Russian army increased from 356,000 to 630,000. By the summer offensive it is estimated that this number was approaching 1 million. Additionally DPR & LPR and Wagner troops also supported this. In 2022 Ukraine had a reserve of a little under 500,000, while Russia had a reserve of 2 million. By 2023, the Ukrainian manpower reserve was done completely. While the Russians had used only 25% of their reserve, which mainly went into expanding the army. What does all this mean? Because of these 4 reasons, the Ukrainian offensive was doomed from the beginning. We didn’t know just how bad it was until recently, but the failure to break through the minefields in June and July were a bad omen, and after 5 months of continuous assaults Ukraine has lost many of it’s veterans and best trained soldiers. We know that the Ukrainian offensive in the south is ultimately over, because the Ukrainian western trained elite brigades have been moved from offensive actions near Robotino, to defensive actions against Russian attacks in Kupiansk and Avdiivka. The fate of Ukrainian offensive capability relies not only on western arms deliveries, which are severely lacking recently, but also on the ability of Ukraine to recall many of its young people who fled Ukraine as refugees, into coming back to fight. Question: How would a Russian T-90 preform against the notorious M1A2 Abrams (SEPV4)?
Answer: It seems highly likely both tanks are able to destroy each other at normal combat ranges under test settings, that is to say we line them up and they fire at perfect angles straight at each other. However, this is not really the reality of combat, it never was, but even less so now than previously. The current production version of the T-90 is far more suited for the reality of modern combat than the M1A2 Abrams is. For starters the vast majority of tank hits now are not on the front, but the sides and the top. The Abrams series have no reinforcement on the top armour at all, with it being 25–38mm thick. Practically any FPV drone with a tiny shaped charge can disable an Abrams, indeed we saw this quire clearly in Iraq when ISIS used toy drones for this exact purpose. The side and rear armour of the abrams like wise is easily penetrated as the special armor on the Abrams only cover the front arc and side of the turret. The TUSK armor upgrade for the Abrams increases side hull protection, but that is basically it. In contrast the T-90 currently produced has ERA protection on the top and indeed every other angle, as well as slat and net armour to catch drones and some RPG warheads. Additionally the T-90 has an integrated electronic warfare suite, which is supposed to blind thermal optics as well as give some jamming against drones. The M1A2 Sep4 Abrams might will be better protected from the front, against APFSDS, but there is little doubt that it is not as well protected against drones like the Lancet, or side shots. It also lacks effective stand off weapons to suppress wide areas of infantry and ATGM teams. Incredibly, the Abrams still do not have a 120mm High Explosive Fragmentation round available. In contrast the T-90M has a highly effective one, as well as an option to fire thermobaric missiles at targets over 5km away, which is a very potent solution to dueling with ATGM crews. In short, the M1A2 Sep4 might destroy a T-90 from the front on a shooting range, but in terms of actually getting into a position to do, the Abrams design appears disadvantaged in the realities of surviveability in a modern war against the most common anti tank threats.

Question: Why was the US so late on the 3rd gen mbt? The Soviets already made the T72 by 1970 and Germany which is a country divided in 2 managed to make the Leopard 2 during 1972 while the US only made the Abrams during 1980?
Answer: The Leopard 2 is from 1979 not 1972. The US and Germany were working on a tank before the Leopard 2 and Abrams was created, which was the MBT-70. The MBT-70 failed however, and we can talk about why. US defense secretary McNamara was suspiciously obsessed with German historical weapons development, and decided that a joint NATO vehicle could be developed between the US and Germany in the 1960s. However, quickly systematic differences in development hampered the project. On the top level the Germans were not happy with the fact that the Americans insisted on using imperial measurements for this tank which was supposed to be developed with Europeans. Additionally it was felt that development in the US was increasingly blowing the budget. Though by modern standards 300 million dollars over budget is called a Lockheed Martin 3 day workshop for interns. On a technical level the Germans didn’t like the American gun launcher or which was far inferior to conventional guns at ranges below 2km. Though it was able to fire missiles, it was also quite unimpressive. Despite having a massive 152mm gun, the missile MGM-51 was only able to reach a range of 3km in the improved version, the missiles are enormous and had a penetration of 600mm in best case estimations. The Soviet Kobra tank fired missile was 125mm had a range of 4.500m and a penetration of 600mm, while also being a faster (400 m/s vs 320 m/s) and more accurate missile. MGM-51 While the MBT-70 could carry 48 rounds, only 16 of them would be available in the autoloader. In contrast the T-72 carried 22 rounds in the autoloader out of its total of 44 rounds. The MBT-70 autoloader was impressive on paper, however neither Germany nor the US could make a reliable one, and so an autoloader from Italy’s OTO Malera was used. Even so, while I am unable to find test results, the reliability was likely poor anyway, as the autoloader was never used in any production tanks with both countries switching back to a manual loader despite agreeing initially on the benefits of an autoloader. The MBT-70 was really not quite as good as the T-64, while being immensely expensive and didn’t solve the problem it was designed for, i.e. making a common tank that could be used in Europe. The insistence on using a measurement system no one else uses in NATO was perhaps particularly annoying. Despite it’s high cost the MBT-70 failed to be what the T-64B was, i.e. a highly available tank with an autoloader, powerful cannon equally capable of APFSDS and firing anti tank missiles, with a laser range finder and composite armour.

Question: Do you know of any medieval ballad sung by bards and knights that is still sung today?
Answer: I do actually. The oldest recorded Danish song is “Drømte mig en drøm I nat”, it means “I dreamt a dream last night”. However, the words ærlik pæl, which is often meant to be silk and fabrics, referring to the singer wearing clothes, could also mean honest judgement, and the line could indeed be about equality before the law. This is supported by the fact that quite unusually, the song is written down in a tome called Codex Runicus which actually contains law texts. It is also note worthy to mention, that this song was written down about AD 1300 while a major reform of the Danish legal system was created in AD 1241. It is not impossible it is in fact related. Either way here is the song, some 700 years old and almost certainly sung by knights or bards, it is still sung today.

Question: What is the best military medal in the history of war?
Answer: There are many ways of thinking about what the “best” medal might be. Rarity, rarity of medals or the actions required for the awarding of a medal. If we go by rarity among the probably most recognizable medals from WW2, the Victoria cross wins rather handsomely. The list below is the number of recipients in the entire period it was awarded not just WW2, though most were awarded in this period for all of the medals. Obviously the Iron Cross was not actually a very difficult medal to obtain, even the knights cross of the iron cross had over 7,000 recipients in WW2 alone, which is more than both the US and UK medals combined. The Hero of the Soviet Union contains recipients who probably rank amongst the most impressive, however it also contains people who got it merely for their status, such as Stalin and Brezhnev. This in my opinion detracts quite a bit from it. Clearly the Soviets felt this way too, as they also felt it was needed to award some people with the award multiple times. Both the medal of honor and Victoria cross are very rarely awarded now, but they are also awarded rather inconsistently and for things not really that impressive. For example, Charles Brown received the US medal of honor, as a marine in 1871, merely for being part of a squad that captured a Korean flag during a minor and very one sided battle, in fact when the flag was captured the Korean fort was likely abandoned. He in fact deserted his duty before he even received the physical medal, being one of the only deserters in the world to receive the highest national award. Frederick Tilston, was the last non-posthumous awarded victoria cross in the European theater of WW2. According to his citation, it was awarded because he threw a hand grenade at a machine gun while wounded, proceeded to be wounded twice more in a battle, but was ultimately awarded the award for his leadership that resulted in a bayonet charge against a trench where 75% of his company died. In Denmark, there is a proverb which goes “Orders are hung on idiots”, unfortunately, the awarding of medals are often subject to arbitrariness and political influence. Question: In military terms, what's the difference between campaigns, battles, operations, and offensives? Are they are pretty much the same thing or is there something that distinguishes them?
Answer: These are all terms which are attempting to explain a period and often geographical section of military activity. Let’s go through them all. Battle: A battle is when 2 forces meet and engage each other. Originally this was quite simple, as armies were very concentrated and would usually meet in a very limited area, fight and determine a local winner. In the modern sense this is almost a useless term. Modern warfare is constantly and widespread. Fighting happens all the time and basically everywhere. Battles in the modern sense refers usually to areas which has a high intensity or where the outcome of the fighting is important. The battle of Kursk for example could easily be described as many battles, and was in reality at least 4 operational movements. Operation: Operation is the most modern term, and refers to military activity at a certain level. Usually today military activity is broken into 3 levels, the tactical (lowest) operational and strategic (highest). Operations are usually a limited scope, but large military force plan, which attempts to achieve one or several strategic objectives. This is usually the highest in which tactics are used, and the lowest level in which strategic goals are achieved. They are as such the binding level of command for modern wars. Offensive: A planned offensive, is usually an operation, in which one side attempts to break the enemy defenses and reach some form of strategic objective. A local offensive is the same but on a smaller scale. Campaign: A more or less obsolete term, that refers to a prolonged and often seasonal effort to conduct some military activity. It is more or less replaced in terminology with operation now, which carries more specific significance. In older history it was often the march of a single army to achieve a single objective. For example Henry V campaign to march across Normandy culminated in the battle of Agincourt.

Name: Carl Hamilton
Question: How does the M60A1 compare to the T72 Ural during the early 70s since they are similar in numbers at the time? How about the M 60A3 and T72A? Which tank is better?
Answer: The T-72 was a whole new generation of tank, it was a revolutionary step above the M60A1 even the most basic version. This was recognized by America at the time as well, which developed the M1 Abrams to counter the T-72 Ural and T-64A. Below the armour analysis from the US in 1979, notice by the way that the US believed that the T-64 came into production in 1973 along the T-72. The T-72 Ural was far superior in practically every way to the M60A1, including having features like an Autoloader and NBC protection. The above analysis actually also assumes this is an M60A1 AOS, as the M60A1 baseline doesn’t actually have a stabilizer, while the T-72 Ural had a two axis stabilizer which was slaved to the sight rather than the gun only, like was the case on the M60A1 AOS and Leopard 1. Additionally the T-72 had clear advantages in the following categories: Weight M60A1: 47.7t T-72 Ural: 41t Speed M60A1: 48 km/h T-72 Ural: 60 km/h Firepower Armour Piercing M60A1: 216mm RHA at 2km using M728 APDS (1974) T-72 Ural: 400mm RHA at 2km using 3BM-15 APFSDS (1972) Firepower High Explosive M60A1: 11.2 kg projectile, with 2.99kg of Comb. A filler, T-72 Ural: 23.2 kg projectile, with 3.15kg of TNT filler, 3OF19 Frontal Hull Armour M60A1: 108mm of RHA armour with 216mm RHAe in a Line of Sight (60 degree construction angle) T-72 Ural: 335–410mm RHAe vs kinetic and 410-510mm RHAe vs HEAT. Frontal Turret Armour M60A1: 250mm RHA in a LOS T-72 Ural: 380–410mm RHAe vs kinetic and 450–500mm RHAe vs HEAT. The M60A3 did little to change this balance. The M60A3 was frankly a very minor upgrade, which included simply a laser range finder, an electronic ballistics computer and a crosswind sensor. The M60A3 did not come with thermal optics by default, this was the TTS upgrade on the M60A3. The T-72A also featured a laser range finder, it did not need advanced computers or a crosswind sensor, because the speed of the 125mm smoothbore gun of the T-72 was vastly faster which made ballistic calculations simpler. While the computer in the T-72A was slightly cruder, it was still able to do automatic ballistic calculations within a second and upon ammunition selection. Additionally the T-72A received armour upgrades, and significant upgrade in firepower both HE and APFSDS, while the M60A3 continued using the obsolete 105mm rifled gun.

Name: Carl Hamilton
Question: I've seen a few videos a while ago showing Ukrainian soldiers punching Russian helmets and causing them to easily dent. Are the helmets denting because they're poorly made, or is it something to do with the material that is used?
Answer: I am guessing you’re referring to this video: There is a few things here, the helmet if it is indeed authentic (because you can get a plastic replica on Aliexpress for 10 dollars) appears to be a 6B47. The 6B47 is a lightweight helmet, that means it’s not a steel helmet. It is an aramid helmet, that means it is primarily made of a highly resistant fiber weave. This is the same material that soft bullet proof vests are made out of. I have read that in order to make the fiber hard it is impregnated with phenol-formaldehyde resin, but the point of a lightweight helmet is to be comfortable. These helmets can still stop 357 magnum rounds at less than 10m distance, which means they certainly also stop fragmentation which is what they are designed for. A 6B47 helmet was tested by Garandthumb on Youtube if you want to see a western test of it. There is quite a lot of space between the helmet and the wearers head which allows a lot of deformation, perhaps some of you remember the meme of Russian soldiers wearing big helmets. Aramid fibers Steel helmets are simply a lot heavier than kevlar helmets are, which is why many countries not just Russia use these. For example the OPS-CORE FAST helmet, is a popular type of helmet with western forces and is also made out of aramid. While this helmet is apparently more rigid than the 6B47, it is also smaller and tighter so it cannot allow much deformation. Even so, it is rated for 300-400 lbs static pressure. This is not a pressure level that is unobtainable from impacts. Russia does have other helmets, such as the Lynx-T and K6–3 which are titanium heavy helmets, they are rated for assault rifle fire to the face, but the reality of warfare is that you don’t need this often. Sometimes you see point man assault squad members wear these when clearing buildings. For outside combat when you are more likely to be shot at a distance, the 6B47 does it’s job okay.

Name: Carl Hamilton
Question: We know of German aces like Wittman, but what about allied aces, especially Soviet aces? Didn't they exist?
Answer: Well, there were many alleged tank aces including Soviet ones like Dmitry Lavrinenko who it was claimed destroyed 52 tanks before he died in December 1941. However, like with Wittman the stories are likely exaggerated. Whether the supposed Ace is American, German or Soviet, it has to be understood that actually verifying kill claims on the ground is exceedingly difficult. It is a known fact that if you count actual claims made by German units at Kursk they destroyed multiple times the entire Soviet inventory in a single battle. People over claim, and while the German claims in WW2 were particularly high, borderline comical, they were by no means the only people to suffer from over-claiming. The reality is that we really don’t know how many tanks people personally destroyed, we barely can accept unit wide claims, and I think the talk of individual ‘heroes’ whether they are snipers, pilots or tankers, honestly is a left over from WW2 propaganda, and has little verifiable historical basis.

Name: Carl Hamilton
Question: What other alternatives could America have taken other than building tank destroyers and creating the Tank Destroyer Force?
Answer: In principle there was nothing wrong with the idea of the tank destroyer doctrine in the way that the war was expected to happen. It was merely that the Germans didn’t have the capacity to fight in the west how the Americans expected it. The original idea was that US armies would have a reserve of densely grouped tank destroyers ready to destroy German armored counter attacks. The reality however was, that Germany essentially never launched any armored counter attacks against the USA, one of the only real major tank engagements at all in France was the battle of Caen, which was handled by the British. Until the battle of the Bulge the biggest tank engagements the entire American force was involved in, was the Battle of Arracourt. In this battle completely green German Panther crews failed to read tactical maps correctly, was bombed non stop by US ground attack planes and generally made a total mess of their own situation. Patton’s vanguard 4th Armour division made a short process of this German group in a matter of a week, and from then the US never encountered another German attack like this in France. Had there been any serious attacks like the German attack on Kursk, the Americans would likely have been ready, the groups of tank destroyers were used at Arracourt and destroyed their targets, they were deployed correctly at the battle of the Bulge. The criticism stems from the fact, that for the majority of the campaign, the American forces met sporadic armour resistance, which could easily destroy a couple of out gunned Shermans before tank destroyers were brought up, but this was never at any point a decisive disadvantage. Would it have been better to have tank destroyer distributed or delivered 76mm shermans earlier? Probably, a little bit, but really it just didn’t matter. The Germans were so overmatched that not even having the 76mm M10 tank destroyer or Sherman, would probably had made no difference at all, and bringing them up earlier would have made just as little of a difference. The big German armor attack was just never going to happen, but had it happened the tank destroyer doctrine would likely have proved just fine, but hindsight is 20/20, no one knew how it would be back then.

Question: During battles in avdivka, a Russian t72 was able to destroy a leopard 2a6 on first shot after its operatives detected the tank with a drone. Has the presence of drones negated the target acquisition advantages western tanks have over Soviet tanks?
Answer: Target acquisition inside a tank requires more than simply knowing the general direction of a potential enemy tank. In fact if you have ever tried playing a game like war thunder with another person, you’ll know that telling someone where something is that you see, without being able to point on their screen is in fact not so easy. Even before drones, you have observation helicopters, ground radars and scouts, which would also find and mark enemy tanks for their own tank units. The advantage western tanks had over Soviet tanks for an honestly rather brief period, was their more sophisticated thermal optics, which allowed them to scan for heat signatures. What has negated this advantage is simply that modern T-72s and other Russian tanks also have thermal optics. This is simply a standard feature of current production tanks.

Name: Carl Hamilton
Question: If Guderian, or Von Monstien, had been in charge of the 6th army, might Stalingrad have been different?
Answer: No, it would not. Manstein, was involved in the breakout attempt, and some people say “they could just have moved sooner”, and “if only Hitler had not been in the way”. Manstein called for 8 fresh divisions saying this would be enough to lead the lifting of the encirclement for Stalingrad. Only 2 fresh divisions could be provided for. Manstein was making plans using imaginary units that never arrived. Had Manstein or Guderian been commanding the sixth army, they would not have been able to conjure more troops out of the air than Paulus could. They would not have been able to increase the transport capacity of the Luftwaffe or increase the availability and supply of new tanks. Stalingrad was not an almost defeat for the Soviet Union, Operation Uranus was a crushing defeat for the Germans. It was not close. There is an idea that it was merely a small encirclement around Stalingrad and then the Soviets waited out the destruction of the Sixth Army. This is false. The Soviets significantly expanded their territorial hold along the entire southern front until mid February. Uranus was also not the only offensive launched, Little Saturn, as well as the Ostrogozhsk–Rossosh offensive and after that the Voronezh–Kastornoye offensive also saw massive Soviet victories, and essentially knocked Hungary out of offensive actions for the rest of the war. No matter who was in charge, the Axis had used up their remaining offensive power, there was not much left at this point. If the line had not broken around Stalingrad, it would have broken at Voronezh. The Germans indeed had some elite armies, and great generals, but they couldn’t be everywhere, the majority of the Axis line was basic infantry, whether they were German, Romanian, Italian or Hungarian, the Soviets could attack any section of the line where German elite units were not located, and simply break through with their tank armies and superior artillery. As indeed is what they did. Nothing Guderian or Manstein could have done at the point of late 1942, was ever going to change the material reality.

Question: Why is the military-industrial complex being demonised? What is wrong with having a vibrant MIC capable of producing large volumes of military equipment and ammunition?
Answer: Well the military industrial complex (MIC) is demonized because frankly it sucks, and it sucks in almost every way you can imagine. As such, MIC companies basically risk nothing. And once a contract is signed the companies can deliver practically nothing and the US government will just have to keep paying them in the HOPE that they will eventually deliver a viable product. For example, if you look at the F-35 development cycle, this was awarded as a contract for development, with a budget of 233 billion dollars over 20 years, that’s an advance agreed pay of 11,65 billion dollars per year, an absurd asking price for a single vehicle. As soon as the US government was invested in the project the MIC simply started asking for more, in fact the development budget by 2021 had gone over 416 billion dollars, that’s nearly double the original budget. Additionally, the end product ended up being extremely expensive, both in operation and in purchase, as well as delayed and full of flaws that has already caused many of them to crash. The MIC pays pentagon in bribes as well as in lucrative jobs in the industry once they quit their position in the pentagon. The MIC pays politicians to maintain the system, and it pays its shareholders stupid amounts of profits. All of these are additional expenses that in no way positively affects the final product, but it is all expenses someone has to pay for, and since all these products are publicly paid but privately owned, you dear American taxpayer is paying for everything. This is the reason why that the world’s largest military budget, does not equal a proportionate increase in military power. While the US might indeed have the most military power in total, it is also pumping in multiple times the amount of funds other nations even like China is, and they are absolutely not getting an equal amount of return. The US military industrial complex, is one of the least cost effective production systems in the world.

Name: Carl Hamilton
Question: Why do military colleges study ancient battles? How can it apply to current strategies, technologies, etc.?
Answer: The same reason why when you study economy you read Smith, Ricardo and Marx, when you study sociology you read Durkheim and Comte. These are not modern theorists, so surely there are more contemporary theories students should be reading? Of course, there are more modern theories, but reading the classics means you can see how the field has evolved over time, which is valuable information to get an idea of the flow of scientific knowledge, and to learn from the very process of progressing. Likewise, when studying military science or history, it is good to know how principles of warfare and tactics worked when all warfare was very simple. Modern warfare is highly complex, but an officer should still be aware of the basics, and such basics are more easily understood when other variables are removed. While the battle of Cannae will not be fought again, it is still valuable to understand the deception of the weak center, as this strategy can easily still be used today, though on a much larger scale. Indeed the tactics of formation battles often has modern analogues at the operational level.

Question: How was Syria before the Civil War? Did the "Assad regime" always had this reputation or did it really start after things went downhill and wartime atrocities started happening?
Answer: Syria was a fairly stable country and one of the most multicultural in the middle east, it had many and large minorities from Armenians in Dier ez-Zor, Druze in southern Syria, Yazidi in eastern Syria, Kurds in Rojava, Alawites in Latakia, Turkmens in Idlib and everybody in Aleppo. Name: Carl Hamilton
Question: What are some features or things that an M1A2 Abrams have that no other tank have that gives them an advantage?
Answer: There are really no features which are unique to the M1A2, indeed it’s design from 1980 is only incrementally updated, but it is essentially still a 1980 tank. It’s difficult to prove an absence, so I will instead make an argument against some of the so called features of the Abrams that others are praising. Uranium armour This is not a feature, this is a hazard. The advantage of uranium is that it is dense, but it is not the only dense material in the world. Many people have convinced themselves that weld a solid slab of dense metal to the front of a tank is high technological achievement. It is not. DU is available to any country with uranium based nuclear reactors, but to most people DU is a nuclear waste. Tungsten has a very similar density to uranium while also being being harder, making it probably a better material for armour in fact, it has the added advantage of being perfectly safe, while uranium is extremely toxic. Probably why that the UK went for using tungsten armour plates instead of DU despite their close relationship with the US, and despite their armour layout being very similar otherwise. You might wonder why the US used their nuclear waste for armour instead of tungsten then, while no one else in the world does this. Fire Control The US were early pioneers of fully digital fire control systems as well as thermal optics, and while this was undoubtedly advantage at some points, this is not in anyway unique features for the M1A2 anymore, these are standard on basically all tanks currently in production everywhere in the world. Blowout Panels This is again not unique to the Abrams, all western tanks feature this, and the Abrams was not the first one to have it either. Gas Turbine Engine Perhaps one of the most unique features of the Abrams is the engine, the vast majority of tanks uses diesel engines, however even where the Abrams is not the only nor the first for this, with the Soviet T-80 series features gas turbine engines before the Abrams, and still to this date has them. Indeed, the M1A2 lacks features many other tanks have, including integrated reactive armour, drone protection, gun launched missiles, automatic loading and more. The usual argument is that the US systems is better, however an opinion or evaluation of performance, is not a feature. 410mm of steel is not a 10mm feature over 400mm of steel for example. It’s a statistically insignificant measuring difference that is likely within the margin of error. In terms of performance the M1A2 falls pretty close to it’s peers in every regard, sometimes below sometimes above, but again this is not a feature.

Question: What is the reason Russia is so interested in capturing Avdiivka in the Donetsk Oblast?

This railroad connects to Russia, and if this area is captured the Russians will have a significantly easier time moving supplies up for potential offensives around Kramatorsk. As such, taking Avdiivka is vital for the offensive actions Russia is planning in the Donetsk area, it’s vital for continued Russian offensives, it is vital for Ukraine’s defense, and it’s vital as a forward base for launching attacks on Donetsk city. Name: Carl Hamilton
Question: How well did King Tiger Tanks perform on the Eastern Front?
Answer: Not very well, despite claims of the superiority of the Tiger II, and there are several reasons for this. The Tiger II was introduced only in mid 1944, and while the first of the type was engaged in Normandy, the majority went to reconstituting the heavy tank battalions on the eastern front, notably the 501st Heavy tank battalion which was completely destroyed in 2 weeks of operation Bagration. Tiger IIs destroyed by the Soviets at height 188 in January 1945 The Tiger II was not mechanically reliable, and therefore were usually extremely difficult to move around. The 501st heavy tank battalion was sent to Poland to fight the Soviets on August 5th, after being unloaded from the train they had to drive 50km on a road to meet up with the 16th Panzer Division. 100% of the tanks suffered a mechanical break down. By August 11th, only 8 out of the 45 Tiger II were operational, 17.8% operational readiness. This shows just how little these tanks could actually be used. The second flaw, is that despite it’s insane weight and complexity, it was vulnerable to even standard Soviet tank guns. The 8 operational tanks went to attack the Soviet bridgehead over the Vistula river near Ogledow, on the road there 3 of these tanks were completely blown up by T-34s in ambush, as well as 2 abandoned after taking damage. In the following days more of the battalion was brought up, and eventually they managed to lose 13 Tiger 2 tanks, including all 8 originally operational, to the far cheaper T-34 and IS-2 tanks. The below image fails to mention that the 16th Panzer division was also engaged in this battle, but shows the loss of Tiger IIs. Soviet heavy tank regiments had 21 IS-2 tanks in each, while the German heavy battalion had 45 Tiger II, as such if it wasn’t for the unreliable nature of Tiger IIs the Germans would have outnumbered the Soviet heavy tanks more than 2 to 1, but in practice it was the other way around. Likewise the two Soviet medium tank brigades, did not have more tanks than the 16th Panzer division on paper. Any numerical difference was caused by German mechanical failures. Finally, very often we see Tiger IIs without tracks, this is often caused by high explosive shots, which disabled the German tanks, 152mm shells could do it with a hit that is within 30m of a tank. Now if you play video games you likely are aware of the ISU-152 which is often portrayed as the Soviet beast equivalent to the Tiger II in rarity. This is however not the case. The Soviets had 4,600 ISU-152 vehicles built, while the German managed just 500 Tiger 2, that means for every 1 Tiger II German fielded, the Soviets had basically 2 full batteries of ISU-152 (9 to 1 advantage), a single direct hit from a 152mm gun, could send the inside of the Tiger II armour flying through the tank, and so while many appear undamaged, the reality is that the crew very much would be dead, not from penetration, but from spalling. As such, the Tiger II on the eastern front had little to no impact on operations, the counter to the Tiger II was developed before the Tiger II was and was readily available, but as the battle of Ogledow showed, it was not even really needed as with proper tactics Soviet tank corps were fully capable of defeating Tiger II battalions even at full strength.
