Name: Carl Hamilton
Question: Why do the British choose rifle guns more compared to the US, Russia, and Germany which choose smoothbore guns for the tanks? What is the advantage of a rifle gun than a smootbore gun?
Answer: The British have a very poor tank industry, and simply have opted for continuing to use inferior guns because they make them domestically. I know this upsets the fanclub of British tanks, however, the british launched the “Challenger Lethality Improvement Programme”, in which they attempted to upgrade the firepower of the Challenger 2. They did this by putting a German 120mm smoothbore gun on it. The German 120mm gun, is in fact from 1979, with the upgrade from 1991, the British L30A1 on the Challenger 2 is from 1998. What does it tell you about the state of your technology, that putting a gun that is 7 to 19 years older than what you just made into your tank, is an upgrade of firepower? Often you see people say that rifled barrels are more accurate because they induce spin. Yes this is true, if you’re comparing to a smoothbore cannon from before World War 1. Modern tank smoothbore cannons fire fin stabilized ammunition, which is highly accurate. Indeed, the main factor in modern APFSDS dispersion, is vibrations in the cannon, not whether it is rifled or fin stabilized. Indeed tank affecionardos, might be interested to know that the main difference in the 125mm Soviet 2A46-1 gun and the 2A46M gun, is that the 2A46M has a different recoil system which reduces vibrations, it lead to a 40% reduction in dispersion if I recall correctly. Other people tout the HESH round as something special. HESH rounds are not special, they are unique only in that they are less versatile and less useful than HE-FRAG in most circumstances. HESH rounds primary virtue is that they are able to hurt armour and structures by squashing against them, imparting additional force to the object, but guess what, so can HE-FRAG. Modern HE-FRAG rounds has a setting called delayed fuze, in which that the HE-FRAG does not detonate on impact, but slightly delayed, causing the explosive to compress on the target. Indeed the Soviets after receiving Chieftain tanks from Iran in the 1980s, ran tests to see the difference. The difference was totally negligible, with 125mm Soviet HE-FRAG outperforming 120mm HESH rounds from the Chieftain, in a HESH role. Below chart is the movement of an homogeneous armor plate, line 2 is 125mm HE-FRAG, line 1 is 120mm HESH, and line 3 is 115mm HE-FRAG. Read about it in the footnote.[1] In reality, the rifled cannon makes HEAT rounds worse, it makes APFSDS worse, (L30A1 is the same length as the L55 120mm German gun, while achieving 100 m/s less velocity on APFSDS), it’s harder to maintain, it’s harder to produce and it wears out faster. The reason why the British continue to use it, is because they have shells for it. No one is developing new HESH rounds, while almost every NATO country has developed a new HE-FRAG round in the last 20 years. It’s an obsolete technology, that people mainly worship because they genuinely do not compare it’s actual performance scientifically with any other platform. If the club takes an interest, you will no doubt soon see the comment section full of anecdotes which can unfortunately not be backed up by evidence, just have to trust in hear say.

Name: Carl Hamilton
Question: Why T-62 MBT is less popular than T-54/55 even had a bigger gun 115mm than T-54/55?
Answer: The T-62 has a bit of a bad reputation in the Anglo-Sphere, but it is far from unpopular among it’s customers in reality. The T-62 just didn’t offer that much over the T-55 which many customers already had. While it is almost certainly a better tank, thanks to it’s firepower, in other respects it is very similar to the T-55. The 115mm gun should not be underestimated though, when it was developed it was indisputably the most powerful tank gun in the world, unfortunately for the T-62, it was surpassed by the 125mm gun just a few years later, and by the time the T-62 was being offered for export, the T-72 was being produced and within 10 years also offered for export. Countries like India looking to upgrade, saw the T-72 as a major overhaul of every system in the tank, while the T-62 was mostly a firepower and a small protective upgrade, over the T-55. As such countries which already had the T-55 mostly just stuck with it until things like the T-72 was available, though countries in the 1970s who did acquire the T-62, found that it was a very capable tank, such as Iraq and Egypt, who both used it to great effect against more expensive western tank which could not compete with its long range fire power. As such, almost every non-Soviet country that has operated the T-62, still does, about 50 years later, quite a good service record, despite what is commonly believed.

Name: Carl Hamilton
Question: North Korea has for many decades been producing tank and artillery shells identical in caliber to those used by the Russian army. Question: How many shells have been produced in North Korea?
Answer: There is absolutely no way to tell this for certain, we don’t even know how many artillery guns and other weapons North Korea really have. However, the North Korean doctrine was to win a conventional war using overwhelming artillery fire power, and prolonged determination. While North Korea has likely built these for a long time, and potentially continuously, North Korea also has a limited industry. That being said, North Korea likely has stockpiles in the millions of shells, potentially double digit millions of shells. Not all of them are in calibers commonly used by Russia though, for example the Koksan shown above, uses a 170mm shell, while the similar Russian 2S7M Malka uses 203mm shells. So while they appear very similar, they would not be able to exchange shells. 152mm and 122mm shells as well as 122mm Grad rockets are likely to be the kind of products that most readily can be used by Russia. Another caveat is that North Korean ammunition likely uses TNT rather an A-IX-2 explosive filler, meaning that they will not have quite the same firepower as modern shells.

Name: Carl Hamilton
Question: Can you describe one of the possible scenarios of further escalation in the Middle East?
Answer: One of the potential worst case scenarios for escalation is that another major country joins in earnest on the side of the Palestinians. The most likely candidate for this right now appears to be Iran, but they are far from alone. Recently we saw the Jordanese police attempting to storm the US embassy in the country, as well as massive protests in Turkey and outbursts in Egypt. Jordanese police protects the US Embassy in Amman This kind of unrest will not be pleasant for the stability of the middle east in general, and we likely have not seen the top of it yet. The governments are forced with some very difficult choices, being too anti-Israel might result in a war with not just Israel but also its western allies. Not being anti-Israel enough, might well result in riots, or even revolts or revolutions. The larger middle eastern world has rested on narratives regarding Israel for so long, that it will be hard to control. However, righteous one might think the public is, uncontrollable public fervor tends to lead to very unfavorable outcomes in history. If one or several actors decide to join the conflict against Israel directly, either voluntarily, due to public pressure, or because of a regime change, they will risk terrible retaliation. While previously Israel beat it’s neighbors handily in their wars, the power has shifted and the countries arrayed against it, are not as disorganized or technologically outclassed as was the case in the past. Particularly Iran has a large capacity, though they are geographically disadvantaged in a potential war, but if Iraq and Syria were to condone an attack, Iran could bring about massive land forces to bear, and their long range weapons are already combat proven. Was this to happen, and did Israel feel that they might indeed lose a conventional war against what ever an escalated alliance might look like, the result would be sadly predictable. Israel will almost certainly use it’s nuclear arsenal damned what anyone thinks. They believe that a true defeat will result in the destruction of Israel, which is not unrealistic, as such they will hold nothing back. Likely, the western countries are aware of this too, and the move of conventional forces to the theater from the USA and NATO, is not because Israel needs this in their current operations, but because the west fears that an escalation which Israel might lose, would lead to a nuclear strike. Whether an escalation would result in a major conventional war in which the allies of Palestine end up being slaughtered by the combined western-Israeli forces, or if they perform so well Israel strikes with nuclear weapons, a major war with religious and long time ideological fervor on both sides, will likely be more bloody than what we have seen in Ukraine so far. Hawks on all sides are wishing for escalation, fantasizing about it, saying this is the opportunity for a final showdown. This is a foolish position no matter which side one is on, the damage will be irreparable, both for the middle east, and for the large diaspora of ethnicity from both sides, will suffer greatly. No one should wish for an escalation, indeed the only sensible choice is de-escalation, negotiation and peaceful solutions. Think not that simply because you feel that one side might win, that would would do so at low cost, while politicians with many goals might win in such a conflict, be assured that the civilians on a far larger scale than what is happening now will be the losers.

Name: Carl Hamilton
Question: Is depriving a region of water considered a conventional tactic in military operations?
Answer: Historically speaking it is indeed a very common tactic, and well known throughout many wars. Often this is done in relatively minor engagements by modern standards such as sieges. However, directly attacking a targets in such a way, that the civilian population in the area no longer has access to drinking water, is not considered customary anymore, and if a nation has signed the Additional Protocol I of the Geneva convention, this is a war crime. It is prohibited to attack, destroy, remove, or render useless objects indispensable to the survival of the civilian population, such as foodstuffs, agricultural areas for the production of foodstuffs, crops, livestock, drinking water installations and supplies and irrigation works, for the specific purpose of denying them for their sustenance value to the civilian population or to the adverse Party, whatever the motive, whether in order to starve out civilians, to cause them to move away, or for any other motive. Article 54(2) of the 1977 Additional Protocol I of the Geneva convention. As with most legal texts there are some caveats to this.

Name: Carl Hamilton
Question: What did the Warsaw Pact Army, Navy, and Air Force look like in the 1960s? What was also their tanks, fighter jets, and equipment compared to NATO?
Answer: The Warsaw Pact was in general being built up at this time, it was mostly the Soviet military, the 1960s was a period of modernization experiments for the USSR, which greatly intensified in the 1970s in a series of sophisticated weapons, but we see the beginning of these in the 1960s. The Soviet army was switching to a fully mechanized fighting force, and mechanized systems began to appear which would increase the fire power of Soviet infantry formations by massive amounts. The BTR-60 from 1959 became the main APC and transport vehicle for Soviet infantry, and from 1966, the BMP-1 the world’s first infantry fighting vehicle, and the vehicle after which the type is named, began appearing which allowed every squad in the unit to have an anti tank missile and 73mm cannon at their disposal at all times, as well as being bullet proof and amphibious. We saw the introduction of the T-64 in 1966, which was probably the most ahead of its time tank. The features of the T-64 revolutionized tank design, from it’s autoloader, smoothbore cannon, invention of APFSDS to the composite armour, none of which would be available even in their early stages in NATO for 10–20 years. Likewise the Soviets mass introduced self propelled anti aircraft weapons like the ZSU-23–4 Shilka, the first radar guided SPAAA in 1960, something NATO would not get for another 16 years with the introduction of the Flak Panzer Gepard. This was complimented by the mobile medium range 2K12 Kub missile launcher in 1967, which would later plague Israeli aircraft in the Yom Kippur war. In the Soviet navy, the Soviet had given up on creating large ships, and were instead moving towards missiles on all levels. Already in the 1950s the Soviets had created the P-15 anti ship missile and mounted it on small boats, in 1967 Egyptian Komar class boats sank a much larger Israeli destroyer from a safe distance, though it would take until 1980 before Harpoon missiles became available to NATO. By 1967 the Soviet had invented the P-70 which was the first submarine launched cruise missile, that could be launched while submerged. As we now missiles was certainly to be the future of naval warfare. In the air force, the Soviets struggled to match NATO quality in several fields. In 1970 they would introduce the MiG-25 and MiG-23 both fairly capable fighters. The MiG-21 from 1959, was the mainstay of Soviet air power, which was fairly versatile though not as capable as the top tier NATO planes of the time, it was cheap and produced in huge numbers. The Soviets also developed the Mi-8 helicopter, the most produced helicopter ever. In terms of infantry weapons, the Soviets developed the RPG-7 which would prove to become the most successful shoulder fired rocket launcher in the world by a very large margin. The PK machine gun, RPK machine gun, the AKM assault rifle, Malyutka ATGM, SPG-9, SVD sniper rifle, D-30 122mm light howitzer and other weapons completely and deeply modernized the Soviet infantry arm, again to a level that most of NATO was not able to achieve for decades. In terms of numbers, the Soviets fielded 136 divisions in 1960 with 35,000 tanks, they had 4,000 fighter aircraft and 1,000 bombers. Compared to the US who had 17 ready divisions, with 13,000 tanks of older quality. Apart from the Soviet navy fielding 400 compared to 100 attack submarines in the US navy, the US navy was superior in numbers and quality in every area except missile technology. But by the end of the 1960s the Soviet navy was a highly modern missile focused navy, while the US scrapped 200 ships by 1970 due to their old age and did not replace them with any new ships. In short, the Soviet military was drastically modernising in the 1960s and would peak in the 1970s in terms of relative power to NATO.

Name: Carl Hamilton
Question: Would the Soviet Union be able to defeat Nazi Germany without the contribution of Ukrainians?
Answer: That’s a rather complicated question, but I will endeavor to give a somewhat sensible answer. I think that the most obvious question would be under which circumstances, Ukraine as a whole would not be part of the USSR. To me the most sensible solution, is around 1918, with the central powers holding most of Ukraine, and the Bolsheviks holding only the Donetsk Socialist Republic. If history splits at this part, with the central powers held part of Ukraine, stay independent and not joining in the Russian civil war, and also somehow not being absorbed by Poland, and all else remains we can think about what the consequences might be. The alternative outcome is that they do join the war, but this is actually what happened and they lost which resulted in most of it being absorbed. If we then move ahead to 1941, I see 3 possible scenarios: There are other considerations compared to reality, in terms of economy for the most part the USSR did win WW2 without Ukraine’s territorial contribution. In reality by August 1941, half of Ukraine was already lost, and eastern Ukraine was lost by October 1941 after the first battle of Kharkov. The territory of Ukraine would barely play a role in Ukraine as a resource for the Soviet Union. The population of Ukraine was divided, with many remaining in the occupied territory and some fleeing to the east. It is pretty difficult to quantify the contribution based on ethnicity, but Peter Samsanov gave these numbers for the irrecoverable casualties of the Red Army: 5,756,000 were Russian (66%). Ukrainians made up 1,377,400 losses (16%), Belarusians 252,900 (3%), Tatars 187,700 (2%), Jews 142,500 (1.6%), Kazakhs 125,500 (1.4%), Uzbeks 117,900 (1.4%) and other nationalities made up less than one percent of the total losses apiece. Others might consider in the direction of famous contributors to development. For example someone told me the T-34 would not have been developed. To this I say, that the chief designer of the T-34 was Mikhail Koshkin, who died in 1940, but the design was already basically finished then. He was Russian. Aleksandr Morozov then took over as lead designer, and did an excellent job, but he was in fact born in Bryansk to Greek parents, whether you want to call him Greek or Russian based on that is up to you. While the Kharkiv Locomotive Factory formed the initial basis for the design team, they spent the second world war in the Urals working from inside the UralVagonZavod factory. In short, this is a counter factual question, so we cannot say if the USSR could have won anyway, no doubt in many ways they would have been far worse off, but depending on the magical powers you choose to change history, it appears to me that they could still have won, even with the reduction in manpower, they would have gained some geographic advantages.

Question: Why do we condemn the Russians taking land, but we are okay with the Israelis doing the same to the Palestinians?
Answer: I will tell you this in principle, most people base their condemnations on having no idea about the situation, history or international principles in question. Most politicians’ actions on the other hand can be explained quite easily, they condemn their political enemies, and they support their allies. It doesn’t matter in anyway what the context is, the condemnation of countries at the political level has at this point lost any and all meaning, it is merely and solely virtue signaling what ever is most expedient at the time. Name: Carl Hamilton
Question: Considering their arsenal of long range missiles, why didn't Russia attack Kyiv or western Ukraine more? Wouldn't taking out key figures in the Ukrainian government be beneficial? Or is this part of a psyop?
Answer: Russia has switched their strategy on the deployment of their strategic missiles more than once in the war. Initially Russia had a substantial but actually quite limited missile strike against Ukraine, this took out some airfields and some AA positions, but was focused mostly on highly concentrated ammunition depots and logistical facilities. Russia was likely trying to limit the damage to Ukraine initially expecting a less hostile welcome if the bombing campaign was not as extensive. Initially the Iskander was the most feared weapon and it still remains in service for high priority targets, but the Shahed-136 now makes up one of the most common systems of strategic bombardment. When Russia realized this was not going to happen, the missile campaign intensified, but much of Ukraines air force and air defense network had dispersed and were not longer as vulnerable. During the summer of 2022, Russian strategic attacks were lowered in quantity and targets were switched to so-called decision making centers, such as the Vinnytsia air force command center. In the fall of 2022, the Russian strategy under supervision of general Suroviken began focusing on the electric infrastructure and supply of oil, in an attempt at worsening the conditions for the Ukrainians during the winter, but a relatively mild winter saved Ukraine from too much trouble along with the aid of western countries in the supply of coal and oil. This coincided with the introduction of the Shahed-136 drone which allowed cheaper alternatives for low priority targets such as electric substations. Likely Russia will return to this strategy this winter as well. But for most of 2023, waves of attacks have been made, usually to shape political goals, for example the destruction of depots in Odesa and other Ukrainian cities has been a high priority after the end of the grain deal. West Ukraine and Kyiv have been attacked multiple times, in west Ukraine depots and particularly training bases have been the focus of attacks, one of the first major strategic strikes was against a base housing foreign volunteers in western Ukraine for example. Kyiv has also been hit multiple times, with the electric power plants being the most obvious targets, while other targets have been more shrouded in mystery and the effectiveness of which is not confirmed by Ukraine. Finally, taking out officials in a war is not nessesarily beneficial, officials can in fact be replaced, and sometimes with more competent people. Additionally, assassinating politicians is a very bad idea, as it often leads to them doing the same to you. Really only the exceptionally stupid, would want to engage in a competition like that, and doubtless neither Russia nor NATO would like to see that.

Name: Carl Hamilton
Question: How many battles did Julius Caesar win as a general?
Answer: Julius Ceasar won 6 out of the 7 major battles in his Gallic campaign, as well as one siege. He took a break during this campaign to invade Britain, win 3 battles and force the British to become Roman tributaries. After returning to Rome, Caesar fought a civil war in which he lead 9 battles, of which 7 he won, as well 4 sieges, and the battle of the Nile. That is 14 major pitched battles in 2 campaigns. Caesar also had other campaigns, he fought in Iberia and Greece before, during his governorship in Hispania Ulterior, he no doubt fought battles as well and obtained Imperium for which he qualified for a triumph in Rome. Caesar gave up his triumph in order to run for consulship due to Cato’s filibustering. Either way, I think we can say that Caesar won at least 14 major battles, and likely far more which history has not recorded in detail.

Name: Carl Hamilton
Question: Who are some generals that had a high regard as battle strategist geniuses but actually aren't?
Answer: Erwin Rommel is probably one of the most over rated so called geniuses. Rommel had a good sense of tactical employment of certain equipment particularly tanks, but he was greatly aided by the fact he mostly fought an outpost of Britain, rather than the full might of any of the allied armies, and his tactics were never tested by the Soviet armored branch, unlike most German generals. Furthermore, he was operationally inept and strategically an imbecile. Rommel was the ultimate “i know better than you”, and circumvented the command chain to get his way. For example, he appealed directly to Hitler in order to launch the attack on Egypt, that totally failed and cost the Axis their foothold in Africa, and undermining the Wehrmacht plan made to occupy Malta and cut off the British navy. At the strategic level Rommel never understood Germany’s actual position, and certainly did not contribute to it. He left this entire theater of command on June 5th despite the Germans knowing that an invasion of France was imminent. He had also previously spent massive resources on creating additional anti air borne defenses, none of which had an impact on the outcome of D-day. Rommel was defeated in Africa, defeated in Italy and defeated in France, before he was a high level leader he was an insubordinate divisional commander who got lucky mostly. His ghost division was called such because no one knew where it was or what it was doing. That is not a good thing. Despite all this, Rommel is often mentioned as one of the greatest generals in World War 2, but I really see no reason for this, when von Rundtstedt and even the self aggrandising Mannstein, clearly had far more success and skill than Rommel did.

Name: Carl Hamilton
Question: What was a feudal army?
Answer: A feudal army was an army in which the organization of the military was according to the feudal hierarchy of the society. That means that the ranking liege lord, would summon his vassals, who in turn would summon their vassals all the way down to the peasant bondsmen. The King of Denmark firetaxing (extorting) Visby after the Danish defeated the Swedish in 1361 It is often considered that a feudal army was an elite cavalry force surrounded by low quality infantry levies. However, that is not nessesarily the nature of feudalism, though it is partially true for some west European kingdoms. A king might call upon his duke, counts and barons, who personally will fight as elite mounted warriors. However the main stay of the army varies entirely on which companies the vassal choose to keep. The English famously maintained pretty skilled archers who were by no means low quality. The French were able to field almost entire armies of professional warriors and mercenaries. Other kingdoms called upon free cities to provide trained companies of engineers and crossbowmen such as Bercelona. The core of a feudal army then is simply that it is made up of vassal obligations, but what that army actually consists of in practice depended on regional specialties and effort put into maintaining their men at arms.

Name: Carl Hamilton
Question: Why did the German Panther (PzKpfw V) have a Schachtellaufwerk suspension design that hard to maintain in the field comparing its rival T-34 or M-4? What is its advantage so Germany choose to apply in this tank?
Answer: The advantage was that it provided a slightly smoother ride. Many will point out that is was considerably smoother in terms of felt force, but it honestly mattered quite little. It was not smooth enough to allow for firing on the move, in the way that stabilizers later would. Tanks still generally had to stand still to fire, that included the Panther and Tiger. The reason why the M4 Sherman and T-34 didn’t feature them is because they didn’t warrant the extra complication, expense and reliability issues. It offered quite little combat advantage, while reducing the number of available tanks due to mechanical reliability, and reduced the number of available tanks due to lower production output. It was a classic case of Germany spending an unnecessary amount of resources on gaining a small advantage in quality at the expense of reducing the number of serviceable vehicles.

Name: Carl Hamilton
Question: What is the best piece of Russian military propaganda from World War II?
Answer: Planting the Soviet flag on the government building in the capitol of the enemy nation which started the war. This was probably a fairly successful piece of propaganda, quite possibly one of the most recognizable pictures and acts of victory in the 20th century as well. I would imagine that nearly everyone with even a mild interest in history has seen the picture on the left, or a variant of it.

Name: Carl Hamilton
Question: What lessons can be learned from the perspectives of German veterans of the 20th century regarding potential wars with Russia?
Answer: Frankly quite little. If you just watched someone loser horribly, why would you ask them for advice on how to beat the people that just beat them? Never the less this is actually what a lot of people did after WW2, and the result were wild and sometimes almost comically wrong interpretations of history. Allow me to furnish you some quotes from US military historian and officer Colonel David M. Glantz Colonel David M. Glantz This German period of war historiography embraced two genre of works. The first included memoirs written during those years when it was both necessary and sensible to dissociate oneself from Hitler or Hitler's policies. Justifiable or not, the writers of these memoirs did just that and essentially laid blame on Hitler for most strategic, operational, and often tactical failures. Thus, an apologetic tone permeated these works. Officers who shared in the success of Hitler's armies refused to shoulder responsibility for the failures of the same armies. Glantz goes on to explain that notable German memoirs like those written by Guderian, Mannstein and Mellenthin, highlights German victories against Soviet forces in which they have no idea what those Soviet forces were like. For example Mellenthin, vividly depicts the German Panzer Corps heroic defeat of Soviet tanks from the 5th tank army trying to cross Chir around the 19th December. However, Mellenthin ‘forgets’ that while the 5th tank army, was occupying the German Panzer corps, the 1st Soviet Guards Tank Army, absolutely destroyed the 8th Italian army and Army Detachment Hollidt, despite having seen constant action for a month and being under strength, leading to the encirclement of Stalingrad. Mellenthin thus presents Germany’s tank reserve being tied up in an action that lead to a massive strategic defeat, as a heroic victory. None of the 3 German authors here mentioned actually used archival material in writing their stories of WW2, which later proved them wrong on numerous occasions. After WW2 the US historical division collected hundreds of memoirs from German veterans, and until the late 1980s were still used as an authoritative guide on what Russian fighting was like, despite not including a single piece of evidence from neither German nor Soviet archives. Here is a great quote from one of the memoirs used by the US historical division. It is surprising that during World War II the USSR did not attempt any large-scale airborne operations. . . . its wartime operations were confined to a commitment of small units.... for the purpose of supporting partisan activities and which had no direct tactical or strategic effect. - Major General Hellmuth Reinhardt DA Pamphlet No. 20-232, Airborne Operations (Department of the Army, October 1951) This of course is not true, during the battle of Rzhev the Soviets made extensive paradrops, though not as grand as those on D-day the Vyazma operation which actually succeeded stands out, and considering what we know of the extensive resources Germany used for anti parisan duty it is also one hell of a claim to say it had no effect. Colonel Glantz have a series of judgements which were caused by a reliance on German accounts which he mentioned often, and eventually led to a paper called “The Soviet-German War, 1941-1945: Myths and Realities”. That isn’t to say German sources aren’t useful, they just don’t teach you all that much about how the Russian fight, likewise you wouldn’t ask the Russians how the Germans fought.
